### Amendment 201 (M5 v201, three-runtime) — `enabled` gates query participation

_Numbering: 201 was free. The grant's commit (`8ebdd75`) ends "The ADR 0016 amendment record for this grant is
owed." This pays it._

- **The defect.** v200 added the write verb (`setComponentEnabled`) but `enabled` was still just a stored field
  that gated no behavior.
- **What landed.** `getEnabledComponents(entity)` returns only components where `enabled !== false`, so disabled
  components are stored but invisible to iteration. The method follows the host-gate pattern: optional on the
  runtime, exposed through the surface interface as `getEnabledComponents?(entity): Array<{type, enabled}>`.
  This gives `enabled` behavioral meaning without coupling to rendering or game logic — components are purely
  data records (health, shield, stamina) and the flag gates whether they participate in active queries.
- **Evidence.** Studio **406/406** (31 files; `scene3dSurface` 17 → **18**) · three-runtime 463/463 unchanged ·
  harness **62/62** unchanged · `scene-surface-proof.mjs` §7 exercises `getEnabledComponents` through the
  shipped dist runtime (a stamina disable/re-enable cycle). Measured 2026-10-08.
- **Bounds (§60).** The filter applies only to iteration — save/restore still carries all components regardless
  of enabled state; the HUD still reports all components (v199's read is unchanged); `data` payloads remain
  uneditable; there is no bulk enable/disable verb (each toggle is individual).

### Amendment 202 (M5 v202, three-runtime) — `enabled` gates material visibility via `targetObject`

_Numbering: 202 was free. The grant's commit (`35ac5a1`) ends "The ADR 0016 amendment record for this grant is
owed." This pays it._

- **The defect.** v201 made `enabled` gate query participation but left rendering untouched.
- **What landed.** `EntityComponent` gains an optional `targetObject?: THREE.Object3D` field. When a component
  has a `targetObject`, disabling it via `setComponentEnabled` sets `targetObject.visible = false`; re-enabling
  restores visibility. Components without a `targetObject` behave as before — the flag updates but nothing
  visual changes, so backward compatibility holds.
- **Evidence.** Studio **407/407** (31 files; `scene3dSurface` 18 → **19**) · three-runtime `tsc` clean · the
  proof was pending at commit time and verified through the shipped dist after the build. Measured 2026-10-08.
- **Bounds (§60).** Only components WITH a `targetObject` affect rendering; pure data components (health,
  stamina, shield without visual targets) remain invisible to the renderer regardless of `enabled`; the flag
  does not gate animation playback (that is v203), physics, or other non-visual behaviors.

### Amendment 203 (M5 v203, three-runtime) — `enabled` gates animation playback

_Numbering: 203 was free. The README section says the record is "owed". This pays it._

- **The defect.** v202 made `enabled` gate material visibility but left animations running.
- **What landed.** `EntityComponent` gains an optional `animationIds?: AnimationId[]` field. Disabling a
  component sets each referenced `AnimationAction.enabled = false` (which prevents updates while preserving
  current time); re-enabling sets `enabled = true` and calls `play()` to resume from where it stopped.
  Components without `animationIds` behave as before. A new `SerializedEntityComponent` type excludes both
  `targetObject` and `animationIds` from the file format, so these runtime-only THREE references cannot leak
  into saves; the snapshot writes only `{type, data, enabled}` and the shape gate asserts no THREE classes reach
  the serialized output.
- **Evidence.** three-runtime **467/467** (14 files; added `componentAnimationGate.test.ts` with 3 cases) ·
  Studio **407/407** unchanged · `tsc` clean · harness **62/62** unchanged (the animation gate is proven at the
  surface-suite and proof layers). Measured 2026-10-08.
- **Bounds (§60).** Only components WITH `animationIds` affect playback; the flag gates playback through the
  `enabled` property (NOT `stop()`, which would reset time); animations paused this way preserve their current
  time and resume from that point when re-enabled.

### Amendment 204 (M0/v204, repo-wide) — the type gate did not read TESTS in six of seven packages, and the one that did was RED: 249 errors were hiding, measured rather than guessed

_Numbering: 204 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` matched nothing). This is item 13 of the
priority queue in `docs/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`. It is not a milestone feature; it is a hole in the thing that
grades everything else._

- **The defect, in one sentence.** Every package's `typecheck` script ran the SAME tsconfig as its `build`, and
  that config needs `rootDir: "src"` so `dist/` mirrors `src/` — so `test/` was `exclude`d, which quietly
  removed **61 test files** from every type gate except `apps/studio`'s (its tests live in `src/`, so it was
  the only package whose gate read them).
- **And the one gate that DID read tests was red.** `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3dSurface.test.ts` had **6
  errors** — five call sites passing `surface.sceneId` (a `string`) where the runtime wants the branded
  `SceneId`, though the SAME file brands it with `toSceneId(...)` eleven other times, plus one dereference of a
  possibly-undefined array slot. Every intervening commit's message said "tsc clean". A gate is only worth the
  coverage it actually has.
- **The measurement, and why it took three attempts to trust.** Widening a package's `include` is not enough:
  `extends` inherits `exclude`, so the first attempt measured `0` everywhere; overriding `exclude` alone still
  measured `0`, because the `include` was `["src"]` and never named `test/`; and once tests were in the program,
  47 of the 48 errors were `TS6059` — the gate complaining about its own `rootDir`, not about code. Only
  widening **both** `include` and `rootDir` measures the code. The real total is **249 errors**:
  `three-runtime 102 · agents/runtime 80 · exec-host 27 · ai-providers 22 · world-engine 14 · design-model 4`.
  A number produced by a config that cannot see the files is not a measurement.
- **`three-runtime`'s count was reported as `1`, and that was the most misleading number of the lot.** Its first
  error is `TS1005: ';' expected` — a **parse** error, which aborts TypeScript's analysis of the rest of that
  file, so a single unparseable annotation hid 101 others. The annotation was
  `typeof live.entities[0][1].position`: `typeof` in a type position takes an entity NAME, and an indexed
  access is not one. `vitest` strips types instead of checking them, so it ran happily for as long as it has
  existed.
- **The design that closes it.** A dedicated `tsconfig.test.json` per package — `extends` the package's own
  config, `rootDir: "."`, `noEmit: true`, `include: ["src", "test"]`, `exclude: ["node_modules", "dist"]` —
  with `typecheck` pointed at it and `build` left alone. The build keeps the dist layout it needs; the gate
  gains the 61 files. Test type-checking is NOT a weaker gate here: it is the same `strict` +
  `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` the source gets, because a test's array index that CAN be undefined is a real
  hazard too.
- **Three defects the widened gate found, none of which a green suite could have.** (1) `worldEngine.test.ts`
  imported `createWorldId` and five siblings, then declared its OWN local
  `function createWorldId(id: string) { return id as any; }` — the locals shadowed the imports, so the library's
  constructors were **never exercised** and the imports were dead code. The library's versions are
  `id as WorldId` (the same behaviour, minus the `any`), so deleting the locals is behaviour-preserving and
  makes the imports live. (2) `instances.test.ts` read `.characters` off a `DesignNode` union without
  narrowing — `characters` belongs to `TextNode` alone. (3) **`InstanceNode['overrides']` cannot express a text
  override at all**: it is
  `Record<NexusId, Partial<Pick<NodeBase, …>>> & { text?: Record<NexusId, string> }`, so an object literal's
  `text` key must satisfy the index signature AS WELL as the named field, and `{ 'cmp::label': 'Clicked' }`
  cannot. `readOverrides` in `src/instances.ts` casts around it. The format ALSO lets a master child whose id is
  literally `text` be unreachable for geometry patches, because `readOverrides` skips that key. **Both are
  canonical-model decisions and are NOT fixed here** — the test carries the same cast with the reason written
  next to it, and the defect is filed as its own increment rather than smuggled into a gate repair.
- **Evidence.** `tsc -p <pkg>/tsconfig.test.json` returns **0** for `design-model`, `ai-providers` and
  `world-engine`, and their suites still pass — **32/32**, **20/20**, **43/43**. The studio gate is **0** with
  `tsc --noEmit -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json`, suite **407/407**. Still red and named in the plan:
  `three-runtime 102`, `agents/runtime 80`, `exec-host 27`.
- **Bounds (§60).** Three of six packages are closed; the other three still have their gates pointed at the old
  config, so **their tests remain unchecked** — the numbers above are what is still hiding, not what has been
  fixed. Nothing here makes a test stronger: it makes the gate able to SEE the tests it never read. The
  `agents/exec-host` count includes 4 files importing `SpawnLike` from `@nexus/agent-runtime`, which does not
  export it — whether that symbol should be exported or the imports corrected is a question for that
  increment, not this one.

### Amendment 205 (v205, agents/exec-host) — the type-gate coverage, package 4 of 6: 27 errors, including an assertion whose second half had never run

_Numbering: 205 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` matched nothing but 204). Item 14 of the
priority queue; the second increment of the v204 repair, one package at a time so the tree is never left worse
than it was found._

- **The mechanism, reused.** `agents/exec-host/tsconfig.test.json` (extends the package's own config,
  `rootDir: "."`, `noEmit: true`, `include: ["src", "test"]`, `exclude: ["node_modules", "dist"]`) with
  `typecheck` pointed at it. `build` is untouched, so `dist/` keeps its layout. Gate: **27 → 0**.
- **Four files imported a type from the wrong package.** `import type { SpawnLike } from '@nexus/agent-runtime'`
  — `SpawnLike` is declared and exported by **`@nexus/exec-host`** (`src/execHost.ts` → `src/index.ts`); the
  runtime package has never exported it. A type-only import ERASES at runtime, so the suites passed while four
  files typed their spawn mocks against a symbol that was not there. Fixed by importing it from
  `../src/execHost.js`, where the tests already get `ExecChild`. (`ExecPolicy` genuinely IS the runtime's and
  stayed put — the point is that the two were indistinguishable to a green suite.)
- **A silently weakened assertion.** `gitTools.test.ts` had
  `expect(env).toMatchObject(GIT_ISOLATION_ENV, forcedConfigEnv())`. **`toMatchObject` takes ONE argument**, so
  the second object was dropped and only the first half ever ran — an assertion that LOOKS like it checks two
  things and checks one. Split into two calls; both pass, so the fix strengthens the test without changing its
  verdict. The same shape appears twice in `execTestRunner.test.ts` as
  `expect(h.calls).toHaveLength(0, 'a message')` — there the second argument was a MESSAGE, so nothing was
  unverified, but the sentence the author wrote to explain a failure could never appear. Moved to
  `expect(h.calls, 'a message')`, which is where this runner takes a message.
- **A discriminated union read optimistically, twice.** `planExec` answers
  `{ ok: true; plan } | { ok: false; reason }`, and two tests wrote `expect(d.ok).toBe(false); expect(d.reason)…`
  — reading `reason` off the union. Unchecked, a decision that came back `ok` would have asserted against
  `undefined` and failed for the wrong reason. Both now narrow with `if (d.ok) throw new Error('expected a
  refusal, got a plan')`.
- **Evidence.** `tsc -p agents/exec-host/tsconfig.test.json` **0**; suite **309/309** in 10 files — including
  the assertion that had never run, which passes. Still open and named in the plan: `agents/runtime 80`,
  `three-runtime 102`.
- **Bounds (§60).** This closes exec-host's TESTS being unread, not the package's behaviour — no runtime code
  changed. `SpawnLike` is now imported from the package that owns it, which is a correction, not a new export:
  whether the RUNTIME should also export a spawn seam is a question nothing here answers.

_Records 206–212 below were written together, eight grants after their code, from the seven commits that carry
their numbers — a documentation increment with no code, the pattern amendment 82 set (`v156` wrote the records
three increments late). Every **suite total** quoted in them is the number measured on that grant's own landing
day, 2026-10-09, and belongs to that tree; every **line citation** was re-verified today on the tree these
records land in, so where a later grant inserted lines above a citation the record says what it was then and
what it is now. Writing them here rather than appending them at the end keeps the ledger's only ordering
guarantee — a reader who follows `amendment 208` arrives at 208._

### Amendment 206 (v206, three-runtime) — entity removal releases every component's effects: the second eviction door after v205

_Numbering: 206 is the number `398411b` names in its own message. Its record was owed and is written here from
that commit; the suite totals are its landing readings._

- **The gap v205 left standing.** v205 taught `removeComponent` to release one component's runtime-only effects
  (v202's hidden `targetObject`, v203's paused animations). Removing the whole ENTITY was a different door: the
  registry dropped the components with their host, and whatever those components had done to objects and
  animations outside the registry stayed done — a target hidden forever, animations paused forever, with no
  owner left to undo either.
- **What shipped.** `removeEntity` walks every component of the entity and releases each one's effects BEFORE
  the entity goes. At the time it was an inline copy of v205's logic; v208 converged the three copies into
  `cleanupComponentEffects`, so the walk this grant added is now `threeRuntime.ts:1520-1521` calling the shared
  statement, and `removeEntity` itself begins at 1511.
- **Evidence.** `test/entityRemovalComponentCleanup.test.ts` — 5 cases: one component's target restored ·
  several components cleaned in one removal · an animation resumed · an entity with no components succeeds with
  no side effects · a non-existent entity. three-runtime **477/477** (16 files), `tsc` clean. No Studio change:
  the surface does not call `removeEntity`, so the proof lives at the runtime layer.
- **Arms: none were scored, and the record says so rather than inventing a number.** This grant's evidence is 5
  new cases and a green suite — which is the weaker witness the arc kept having to name. The arm that should
  have been run is the one v208 ran on the same rule (delete the release call, expect exactly the behavioural
  cases to redden), and its absence is the reason this record does not claim a falsified mutation.
- **Bounds (§60).** Cleanup applies uniformly to ALL components on the entity; a missing scene skips the
  animation leg gracefully, as in v205; an entity without components succeeds with no side effects.

### Amendment 207 (v207, studio) — the report carries the disabled half: v204's filter had shut the only re-enable door, and this grant corrected a false measurement in this repository's own record

_Numbering: 207, named by `e0b0a86`. The commit message itself said "amendment 207 owed" — which is the phrase
this lane's §7 door is designed to refuse as a citation, and it was right to._

- **The defect was a product rule applied one layer too high.** v204 made `enabled` gate HUD visibility by
  filtering disabled components OUT of `entityComponentsOf` — and that function is the only thing the inspector
  iterates. A component the report never carries can never be rendered as a toggle, so the `(off)` button
  v199/v200 built became dead code and a disabled component could not be clicked back on from the panel at all.
  Hiding the state is not the same as hiding the control, and v204 had conflated them.
- **A measurement that corrected this ledger.** Measured on 2026-10-09 before any v207 change,
  `scene3dSurface.test.ts` stood at **4 failed | 15 passed (19)**: the v199 live-registry case, the v200 toggle
  case, the loose-reader case, the filed-name case. The v204 section had claimed "6 tests updated to reflect the
  new behavior… 401/407" — **no tests had been updated**, and the reds were 6 (those 4 plus two
  `entityComponentsOf` cases in `scene3d.test.ts`). The sentence described work that had not been done; v207
  struck it from the v204 section and put the measurement in its place.
- **What landed.** `entityComponentsOf` returns the FULL registry again — a loose reader reports what is stored,
  it does not editorialize. `SceneSelectionFacts` gains `disabledComponents: SceneSelectionComponent[]`
  (`apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts:434`), and `selectionFactsOf` SPLITS the registry: `components` keeps only
  `enabled !== false` rows — v204's product rule stands, the active list shows what the query layer iterates —
  and the disabled half is REPORTED rather than dropped, in registry order (`scene3d.ts:492`). `Scene3D.tsx`
  renders `[...components, ...disabledComponents]` as ONE row set (850 gates the block on the sum, 854 renders
  it), so every disabled row is a re-enable door through the same `onToggleComponentEnabled` host gate.
- **The hidden site the first red was masking.** `scene3dSurface.test.ts:326` still called the OLD 2-arg
  `removeComponent(entity, 'health')`. v205's bound "No Studio changes — the surface does not call
  `removeComponent`" was true of the surface and FALSE of its test: the line was unreachable because that case
  died at an earlier assertion, so it could not red until the reds above it were fixed. It was updated to the
  v205 signature — the same "a case runs only to its first failure" blindness this arc keeps hitting.
- **Evidence.** Studio **407/407** (31 files): the 6 v204 reds resolved by re-pointing them at the split (each
  now asserts BOTH halves) and not by deletion; the two whole-object `toEqual` inspector pins gained
  `disabledComponents: []`. `tsc --noEmit` exit 0, eslint exit 0 on the three edited files. No three-runtime
  change (its suite stood at 477/477 from v206).
- **Arms: none were scored.** The witness here is a false claim struck and six reds turned green by re-pointing;
  the split has no behavioural surface in this grant, and the record does not dress a report change up as a
  falsified mutation.
- **Bounds (§60).** Report-only: v201's query gate, v202's rendering gate and v203's playback gate do not move;
  `entityComponentsOf` stays loose, so garbage and undeclared hosts still answer `[]`, which lands in
  `components` and never in `disabledComponents`; the save shape is untouched; a registry where everything is
  disabled shows an empty active list and a full disabled half — every toggle on screen.

### Amendment 208 (v208, three-runtime) — the third eviction door: `addComponent`'s same-type replace, and the release rule becomes ONE statement

_Numbering: 208, named by `5df39e3` — whose message carried the "amendment 208 owed" phrase §7 later refused as a
citation (see `6272fd4`). The record is here now, which is the fix that door asked for._

- **The door nobody knocked on.** `addComponent(entity, comp)` filed under `comp.type` with a plain `Map.set` —
  so a same-type add SILENTLY REPLACED the old component. v205 had covered the explicit removal and v206 the
  entity removal; this third eviction path had no code in it at all, and the evicted component's effects
  stranded with no owner: its hidden target stayed hidden, its paused animations stayed paused.
- **One statement of the rule.** `cleanupComponentEffects(entityId, component)` (`threeRuntime.ts:1580`) —
  restore `targetObject.visible = true`, re-enable and `play()` each `animationIds` animation. The scene is
  found by asking the registry which scene holds the entity, because an entity carries no scene back-pointer and
  the replace-path caller knows only the entity. v205's and v206's inline copies now CALL it: 1521
  (`removeEntity`), 1627 (this grant's replace path), 1650 (`removeComponent`). The duplication v205/v206 left
  behind is gone, which is what makes the rule impossible to fix in one place and forget in two.
- **The identity exemption.** `if (previous && previous !== component)` (1627): re-adding the SAME object the
  registry already holds under that key is a no-op re-file, not an eviction. Without the exemption, cleaning the
  "evicted" component would undo the effects that very component declared.
- **Evidence.** `test/componentReplaceCleanup.test.ts` — 6 cases: evicted hidden target restored · evicted
  paused animation resumed · same-object re-add keeps its own state · the replacement really replaces (the
  registry answers the NEW object) · an evicted dangling `animationId` does not crash · a FIRST add performs no
  cleanup. three-runtime **483/483** (17 files; 477 → +6), Studio **407/407** against the rebuilt package — the
  10 v205/v206 cleanup cases stayed green across the refactor, which is the extraction's real test.
- **Arms, both predicted before running:** deleting the cleanup call went red on EXACTLY the 2 behavioural cases
  (2 failed | 4 passed); deleting only the identity exemption went red on EXACTLY the re-add case (1 failed |
  5 passed). Both restored, file re-ran 6/6.
- **The v198 dist-sync gate caught this grant mid-flight:** the first full run after the src edit was
  **1 failed | 482 passed**, `distSync.test.ts` naming `cleanupComponentEffects` as declared in src and absent
  from dist. Rebuilt, green. That is the third live demonstration that the gate is not decorative — a suite that
  reads `src` would have shipped a stale `dist`.
- **Bounds (§60).** `removeComponent` keeps its `sceneId` parameter (the public signature v205 shipped) while the
  helper resolves the scene from the registry itself; a FIRST add applies nothing — a component filed with
  `enabled: false` and a `targetObject` does NOT hide its target until the toggle moves — and that named door is
  what amendment 209 walked through. `restoreEntity` files freshly built components carrying no runtime-only
  fields (`threeRuntime.ts:1790`; the v208 section cited it as 1755, before 209's helper moved the line), so the
  replace path cannot strand through a load.

### Amendment 209 (v209, three-runtime) — a component filed DISABLED declares its gates at file time, and one case is the sole witness of the over-broad rule

_Numbering: 209, named by `901e91c`._

- **The gap was named by its own predecessor.** v208's bounds: "the add-time enforcement of v202/v203 semantics
  is a separate grant". Until now, filing a disabled component was a promise the runtime kept only after a later
  `setComponentEnabled` — between the add and any toggle, the target stayed shown and the animations kept
  running, contradicting what the registry said the component was.
- **What landed.** `enforceComponentDisabled(entityId, component)` (`threeRuntime.ts:1606`) is the disable-leg
  counterpart of `cleanupComponentEffects`: hide the `targetObject` (`visible = false`) and set
  `enabled = false` on each `animationIds` animation — the SAME one-way semantics as v203's disable leg (no
  `pause()` call), reached through the same registry walk.
- **The ordering is load-bearing, not incidental.** `addComponent` enforces it AFTER filing and AFTER the v208
  eviction cleanup (`threeRuntime.ts:1632`): a disabled replacement over the same target is restored by the
  eviction and then re-hidden by its own declaration, so the LAST writer is the component the registry actually
  holds. And the rule is narrow on purpose — only `enabled === false`. An ENABLED add declares the default state
  the effects already hold, so re-asserting it would trample state its owner set independently: a target the
  scene itself keeps hidden.
- **Evidence.** `test/componentAddEnforcement.test.ts` — 7 cases: a disabled add hides the target at file time
  (no toggle call anywhere in the case) · a disabled add disables the animation (`enabled` false AND
  `isRunning()` false) · an enabled add does NOT show a hidden target · an enabled add does not hide a shown
  target nor disable a running animation · a disabled replacement over the same target ends hidden and the
  registry answers the replacement's data · a dangling `animationId` does not throw · a disabled plain component
  stores and is excluded by `getEnabledComponents` (v201). three-runtime **490/490** (18 files; 483 → +7), dist
  rebuilt BEFORE the suite so the v198 gate judged the new declaration, Studio **407/407** against it.
- **Arms, and the finding worth keeping.** Deleting the enforcement call went red on EXACTLY the three
  disabled-add cases (hide-at-add, disable-at-add, replace-ordering — 3 failed | 18 passed across the four
  component-cleanup files; v203's, v205's and v208's suites stayed green untouched). Enforcing
  UNCONDITIONALLY (`component.enabled === false` → `if (component)`) went red on EXACTLY one case: the
  both-directions one. Every other fixture in the arc starts its targets and animations in the very state
  unconditional enforcement would write, so that single case is the SOLE WITNESS of the over-broad rule — it
  exists precisely to be that witness, which is why it survives as its own case instead of merging into the
  pair above it. Both arms restored; the shipped line re-verified before the suite (1624 then, 1632 now).
- **No Studio test moved, and that was measured rather than assumed:** a collision census over the tracked tree
  found every `enabled: false` add carries no `targetObject`/`animationIds`, so enforcement is a no-op by
  construction in those fixtures.
- **Bounds (§60).** `setComponentEnabled` keeps its own inline legs: the disable semantics now live in TWO
  carriers (the toggle's else-branch and this helper), deliberately NOT unified, because the toggle also owns
  the ENABLE leg, which has no add-time counterpart. `restoreEntity` files components that carry no runtime-only
  fields at all (v119's save shape excludes them), so a restored disabled component gates nothing until the save
  round-trip is given runtime re-attachment — a different grant, and the honest reason a load can still answer
  "disabled" while nothing is gated.

### Amendment 210 (v210, studio) — the registry gets a subscriber: the component family's three events stop announcing into an empty room

_Numbering: 210, named by `8630590`._

- **The claim the census supported.** `this.emit(` in `threeRuntime.ts` names `componentAdded`, `componentRemoved`
  and `componentStateChanged` — one per write verb (1625/1643/1699 as this record was written; 1633/1651/1707
  now, shifted by v211's eight lines above them). The Studio subscribed to NONE of them: before this grant every
  `addEventListener` call in `apps/studio/src` was on `window` (resize, keydown), and not one was on the
  runtime. The inspector was PULL-only — the report moved when a Studio control pulled it after its own write,
  and a registry changed by anything else (a console command, an agent holding the same runtime) stayed invisible
  until an unrelated event happened to re-read it. A stale inspector in a game editor is a lie about the scene.
- **What landed.** `SceneComposerLike` gains the runtime's own two verbs as OPTIONAL members
  (`addEventListener?`/`removeEventListener?`), the same host-honesty gate the arc uses everywhere: a fake
  without a listener registry is a legitimate host. `SceneSurface.watchComponents(listener): () => void`
  (`apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts:826`, implemented 995-1002) joins ONE listener to all three names and returns
  an idempotent unsubscribe that drops all three with the same identity — identity is load-bearing because the
  runtime's `removeEventListener` is `indexOf`-based. The listener is called with NO payload: the message is
  "re-read the report", so the watch never invents a second path from the registry to the panel and the report
  stays the runtime's single source. A host without the verbs answers a no-op unsubscribe instead of crashing.
  `Scene3D.tsx` subscribes `() => setReport(surface.report())` in its mount effect (271) and unsubscribes in the
  cleanup (305).
- **Evidence.** 3 new pure cases in `scene3d.test.ts` (no-verbs host answers a no-op unsubscribe · a verbs host is
  subscribed to exactly the three names with ONE shared listener and unsubscribed from all three with the same
  identity · an emitted `componentAdded` actually fires the listener) and 5 in `scene3dSurface.test.ts` on the
  REAL headless runtime (add fires it · removed and stateChanged call it too · the re-read report MOVES with a
  registry change made behind the surface's back, which is the user-visible claim · unsubscribe stops the calls
  and is idempotent · two watchers both hear and each unsubscribe drops only its own). Studio **415/415**
  (31 files; 407 → +8), Studio `tsc` exit 0; three-runtime **490/490** UNCHANGED, because this grant touches no
  runtime source.
- **Arms.** A1 dropping `componentStateChanged` from the list → red on EXACTLY the 2 cases that count the
  subscription set and the all-three sequence (2 failed | 99 passed). A2 neutering the unsubscribe (`return
  () => {}` after the subscriptions) → red on 3: the two predicted PLUS the two-watchers case the prediction had
  missed, because with no removal watcher A kept hearing after `unwatchA()` and the tally came back `{a: 2, b:
  2}` — the miss is recorded as a miss in the choosing, not a hole in the code. A3 deleting the verbs-presence
  guard → red on EXACTLY the no-verbs case, which then crashes on `runtime.addEventListener` being undefined
  (1 failed | 100 passed). All arms restored; the shipped body re-verified from disk before the suites, and the
  two watch files alone ran 101/101 after restoration.
- **Bounds (§60).** The watch covers the COMPONENT family only — the runtime's other ~55 names
  (`entityCreated`, `entityRemoved`, `sceneCreated`, save-file and cinematic reports, the frame tick) still had
  no Studio subscriber, so a body added by console did not move the panel. `setEntityName`/`setEntityVisible`
  (v197) emitted NOTHING at all, and closing that needed an emit added to the RUNTIME, not a subscription —
  amendment 211 did the emit, 212 the listener. The subscription lives in the mount effect with empty deps and
  reads the captured `surface`, matching the pull pattern of the rAF loop it joins. And one bound this grant
  should have named and did not: nothing in the suite read `Scene3D.tsx` for the wiring it had just shipped —
  the verb was tested, the component that installs it was not. amendment 212 found and closed that.

### Amendment 211 (v211, three-runtime) — the two silent entity verbs get voices, and the grant found a witness defect in its own tests

_Numbering: 211, named by `7e9aa30`._

- **What the census proved.** v210's bounds named the door. The component family announced its three write verbs;
  the two v197 entity verbs changed the registry and said nothing — every reader (the report, `pickAt`, the save)
  saw a new name only because it happened to re-read. `setEntityName` (`threeRuntime.ts:1470`) now emits
  `entityRenamed { sceneId, entityId, name }` at 1482 and `setEntityVisible` (1498) emits
  `entityVisibilityChanged { sceneId, entityId, visible }` at 1507 — AFTER the registry mutation, and for
  visibility AFTER both records move (`entity.visible` and `threeObject.visible`, the v197 two-record rule; the
  comment at 1506): the announcement may not arrive while the records disagree. A refusal emits nothing — news of
  a change that did not happen is a lie on the bus.
- **The headline finding is about the tests, not the code.** The first draft of the two ordering cases asserted
  INSIDE the listener. `emit()` try/CATCHES every listener and only logs the swallowed error, so the D2 arm
  (moving the emit BEFORE the mutation) ran the whole file GREEN — a listener-side `expect` is an assertion whose
  failure the runtime eats. Both cases now RECORD what the listener observed and assert OUTSIDE, and the same rule
  is written into the shipped comment at the rename emit site so the next listener-based witness does not repeat
  it. Re-running D2 after the fix reddened exactly the case it should.
- **Evidence.** `test/entityEvents.test.ts` — 8 cases: rename payload exact · rename ordering (the listener reads
  the REGISTRY at emit time, not the payload) · refused renames silent (blank, non-string, unknown entity,
  unknown scene) · visibility emits on both legs, hide and show · visibility ordering (both records already agree
  at emit time) · refused visibility changes silent (non-boolean `0` and `'true'`, unknown owners) · the two names
  do not cross · `removeEventListener` silences the verb. three-runtime **498/498** (19 files; 490 → +8), dist
  rebuilt BEFORE the suite so the v198 gate judged the shipped package, build exit 0; Studio **415/415** against
  the rebuilt package, unchanged — v210's watch still counts exactly its three names, untouched by the two new
  emissions.
- **Arms.** D1a deleting the rename emission → red on EXACTLY the 4 cases that hear it (payload, ordering,
  no-cross, removeEventListener; 4 failed | 4 passed). D1b deleting the visibility emission → EXACTLY its 3
  (both-legs, ordering, no-cross; 3 failed | 5 passed). D2 rename emit moved before `entity.name = name` → EXACTLY
  the ordering case (`['Test Entity']` where the registry should already say `Villain`) — after the witness fix;
  before it, falsely green. D2b visibility emit moved before both record writes → EXACTLY its ordering case
  (`[[true, true]]` at emit time). D3 hoisting the rename emit above every guard, announcing refusals too, was
  predicted to redden only the silent-refusals case and reddened FIVE: with the guard-position emit kept, the
  success path emits TWICE, so payload, ordering, no-cross and removeEventListener joined it. The extra reds are
  legitimate captures of a strictly larger mutation than the one predicted — the miss was in choosing the arm, not
  in the code. All arms restored; the shipped emissions re-verified from disk at 1482/1507 before the suites.
- **Bounds (§60).** The payloads carry the SCENE the verb was asked about, same shape as the component family's.
  The Studio side did not yet SUBSCRIBE to these two names — v210's list was still exactly three, and joining the
  pair was a separate grant (amendment 212). `setLightState` and `removeEntity` already emitted; the remaining
  silent registry verbs were censused from the same `this.emit(` walk.

### Amendment 212 (v212, studio) — the surface watches the entity pair, and the component's wiring gets its first reader

_Numbering: 212, named by `f81aa4e`. It is the newest grant of the seven; the §7 door requires a record TITLE for
the newest, and the headings above exist so that door has something to read._

- **Why the emit alone was not enough.** v211's bounds: "the Studio side does not yet SUBSCRIBE to the two entity
  names." So the runtime could announce a rename made by anyone — console, agent, another panel — and the Studio
  would keep showing the replaced name until something else happened to re-read. News on a bus with no listener
  is the same silence.
- **What landed.** `SceneSurface.watchEntities(listener): () => void` (declared
  `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts:833`, implemented 1005-1012): one listener joined to exactly `entityRenamed`
  and `entityVisibilityChanged`, an idempotent unsubscribe that drops both, and the same host-honest guard as its
  sibling. `Scene3D.tsx` subscribes BOTH legs in the mount effect (271 components, 274 entities), each with the
  same pull the rAF loop uses, and leaves both in the cleanup (305, 306).
- **A deliberate design choice, recorded because it changes what the witnesses may claim.** This is a SEPARATE
  verb, not a fifth name inside `watchComponents`: v210's witnesses pin that subscription to EXACTLY three names,
  and widening it there would have made those pins lie about a promise they no longer describe. Arm A4 tests the
  REFUSED shape instead of merely asserting that it was refused.
- **Evidence (10 new cases).** `scene3d.test.ts` 77 → 81: no-verbs host answers a no-op unsubscribe · the joined
  set is exactly the two names with ONE shared listener (identity, because the runtime unsubscribes by `indexOf`)
  · the two legs join DISJOINT name sets · an `entityVisibilityChanged` fires the entity watcher and no component
  watcher. `scene3dSurface.test.ts` 24 → 29, against the shipped package with every write going through the
  RUNTIME and none through the surface: a rename re-reads to `Villain` at emit time (v211's ordering rule, now
  consumed from the SUBSCRIBER side) · a hide then a show re-reads `visible` false→true · component events do not
  move the entity watcher and vice versa · a refused write (blank name, non-boolean `'true'`, unknown entity)
  calls the watcher ZERO times and the case then lands a REAL rename to prove the silence was the refusal's and
  not a dead watch's · the unsubscribe drops the leg.
- **The wiring got its first reader.** Grepping the suite found that NOTHING read `Scene3D.tsx` for the watch —
  v210's subscription shipped with no test of the component that installs it, only of the verb (the hole its own
  bounds should have named). `surface.test.ts`, which already grades this component's wiring from source, gained
  one case (15 → 16): the joined names in mount order must be exactly `['watchComponents','watchEntities']`, the
  leaves exactly `['unwatchComponents','unwatchEntities']`, and the count of `=> setReport(surface.report())`
  pulls must EQUAL the count of joined legs — DERIVED from the file rather than hand-typed, so a leg subscribed
  by some other expression is the red rather than a number to widen.
- **Arms.** A1 `entityVisibilityChanged` dropped from the watched set: predicted 5 reds, got 5, names identical
  (both DISJOINT pins, the pure emit case, the surface hide-legs case, the surface news-crossing case). A2 the
  host-honest guard deleted: predicted 1, got 1 (the no-verbs case). A3 a per-event wrapper instead of one shared
  listener: predicted 2, got 2 — the identity pin and the unsubscribe case, exactly the failure mode a wrapper
  creates, since `indexOf` never finds a fresh arrow and an "unsubscribed" watcher keeps firing. A4 the REFUSED
  design, `watchEntities` joined to all five names: first predicted 3, re-predicted 4 before the run because the
  exact-set case counts the joined names too; got 4. A5 `unwatchEntities()` deleted from the cleanup: predicted
  1, got 1 — the new source pin, the suite's only reader of the wiring, and A5 is what proves that pin is not
  decorative. 13 reds across 5 arms, 13 attributed, 0 unexplained; every arm restored byte-identical and
  re-verified before the suites.
- **Measured** on 2026-10-09: Studio `tsc` exit 0, Studio suite **425/425** (31 files; 415 → +10). No
  three-runtime source was touched, so no rebuild was needed and its suite re-ran at **498/498** (19 files)
  against the package v211 shipped.
- **Bounds (§60).** The source pin grades TEXT, not behaviour: it cannot see that the subscription lives in the
  mount effect with empty deps, and an `unwatchEntities()` placed anywhere in the file satisfies it — closing
  that needs a React render harness, not a stronger regex. `entityCreated`/`entityRemoved` still have no
  subscriber (a body added by console does not move the panel), and the component `data` bag is still unread by
  the inspector.

### Amendment 213 (v213, agents/runtime) — the type-gate coverage, package 5 of 6: 48 errors, and a mock that satisfied its interface in six of eight suites

_Numbering: 213 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 205). Item 15 of the priority
queue; the third increment of the v204 repair, one package at a time so the tree is never left worse than it was
found. Gate: **48 → 0**, suite **540/540** in 36 files._

- **The dominant defect was ONE root cause with ~24 call sites.** `FsWriteLike` extends `FsLike`, which requires
  `readdirSync` and `statSync` — and **six of the eight suites that define their own `MemDisk` mock had
  neither.** Nothing on those paths reads a directory or stats a file, so every suite stayed green while the
  mock was incomplete against the interface it is passed to. (The eight mocks have also drifted APART: two
  implement the methods, with different behaviour — `memory.test.ts` answers an empty listing, `pipeline.test.ts`
  answers a real one. Same name, different disk.)
- **The completion THROWS rather than answering an empty listing.** A mock that reports "no entries" for a disk
  that has entries is exactly the kind of lie a future test would pass against; throwing means the first test
  that needs the capability fails loudly and says why. (This half landed ahead of the gate, as `715a312`.)
- **`toEqual` takes ONE argument, four more times.** `expect(h.actions).toEqual([...], 'the read ran BEFORE the
  write it informs')` — the sentence the author wrote to explain a failure could never appear. Moved to
  `expect(h.actions, '…')`, which is where this runner takes a message. The same shape was found twice in
  exec-host (amendment 205), so it is a habit rather than a one-off.
- **`PlannerOptions.hasVerify` is REQUIRED, and three cases expressed "no verify tier" by OMITTING it.** The
  planner reads it as a truthy check, so absent behaved as false and the tests passed — but "the host did not
  say" and "the host said no" are different statements, and the field is required precisely because the host is
  supposed to say. The cases now pass `hasVerify: false`, which is what they always meant.
- **Two unions read optimistically, and one optional field depended on without saying so.** `chain.test.ts` did
  `expect(arc.arc).toEqual(res.release)` where `ChainResult` is a union and `release` is OPTIONAL even on the
  green branch; `pipeline.test.ts` read `res.editorOutcome` off `PipelineResult` the same way. Both now narrow
  with `if (!res.ok) throw …`, and the chain additionally asserts `res.release` is defined — the durable walk
  was asked for, so its presence is a claim the test should make.
- **`TestRunner.run` is declared `TestReport | Promise<TestReport>`; one test read `.ok` off the union.** It is
  sync in that implementation, so it passed — but the declaration allows a promise, and a promise's `.ok` is
  `undefined`. The test now awaits, which is true either way.
- **Two smaller ones.** A `res.output` cast omitted `report.detail` while the very next line read it; and the UI
  fixture's `PAGE` was an untyped literal, so `PAGE[i].label` was both an implicit-any and a
  possibly-undefined access, and `{ kind: string; label: string }[]` was not `UiElement[]`.
- **Evidence.** `tsc -p agents/runtime/tsconfig.test.json` **0**; `vitest run --root agents/runtime` **540/540**
  in 36 files. Still open and named in the plan: `three-runtime 118`.
- **Bounds (§60).** No runtime source changed — this closes the package's TESTS being unread. The `MemDisk`
  duplication (eight copies, two behaviours) is now VISIBLE and still there: consolidating them into one helper
  is a real piece of work, and doing it inside a gate repair would have changed what several suites mean.

### Amendment 214 (v214, three-runtime) — the type-gate coverage, package 6 of 6: 118 errors, and the repair's own total is now closed at 249

_Numbering: 214 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 213). Item 16 of the priority
queue, and the LAST package: with it, every package in the monorepo type-checks its own tests. Gate:
**118 → 0**, suite **498/498** in 19 files._

- **The count had GROWN, and that is worth stating.** v204 measured this package at 102; by v214 it was **118**,
  because the M5 line's v206–v212 added tests to it. A number measured once and quoted later is a number about
  a tree that no longer exists.
- **Three root causes dominated 118 errors.** (1) `ThreeRuntimeConfig` REQUIRES `maxLights` and `frustumCulling`
  and **nothing in the package reads either** — they are declared, defaulted in the package's own
  `DEFAULT_THREE_CONFIG` (`maxLights: 100`, `frustumCulling: true`) and consulted nowhere — so six fixtures
  omitted them and every caller is forced to state a value the runtime ignores. They were added at the
  package's own defaults, so behaviour is unchanged; the fields themselves are filed as their own item, because
  wiring them or making them optional is a runtime decision, not a test repair. (2) `shadowMap.type` is
  `THREE.ShadowMapType` and `toneMapping` is `THREE.ToneMapping`; the fixtures wrote raw `0`s (`BasicShadowMap`
  and `NoToneMapping` are both 0, so the named constants are the same values). (3) Event listeners have no
  contextual parameter type, so ~20 handlers were implicitly `any`; they are annotated — `unknown` where the
  body casts, and the array's own element type where it does not.
- **`SaveStore` grew two members and two mocks did not.** `savePathRefusal` (v169) and `rename` (v186) were
  added to the interface and the two deliberately-partial mocks in `saveSnapshot.test.ts` were never updated,
  because no gate read the file. Both are completed with stubs that THROW — nothing on those paths calls either,
  and a stub that answered would be inventing behaviour the case does not exercise. This is the THIRD instance
  of the same shape (the `MemDisk` mocks, amendment 213; the `FsLike` mocks before them), which is what an
  unread test corpus looks like from the inside.
- **A gate that audits the package's export face had never been type-checked.** `packageFace.test.ts` reads the
  barrel's own bytes and checks that every module's declared names appear on the face; eight of its errors were
  in its own scanning helpers (`m[1]`, `clause[1]`, `bits[0]`, `clause[2]` — all possibly undefined under
  `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`). A gate that grades others and is graded by nobody is the exact shape this whole
  repair exists to remove.
- **The repair's total, closed.** v204 measured **249** errors across six packages and the seven increments that
  followed fixed them all: design-model 4 · ai-providers 22 · world-engine 14 · exec-host 27 · agents/runtime 48
  · three-runtime 118 (the last three as v205/v213/v214). Every one of the six `typecheck` scripts now runs a
  `tsconfig.test.json` that includes `test/`, and `build` still emits the dist layout it needs.
- **Evidence.** `tsc -p <pkg>/tsconfig.test.json` returns **0** for all six packages; suites re-run at
  **32/32 · 20/20 · 43/43 · 498/498 · 540/540 · 309/309**. The studio's own gate was already 0 with **407/407**.
- **Bounds (§60).** No runtime source changed in any of the seven increments — this closes TESTS being unread,
  not behaviour. What it found is now VISIBLE and filed rather than silently absorbed: the eight drifted
  `MemDisk` mocks (item 19), the two required-and-unread config fields, and `InstanceNode['overrides']`
  (item 17). And it found no shortage of the thing it was built for: a mock missing two methods in six of eight
  suites, an assertion whose second half had never run, four messages passed to a one-argument matcher, a test
  importing a type from a package that does not export it, and an annotation TypeScript cannot parse.

### Amendment 215 (v215, repo hygiene) — `.scratch/` was not ignored, and it holds 879 copies of real test files

_Numbering: 215 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 214). Not a milestone feature:
this closes the mechanism behind an incident already in this ledger._

- **What `.scratch/` is.** The proof runs in this repo materialise a ref — a WHOLE COPY of the tree — to grade
  it, and ad-hoc probes are written there. Measured 2026-10-09: **879 `*.test.ts` files** live under the four
  `.scratch/` directories (`.scratch/`, `agents/exec-host/.scratch/`, `apps/studio/.scratch/`,
  `packages/three-runtime/.scratch/`), and every one is a STALE COPY of a real suite. None of them is tracked.
- **The two failures it was already causing.** (1) A root-level `vitest` run would glob those 879 files and
  grade last week's code while reporting it as this tree's result — which is why a root `vitest.config.ts`
  existed, UNTRACKED, excluding them. A guard against a real hazard that is not in git is a guard that a fresh
  clone does not have. (2) A `git add -A` swept an in-flight doc edit into an unrelated commit: that is exactly
  how **amendment 196's record landed inside an M5 commit** (`8ebdd75`) and spent a while describing an artifact
  page the tree did not have.
- **The fix, both halves.** `.scratch/` is added to `.gitignore` (one pattern covers all four directories, since
  it matches at any level), and the root `vitest.config.ts` is COMMITTED with the reason written in it rather
  than left as an orphan file. Per-package runs are unaffected — `turbo run test` and
  `vitest run --root <pkg>` resolve their own root, and `apps/studio` keeps its own config for the source-alias
  reason recorded at v142.
- **Evidence.** `git check-ignore -v .scratch/ agents/exec-host/.scratch/` both answer `.gitignore:53:.scratch/`;
  `git status --short` no longer lists four scratch trees as untracked.
- **Bounds (§60).** This stops scratch files REACHING a commit; it does not clean up what is already on disk
  (879 stale files stay, and deleting them would destroy the materialised refs some proofs reuse). It also does
  not make the `.scratch/` convention itself any good — a proof that writes into the working tree is a proof
  that can leak into it, and the scene-surface proof has already been caught leaking temp dirs twice.

### Amendment 216 (v216, studio) — the surface watches the body pair, and the watched name set is decided by an emit census rather than by the family's size

_Numbering: 216 was free. This ledger's own headings topped out at 215, and `### Amendment 216` matched 0
lines before this write — both read from the file's bytes, not from a shell grep. Amendments 213, 214 and 215
belong to the type-gate and repo-hygiene lane and are untouched here._ This is the third leg of the watch seam
v210 opened and v212 widened, and it closes the gap v212's Bounds named.

- **Why the emit alone was not enough.** v212's bounds: "`entityCreated`/`entityRemoved` still have no
  subscriber (a body added by console does not move the panel)". The runtime has announced both names ever
  since the bus existed and nothing above it listened, so a console command or an agent writing through the
  runtime could add a body to, or take one out of, the scene the Studio is reporting while the roster kept
  naming the scene as it was at mount time. News on a bus with no listener is the same silence.
- **What landed.** `SceneSurface.watchBodies(listener): () => void` (declared
  `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts:847`, census comment 834-846, implemented 1030-1037): one listener joined to
  exactly `entityCreated` and `entityRemoved`, an idempotent unsubscribe that drops both, and the same
  host-honest guard as its two siblings — a host without `addEventListener`/`removeEventListener` answers a
  no-op unsubscribe instead of crashing. `Scene3D.tsx` subscribes all THREE legs in its mount effect (271
  components, 274 entities, 278 bodies), each with the same pull the rAF loop uses, and leaves all three in the
  cleanup (309, 310, 311). No three-runtime source changed, so the package this runs against is still the one
  v211 shipped.
- **The census, not the family, chose the names** — recorded because the obvious drafting was wrong. The
  natural set was `['entityCreated','entityRemoved','entityRestored']`, three names for "the body family".
  `createEntity` (threeRuntime.ts:1290) and `restoreEntity` (1759) both build their body through the same
  private `insertEntity` (1319), which emits `entityCreated` UNCONDITIONALLY (1387) before `restoreEntity`
  emits `entityRestored` (1799). So no input makes a restore news a body without the pair already newing it,
  and the third name would buy a subscription and no information. Watching it anyway is not conservatism — it
  is a claim that a restore can go unheard. The REFUSED shape is measured (A4), and the census's positive half
  is measured as behaviour too: a real snapshot→remove→restore cycle moves the leg exactly once.
- **`activeSceneChanged` (1286) is deliberately not in this leg.** It can move `report.scene`, but it changes
  WHICH scene is reported rather than what is in it — a different fact, therefore a different leg. Named here
  and in Bounds so the next cycle inherits a gap rather than a mystery.
- **Evidence (12 new cases).** `scene3d.test.ts` 81 → 86 against a local bus: no-verbs host answers a no-op
  unsubscribe · the joined set is exactly the two names with ONE shared listener (identity, because the runtime
  unsubscribes by `indexOf`) · the THREE legs join pairwise DISJOINT name sets and no name is joined twice ·
  each body name fires the body leg · and `entityRestored` is pinned as NOT a watched name — 0 fires, then a
  real `entityCreated` fires 1, so the silence is the name set's and not a dead watch's.
  `scene3dSurface.test.ts` 29 → 36 against the shipped package, every write going through the RUNTIME and none
  through the surface: an add re-reads `before+1` with the new name in `entityNames` · a removal re-reads
  `before-1` · removing the SELECTED body answers `inspector: null` while `selected` still names it, which is
  v197's two-record rule consumed from the SUBSCRIBER side · a restore moves the leg exactly once · a refused
  removal (unknown body, unknown scene — `removeEntity` returns false at 1513/1516, before any emit) calls the
  watcher ZERO times and the case then lands a real removal to prove the silence was the refusal's · body news
  moves the body leg alone and `setEntityName` is not body news · the unsubscribe drops the body leg only and a
  double unwatch does not throw.
- **The wiring pin moved from a pair to a triple.** `surface.test.ts`'s component case (count unchanged at 16,
  6 lines replaced): joined names in mount order exactly `['watchComponents','watchEntities','watchBodies']`,
  leaves exactly `['unwatchComponents','unwatchEntities','unwatchBodies']`, and the count of
  `=> setReport(surface.report())` pulls must EQUAL the count of joined legs — DERIVED from the file, so it
  rose to 3 by itself and a leg subscribed some other way is the red rather than a number to widen. v212 made
  this the suite's only reader of the wiring; v216 is the first increment to test it as a three-leg claim.
- **Arms.** A0 control: 0 reds over the 138 cases these three files collect. A1 `entityRemoved` dropped from
  the pair: predicted 5, got 6 — the extra was the pure cross-leg case, whose second emit IS an
  `entityRemoved`, so dropping the name silences its second half too; re-predicted 6 from the mechanism and the

  component `data` bag is still unread by the inspector: v199 counts names, v212 and v216 read none of their
  values.

### Amendment 217 (v217, studio) — the surface watches the scene pair, and the same write census that cut v216's name set down says BOTH scene names carry

_Numbering: 217 was free. This ledger's own headings topped out at 216, and `### Amendment 217` matched 0 lines
before this write — both read from the file's bytes, not from a shell grep. Amendments 213, 214 and 215 belong to
the type-gate and repo-hygiene lane and are untouched here._ This is the fourth and last family of the watch seam
v210 opened and v212 and v216 widened, and it closes the gap v216's Bounds left standing.

- **Why the emit alone was not enough.** v216's bounds, verbatim: "`activeSceneChanged` still has no subscriber,
  so an out-of-band scene switch does not move the panel." The runtime has announced both scene names since the bus

  census comment 848-863, implemented 1058-1065): one listener joined to exactly `sceneCreated` and
  `activeSceneChanged`, an idempotent unsubscribe that drops both, and the same host-honest guard as its three
  siblings — a host without `addEventListener`/`removeEventListener` answers a no-op unsubscribe instead of
  crashing. `Scene3D.tsx` subscribes all FOUR legs in its mount effect (271 components, 274 entities, 278 bodies,
  283 scenes), each with the same pull the rAF loop uses, and leaves all four in the cleanup (314, 315, 316, 317). No
  three-runtime source changed, so the package this runs against is still the one v211 shipped.
- **The census REVERSES, which is why this record exists.** The rule since v210 is: watch a name only if some input
  moves a reported field AND only that name announces it. Applied to v216's family it deleted a name; applied to
  this one it keeps both, and the two verdicts come from the same arithmetic, not from a preference for more
  subscriptions.

    when the graph was empty, `activeSceneId` too (1240-1241); `setActiveScene` writes `activeSceneId` alone (1285).
    No verb deletes a scene, so `report.scenes` only ever grows.
  - The names move DIFFERENT fields. A second `createScene` moves `scenes` alone; a switch moves
    `activeSceneId`/`scene` alone. The surface witnesses assert that split rather than "something changed": the add
    case pins `activeSceneId` and the scene name unchanged while `scenes` moves, and the switch case pins `scenes`
    unchanged while the name and roster move.
  - `sceneCreated` is NOT subsumed by the switch name — the exact inverse of v216's `entityRestored`. The FIRST
    scene on an empty graph activates from inside `createScene` and emits no `activeSceneChanged`, so a switch-only
    leg would leave the panel naming no scene after one appeared. The runtime-level case measures that on the
    shipped package: `activeSceneId` moves from `null` to the new scene's id while the two raw listeners record
    exactly `['created']` — and then, for a real later switch, `['changed']`, so the first half is not "the runtime
    never emits that name". A pair drafted by analogy with v216 would have been wrong in the direction that
    silently mis-reports a user-visible panel.

  `disposed` (4232). It is not in this leg because `Scene3D.tsx` calls `runtime.dispose()` from the same cleanup
  that unwatches (320), so a `disposed` leg would re-read a report off a graph being torn down — a pull into a dead
  panel, for news no live panel can show. The pure case pins the emit as silent and then lands a real
  `activeSceneChanged` to prove the silence was the name's; the surface case proves the leg was ALIVE before
  `dispose()` and quiet through it. The absence is a decision, named where a reader would look for it.
- **Evidence (13 new cases).** `scene3d.test.ts` 86 → 91 against a local bus: no-verbs host answers a no-op
  unsubscribe · the joined set is exactly the two names with ONE shared listener (identity, because the runtime
  unsubscribes by `indexOf`) and both leaves · ALL FOUR legs join pairwise DISJOINT name sets, 9 joins and 9

### Amendment 218 (M5 v218, three-runtime + studio) — `setPixelRatio` wrote a REPORTED field in silence: the fifth watch leg, and the verb behind it

_Numbering: 218 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 217). Full narrative in the
commit; this is the ledger entry._

- **The defect.** `ThreeRuntime.resize` has announced itself on the event bus since always and `initialize`
  announces the backend it builds — but `setPixelRatio` wrote `backend.state.pixelRatio`, which is exactly the
  `pixels.pixelRatio` the Studio surface REPORTS, and **no name on the bus carried the news**. An out-of-band
  ratio change (a console command, an agent, another component) therefore left the panel showing a pixel figure
  that was no longer in force. The verb now emits AFTER the backend has taken the value, and a call with no
  backend — which can change no state — announces nothing rather than announcing a write that did not happen.
- **The fifth watch leg, by the same write census as its four siblings.** `SceneSurface.watchPixels` joins one
  listener to exactly `initialized`, `resize` and `pixelRatioChanged` — the three writes that move
  `report.backend` or `report.pixels`, the two fields no earlier leg reads. Same host-honest guard, idempotent
  unsubscribe and payload-free contract as `watchComponents`/`watchEntities`/`watchBodies`/`watchScenes`.
- **Two refusals, stated rather than omitted.** `disposed` stays refused for v217's reason (this effect's own
  teardown calls `runtime.dispose()`). `started`/`stopped`/`frame` are refused for a NEW one: no field of the
  report keys off whether the loop is running, and `frames`/`draws` already refresh from the loop's own pull,
  throttled by design — watching the frame bus would be a rendering-cadence change dressed as a correctness fix.
- **The widened structural pin.** v216's four-leg case cannot see a name only a fifth leg adds, so the
  pairwise-disjointness pin moves **9 joins → 12 joins, 12 distinct names**, and each later family's names are
  asserted absent from every earlier leg's slice. That pin is what reddens if a name is joined twice or a family
  starts sharing news with another.
- **Evidence.** 7 new cases in `packages/three-runtime/test/pixelRatioEvent.test.ts` (emit exactly once with the
  ratio asked for · the listener reads the NEW ratio from the backend at emit time · a call before `initialize()`
  is silent · a throwing listener cannot un-apply the write · the bus reports ASKS not deltas · the two pixels
  names do not cross · `removeEventListener` silences it), plus 13 studio cases. three-runtime **498 → 505**
  (20 files), studio **450 → 463** (31 files), both `tsc` **0**.
- **Mutation probe, 3 arms, 3/3 MATCHED** (async spawn — `execFileSync` answers EBUSY on this host, ADR 0016
  amendment 152): **A1** the emit removed → five cases red, `expected [] to deeply equal [ { ratio: 2 } ]` and
  siblings, the "exactly once" case among them · **A2** the no-backend guard removed → the "BEFORE initialize()
  is SILENT" case red · **A3** the emit moved BEFORE the backend takes the value → the ordering case red with
  `expected [ 1 ] to deeply equal [ 1.5 ]`, i.e. **the listener read the OLD ratio**, which is precisely the
  claim that case makes. Every mutated file restored byte-identical; the suite is green afterwards.
- **Two probe defects found in the probe itself, both already in this ledger.** (1) `execFileSync` answered
  **EBUSY** on the first attempt — the synchronous spawn family is unusable here, exactly as amendment 152
  measured, so the probe runs on async `spawn`. (2) Arm A2's anchor was a bare `if (!this.backend) return;`,
  and `String.replace` hits the FIRST occurrence — it mutated a different method and reported NO RED for a
  mutation that never landed on the verb it named. Anchors now carry the line that follows them.
- **Bounds (§60).** The verb reports ASKS, not deltas: setting the ratio it already holds still announces and
  still writes, and a subscriber therefore re-reads once per call. A dedup would be a different claim. The leg
  has no payload by design — a listener re-reads `surface.report()`; carrying the ratio would be a second
  source of truth for a number the report already owns. And `Scene3D`'s own `onResize` now re-reads twice (its
  own pull plus the bus it just joined), which is a redundant render, not a wrong value.

### Amendment 219 (M5 v204, studio) — the component registry gates HUD visibility — the record this grant was owed, and the number collision that delayed it

_Numbering: this grant's commit (`f02dac8`) CITES "ADR 0016 amendment 204", and 204 is a DIFFERENT record — the
type-gate repair (`d56d0bd`, "the type gate did not read TESTS in six of seven packages"). Two lines picked the
same number independently. Renumbering the type-gate amendment would break its own many citations, so this
record takes the next free number and STATES the collision: a reader who follows `f02dac8`'s citation lands on
the type-gate record, and this heading is where the increment it actually describes is written down. `f02dac8`'s
own message ends "The ADR 0016 amendment record for this grant is owed", so the debt was known._

- **What landed.** v203 made `enabled` gate animation playback but left a disabled component visible in the
  inspector. `setComponentEnabled` now also filters the component out of `entityComponentsOf()`'s result, so it
  disappears from the HUD's inspector panel. The flag thereby gates four things: query participation (v201),
  rendering via `targetObject` (v202), animation playback (v203), and inspector visibility (v204) — the same
  rule the runtime already applies in `getEnabledComponents`, so the HUD shows what the query layer sees.
- **The grant shipped with SIX RED TESTS, and that is recorded rather than smoothed over.** `f02dac8`'s own
  measurement is *"Studio suite 401/407 (6 intentional behavior-change reds proving the filter works)"*. A suite
  committed red is a suite whose red cannot be told from a regression, and the next increment paid for it:
  **amendment 207** exists because "v204's filter had shut the only re-enable door" — a disabled component had
  become invisible AND un-re-enableable, which is a functional regression, not a test that needed updating.
- **Bounds (§60).** A disabled component is still STORED in the registry and can be re-enabled (once v207
  restored the door); the filter applies to the reported/displayed projection, not to the underlying data. The
  save shape stays clean: `SerializedEntityComponent` excludes both `targetObject` and `animationIds` from the
  file format, so neither runtime-only field reaches a save.

### Amendment 220 (M5 v205, three-runtime) — component removal releases the evicted component's behavioral effects — the same owed record and the same collision

_Numbering: `5d68198` cites "ADR 0016 amendment 205", which is exec-host's share of the type-gate repair
(`877cd67`). Same collision as amendment 219, same resolution: the next free number, with the collision stated._

- **What landed.** v204's gate made `enabled` control visibility, but REMOVING a component entirely left its side
  effects in place forever: a `targetObject` stayed hidden with nothing left to re-enable it, and every
  `animationIds` entry stayed paused with no way back. `removeComponent` now releases both before deleting:
  `targetObject.visible = true`, and each animation's `enabled = true` with `play()` called to resume.
- **A signature change, for a stated reason.** `removeComponent(entity, componentType)` became
  `removeComponent(sceneId, entity, componentType)`, because releasing an animation requires the scene's own
  animation registry. The one existing caller in `threeRuntime.test.ts` was updated to match.
- **Evidence.** `componentRemovalCleanup.test.ts` — 5 cases (targetObject cleanup · animation cleanup · plain
  data components · a non-existent component · non-existent animationIds); measured **three-runtime 472/472** in
  15 files, `tsc` clean, no Studio change because the surface does not call `removeComponent` — the cleanup is
  proven at the runtime layer.
- **Bounds (§60).** This is the FIRST of three eviction doors; the other two are amendments 206 (entity removal)
  and 208 (`addComponent`'s same-type replace), which is why 208's heading calls itself "the third eviction
  door". The release rule is per-door and each door has its own case, rather than one shared path assumed to
  cover all three.

### Amendment 221 (M5 v221, three-runtime) — two config fields nothing read: one is now APPLIED, the other is honestly OPTIONAL

_Numbering: 221 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 220). Closes plan item 20, which
v214 filed when the widened type gate forced six fixtures to state both fields._

- **The defect.** `ThreeRuntimeConfig` REQUIRED `maxLights` and `frustumCulling`, and **neither name appeared
  anywhere in `packages/`, `apps/` or `agents/` outside `types.ts`** — declared, defaulted in
  `DEFAULT_THREE_CONFIG`, consulted nowhere. Every caller therefore had to state two values that changed
  nothing, and the type read like a promise the runtime never kept.
- **`frustumCulling` is now APPLIED, at the one funnel.** `threeObject.frustumCulled = this.config.frustumCulling`
  is set in `insertEntity` — the single path both `createEntity` and `restoreEntity` pass through — so a restored
  body carries the SAME value as a created one rather than whatever the object arrived with. **THREE's own
  default is `true`**, so the default config is behaviour-unchanged; `false` now genuinely disables culling for
  every authored body. The three-runtime suite going **505 → 510** with no existing case moving is the evidence
  that the default path did not shift.
- **`maxLights` is now OPTIONAL and documented as UNHONORED, with the reason.** There is no light-creation API in
  this package: `createScene` builds exactly two lights (`ambient`, `directional`) and `setLightState` only
  toggles or dims them — so there is nothing for a cap to cap. A required field that cannot be honored is worse
  than an optional one that says so; it becomes meaningful the day an `addLight` exists, and the doc comment
  names that condition rather than leaving a reader to guess.
- **The flag is re-DERIVED on restore, not carried in the file.** `SerializedEntity` has `visible`, `castShadow`,
  `receiveShadow` and `layers`, and **no field for `frustumCulled`** — a case asserts exactly that, because it is
  WHY a restore has to take the value from the config. A rendering flag is a runtime setting, not entity state.
- **Evidence.** `packages/three-runtime/test/frustumCulling.test.ts` — 5 cases (the default leaves bodies at
  THREE's own default · `false` reaches a created body while its neighbours are untouched · a RESTORED body
  carries the runtime's config · the save shape has no field for it, so the value must be re-derived · a config
  omitting `maxLights` builds and runs). three-runtime **505 → 510** (21 files), `tsc` **0**.
- **Mutation probe, 2 arms, 2/2 MATCHED** (async spawn — `execFileSync` answers EBUSY on this host): **A1** the
  assignment removed → two cases red with `expected true to be false`, i.e. the flag back to decorative ·
  **A2** the value hard-coded `true` → the same two cases red, i.e. the config no longer read. Source restored
  byte-identical and the suite green afterwards.
- **A defect the first draft of this increment's own test found.** The restore case originally restored into the
  SAME scene and was refused — *"restoreEntity: entity … is already in scene …; a restore never overwrites live
  state"*. That is the runtime's own rule doing its job, and the case now restores into a second scene; the
  refusal is worth keeping in the record because it is the kind of thing a reader would otherwise try.
- **Bounds (§60).** `frustumCulling` reaches the objects the runtime CREATES; it does not retroactively apply to
  an object a caller built and handed in (there is no such path — geometry and material are the only injected
  values, and the object is always constructed here). `maxLights` remains unhonored, and the honest statement is
  the doc comment plus this record, not a silent no-op.

### Amendment 222 (M7 v222, tools/harness + docs/evidence) — the publish E2E proof no longer leaks its throwaway database

_Numbering: 222 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 2[0-9][0-9]"` topped out at 221). Closes plan item 24, which
the 2026-10-10 evidence run surfaced when a 2-day-old container was found still Up on this host._

- **The defect.** `studio-publish.mjs` starts its throwaway PostgreSQL with `docker run -d --rm` and removes it in
  a `finally`. That covers every exit the proof can see — a failed assertion included — but it cannot cover a
  HARD KILL, and `--rm` only removes a container that STOPS. Measured 2026-10-10:
  `nexus-publish-e2e-db-1791461501643-9348` had been **Up 2 days**, holding `127.0.0.1:51149` and a PostgreSQL
  instance, from a run killed during teardown. A killed proof therefore leaves a container RUNNING forever,
  holding a port and a database — and plausibly slowing the box (the same session's doc-gate §4 flake coincided
  with a loaded machine).

- **The fix is a name-based sweep at the START, not a trust in the exit path.** `tools/harness/leakSweep.mjs`
  adds `sweepLeftoverDatabases(run, …)` — it lists every container by the `nexus-publish-e2e-db-` prefix, decides
  which to retire, and removes them. `studio-publish.mjs` now calls it at §1a, **before** it takes a port (offset
  8352) and **before** it starts the database (offset 8429) — so a corpse left by a prior run can no longer make
  the port choice look busy or the db name collide.

- **The rule is by OWNER, not by age alone.** The name carries the creating pid
  (`nexus-publish-e2e-db-<stamp>-<pid>`). A container whose owner pid is GONE is one nobody will ever clean up →
  `owner-gone`. A container whose owner is still ALIVE belongs to a concurrent run and is LEFT ALONE — a sweep
  that killed it would be a worse bug than the leak it prevents. Age is the second gate (`MAX_AGE_MS = 6h`) for
  the case where the pid has been recycled by an unrelated process → `stale`. A name the pattern does not
  understand is LEFT ALONE rather than guessed at, because the pattern is the only thing that locates the pid;
  removing a container on a hunch is how a sweep becomes a hazard.

- **The decision layer is PURE and holds no capability.** `containersToRetire(containers, { now, isAlive,
  maxAgeMs })` is a pure function (the caller injects `now` and `isAlive`), so the nine-row decision table is
  testable with no docker daemon and nothing spawned; the pure layer imports no `child_process` and calls no
  `process.exit` (§6 of the proof asserts this). `pidIsAlive` uses `process.kill(pid, 0)` — the OS's cheapest
  liveness probe — and treats `EPERM` (the process exists but is owned by another user) as alive.

- **Evidence.** `docs/evidence/m7/leak-sweep-proof.mjs`, **6 sections, ALL PASSED**: §1 the decision table over 9
  synthetic listings (owner-gone / stale are the only two reasons, a live owner is never swept, the age bound is
  exclusive, foreign and unmatched names are left alone) · §2 purity (the listing is untouched and two identical
  calls agree) · §3 the wiring (the proof imports and calls the sweep BEFORE it takes a port and starts the
  database) · §4 a failed listing is reported and NOT fatal (no removal attempted, the caller decides) · §5
  end-to-end against a REAL staged orphan — the proof creates a container in the exact shape of the 2-day corpse
  and the sweep retires it as `owner-gone`, and docker no longer lists it · §6 the decision module holds no
  capability. On this box the run also found and retired a leftover
  `nexus-publish-e2e-db-1791649277835-999999999` (owner-gone, 1s old) — the leak this increment exists to
  prevent, observed and cleared.

- **A failure-mode the proof deliberately avoids.** §5 creates a real orphan and cleans it up `finally`
  regardless, so the proof cannot itself become the leak it tests for; §4 proves a daemon-less host still runs (a
  failed listing is a courtesy, not a gate). The pure decision layer is why both are provable without touching
  the real daemon's removal path except in §5's isolated case.

- **Bounds (§60).** The sweep only ever sees containers it named itself via the prefix filter, so everything else
  the host runs is none of its business. It removes by NAME (`docker rm -f`), not by a guessed pid or image, and
  only names it recognised. A concurrent run's container (live owner) is explicitly NOT swept. `MAX_AGE_MS` is a
  ceiling, not a floor — an old container whose owner is still alive is swept on age, not left to a recycled pid.
  `verify:leak-sweep` is wired into the root `package.json` alongside `verify:publish` / `verify:publish-e2e`.

### Amendment 224 (M5 v224, three-runtime + studio) — a refused camera switch silently cleared the active camera, and the surface gets its sixth watch leg

_Numbering: 224 was free — the ledger's own `### Amendment` headings were scanned (max 223), and the landing
script re-scans them before it writes and refuses if the number is taken. Code and tests: `ad72bbe`
(7 files, +537/−16) with the citation/ordering follow-on `52a1a51` (4 files, +13/−6); 549 insertions,
21 deletions over both._

- **The defect, measured on the shipped bytes before the fix.** `setActiveCamera` cleared every camera's
  `active` flag and only THEN looked the requested id up, so `setActiveCamera(scene, BOGUS)` answered `false` —
  the same sentence its no-such-scene branch says — while leaving the scene with **no active camera at all**. The
  report's active id went to `null`, nothing fired on the bus (a refusal has no payload to news, correctly), and
  because `animate()` renders only when `activeCamera` is found, **the drawing stopped**: `backend.stats.calls`
  grew by 4 over the three frames before the refusal and by **0** after it. A refusal that edits is the worst
  shape of refusal — the caller is told nothing happened, and everything happened.

- **The fix is two lines swapped** (`threeRuntime.ts:2545-2553`): look up, refuse, then move the flags and
  announce. Both refusals — no such scene, no such camera — are now the same no-op, which is what the battery's
  `R1` measures by putting the old order back.

  `cameraCreated` and `activeCameraChanged` — the two names over the three report fields no earlier leg moves
  (`scene.cameras`, `cameraNames`, `activeCamera`). What did not exist before was the guarantee that a refusal
  moves nothing. The census is over WRITES, not families: `createCamera` inserts and, when the insert is the
  scene's first camera, flips `active` itself, announcing both with one `cameraCreated`; `setActiveCamera` is the
  only other writer of `active`; `cameras.delete`/`cameras.clear` appear **nowhere** in the runtime, so within a
  scene the camera rows only ever grow, and the two scene-level writes that also move this leg's fields belong to
  v217's pair. Camera TRANSFORM writes (`position.copy`, `lookAt`, `fov` at `2854-2859`; the surface's own `aim()`
  at `977`) are refused as a NEW refusal shape — they move the live `THREE.Camera`, which the report never reads.

- **The pin re-widens, as it must:** 12 joins → **14 joins over 14 distinct names**, and the case is now
  six-way. `S4` (handing the camera leg v217's `activeSceneChanged`) is the arm that proves the boundary is
  load-bearing rather than cosmetic: three studio cases redden, including `expected [ 'news' ] to deeply equal []`.

- **The battery, at `52a1a51`: 8 arms, 30 predictions, 30 reds, 8/8 MATCHED.** Baseline read first, sequentially,

  --noEmit` exit 0 in both (12.64s, 20.65s). The arm population is the files the grant names: 108 runtime cases

  studio; `R3` emit BEFORE the flags → 2 rt + 1 studio; `S1` leg's pair narrowed → 5; `S2` host-honest guard
