### Amendment 225 (M5 v225, three-runtime) — the two `create*` seams refused nothing: a taken id silently evicted the live record, and the camera one left the scene with no active camera

_Numbering: 225 was free — the ledger's `### Amendment` headings were scanned (max 224) before writing. Code
and tests: this grant (2 files, +97/−4) — `threeRuntime.ts` and the new `test/cameraIdCollision.test.ts`._

- **The defect, measured on the shipped bytes before the fix.** `createCamera`'s optional `id` is the restore
  wedge (`defineCinematic` refuses a shot naming a camera the scene lacks, so a saved cinematic could only be
  read back by re-issuing the ids), and a TAKEN id was answered by `Map.set` alone. A probe run against the
  unmodified runtime — two cameras, `Cam A` active, then
  `createCamera(scene, 'Cam A REPLACED', 'perspective', {}, a.id)` — printed:

      threw=null
     returned=camera-…/Cam A REPLACED/active=false
     size 2 -> 2
     account Cam A:true,Cam B:false -> Cam A REPLACED:false,Cam B:false
     activeNow=NULL
     cameraCreated fired 1x
     activeCameraChanged fired 0x

  So a restore that named the scene's ACTIVE camera left the scene holding two cameras with `active=false` on
  BOTH — nothing for `animate()` to draw from — while the bus announced a create and never mentioned the seat
  that had just been vacated. The solo probe (the overwritten id is the ONLY camera) came back `active=true`,
  because the `size === 1` branch fires on the replacement — so the bug bites exactly in the state a cinematic
  restore arrives in, a scene that already has a camera.

- **`createScene` has the same hole, one level up.** Its `id` is the wedge `loadSaveFile` depends on — the
  loader refuses to invent the scene a file describes, so the caller re-issues the saved id first — and a
  taken one evicted the live scene with its entities, cameras, animations and lighting, announcing the
  replacement with a plain `sceneCreated`. When the evicted scene held the active seat, the graph's
  `activeSceneId` went on naming an id whose contents had been swapped underneath it.

- **The fix is the rule this runtime already states four times, applied where it was missing:** "a restore
  never overwrites live state" (`restoreEntity:1792`, `loadSaveFile:1963`, `restoreNPC:3168`,
  `restorePlayer:3357`). Both create* verbs now REFUSE a taken id, and they throw rather than answering a
  record built around a substitution — the same answer shape every other refusal in this class gives.

- **Nothing in the corpus relied on the overwrite, which is the measurement that makes the rule safe:** all
  521 existing three-runtime cases pass with both guards in place, because every legitimate use of the seam
  already restores into a graph that does not hold the id (the `saveSnapshot` round-trips name a saved id in
  a SECOND runtime, exactly as the loader's protocol requires). The Studio's 474 cases pass unchanged, graded
  through the `@nexus/three-runtime` → `src` alias (`apps/studio/vitest.config.ts`), so the change is measured
  on the seam a user's panel reads too.

- **The battery: 4 arms, 4 predictions, 4 reds, 4/4 MATCHED, zero re-predictions.** Graded against the
  increment's own file (`test/cameraIdCollision.test.ts`, 10 cases) after the increment suite was green, the
  source snapshotted, mutated, re-read and restored for each arm. `A1` camera guard deleted → 4 red (the four
  cases that expect the throw); `A2` scene guard deleted → 3 red (the three `createScene` throwing cases, and
  NOT the restore-wedge case, which was never the bug); `A3` camera guard widened to every scene in the graph
  → 1 red (camera ids address ONE scene's camera set, so a second scene holding the same id is a different
  camera); `A4` both guards answering `null` instead of throwing → 7 red. Restore verified by content
  comparison, byte-identical, and HEAD unchanged throughout. The runner, needles and predictions live in this
  session's ignored `.scratch/`; the four arms are transcribed here and in the evidence record, so a clean
  checkout cannot re-run them.

- **The probe that measured the defect is named because it was an untracked artifact in the tree.** A
  previous session left `test/zzPreFixProbe.test.ts` — its own header says "TEMPORARY pre-fix measurement
  probe — deleted before any gate or full-suite run" — and stopped before deleting it. It was run once to
  harvest the figures above (2 of its 3 cases printing; the third was mis-armed against `defineCinematic`'s
  two-argument signature and threw `scene [object Object] does not exist`, which is the runtime's own arg
  check working) and then deleted, before any gate or full-suite run.

- **Bounds.** A caller passing NO id can never be refused: the generated id is unique per call, so the guard
  fires only on the restore wedge. The collision is scoped the way the ids are scoped — scenes per graph,
  cameras per scene — and both scopes have a case. What this grant does NOT do: there is still no
  `removeCamera`/`removeScene` verb, so the only way a camera leaves a scene is disposal; `loadSaveFile`
  still requires the caller to create the scene first (a loader that invented one would be inventing the
  world the file was meant to describe); and the id is still honoured as the MAP KEY, so a refused restore is
  told by name rather than silently re-keyed.

### Amendment 226 (v226, repo hygiene) — `.workbuddy-ai/` was not ignored, and it holds another tool's memory files

_Numbering: 226 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment [0-9]*"` topped out at 225). Not a milestone feature: the
same mechanism amendment 215 closed for `.scratch/`, found again during the v225 cycle while the tree was being
cleaned for a commit._

- **What `.workbuddy-ai/` is.** Another tool's OWN long-term memory directory, sitting untracked in the working
  tree: eight `memory/*.md` files dated 2026-09-28 through 2026-10-10 plus a `MEMORY.md` index. None of it is part
  of this project's build, its tests or its docs — it is a second agent's notebook ABOUT this repository.
- **The hazard is the one amendment 215 already recorded, one `git add -A` wide.** An untracked foreign tree in
  the working directory is one careless add from landing inside an unrelated commit: `.scratch/` did exactly that
  to **amendment 196's record** (`8ebdd75`), which spent a while describing an artifact page the tree did not
  have. It is ignored here for the same reason and at the same one-line cost.
- **It was found by needing it gone.** The v225 cycle's own commit staged five NAMED files rather than `-A`
  precisely because `git status --short` showed `.workbuddy-ai/` as untracked alongside the increment's changes;
  the doc gate's dirty-tree precondition (`table-recount-proof.mjs` §2) also asserts on the tree, so a foreign
  tree that could be swept is worth naming in `.gitignore` rather than avoided by hand each time.
- **Evidence.** `git check-ignore -v .workbuddy-ai/` answers `.gitignore:58:.workbuddy-ai/`; `git status --short`
  no longer lists the eight memory files as untracked. Measured after the change: `table-recount-proof.mjs` §2's
  precondition still reads 0 modified and §7 still reads "the newest grant 225 IS titled", so the hygiene line
  moved nothing the gate counts.
- **Bounds (§60).** This stops the directory REACHING a commit; it does not delete it (it is another tool's
  working state, and destroying it would be worse than ignoring it). It also teaches nothing to whoever runs
  `git add -A` — the next foreign directory will need the same line, which is the argument for staging by name
  rather than by glob, recorded here rather than repeated.

### Amendment 227 (M5 v227, three-runtime + studio) — a save file's cinematic half was the only half that named an ABSOLUTE scene id, so a file carrying a cutscene could only be loaded into the very scene it was saved from

_Numbering: 227 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment [0-9]*"` topped out at 226). Code and tests: `threeRuntime.ts`,
`scene3d.ts`, `saveSnapshot.test.ts`, `scene3d.test.ts`, `scene3dSurface.test.ts` (5 files)._

- **The defect, measured on the shipped bytes before the fix.** A save file is a set of contents about ONE scene,
  and every half of it is restored against the scene the CALLER names: `entities`, `npcs`, `worldState` and
  `player` all take `loadSaveFile`'s `sceneId` argument. The cinematic half was the one exception. A sequence's
  `sceneId` records where the save was taken (`types.ts:754-761` — it exists because a shot's `cameraId`
  addresses one scene's camera set and nothing else), and the loader demanded that exact scene exist. A file
  carrying a cutscene could therefore only be loaded into the very scene it was saved from — the one half of
  the format no host could restore anywhere else. A probe against the unmodified runtime, loading the
  Studio's own save back through the Studio's own surface, printed:

      PROBE STUDIO PATH REFUSED restoreCinematic: "seq" belongs to scene stage, which is not the active
      scene (studio-scene); … the restore rolled back: nothing had been registered
      PROBE STUDIO PATH scenes 2 · cameras in fresh 0
      PROBE PROTOCOL PATH OK {"sceneId":"stage", …,"sequences":["seq"], …}

  So the format declares cinematic SAVABLE (`saveFeasibilityAudit` lists it), the Studio's save claims to carry
  it, and the Studio's own load could not read one back — because the Studio's whole design is a SIBLING
  restore: "the demo scene and its frame loop stay exactly what they were". The documented protocol
  (createScene under the saved id, re-issue the shot's camera) is exactly what a sibling-restoring host cannot
  do.

- **The fix is one line plus a helper.** `loadSaveFile` now restores the cinematic half against the scene the
  caller names: `retargetCinematic(file.cinematic, sceneId)` returns a COPY with every sequence's `sceneId` set
  to the target, and `restoreCinematic` keeps its own contract untouched (restore the snapshot into the scenes
  it names). The field is still WRITTEN by `buildSaveFile` and still VALIDATED on the way in; what changes is
  that the restore reads the caller's scene for it. A COPY, because the file is the caller's value and
  rewriting it in place would silently edit something the loader did not own — a case pins that, and arm R2
  grades it.

- **The camera half stays the caller's, and now it is the only thing left.** The format carries no camera
  objects — a shot names a `cameraId` and the name, type and FOV behind it are not in the file — so the loader
  refuses a shot naming a camera the target scene lacks, by name. The Studio's `load()` previously did none of
  this; it now re-issues every camera the file's shots name (under the file's id, with a name SPELLED from the
  id, since the save cannot say what it was), and makes the sibling the ACTIVE scene when the file describes a
  cutscene that was RUNNING — `playCinematic` plays only on the active scene. It ANSWERS what it re-issued
  (`SceneLoadReissued`), so a host can say "2 cameras re-issued by id" rather than showing a camera whose
  name is invented.

- **Two honest bounds the tests pin rather than hide.** (1) The surface's OWN save is still refused, by name,
  when its cutscene is still live: a sequence is registry state in ONE runtime, `defineCinematic` refuses a
  taken id, and "a restore never overwrites live state" is the rule this runtime states five times now. The
  round-trip that works is the one a host can actually perform — a file from ANOTHER runtime. (2) A host with
  no `setActiveScene` verb cannot resume a running cutscene at all, so the surface refuses that file in its
  own voice rather than meeting the runtime's scene-id-shaped refusal three calls later.

- **The battery: 5 arms, 5 predictions, 5 reds, 5/5 MATCHED — after one re-derivation, recorded rather than
  smoothed.** The first derivation under-counted every arm for two reasons the mechanism then made plain: the
  studio suite runs the REAL runtime through the `@nexus/three-runtime` → `src` alias
  (`apps/studio/vitest.config.ts`), so a runtime mutation reddens studio cases too; and the STOPPED-sequence
  case names a camera exactly as much as the running one. Re-derived: `R1` loader stops re-pointing → **8** red
  (4 runtime + 4 studio) · `R2` re-point mutates the caller's file → **2** (the case exists in both suites)
  · `S1` surface stops re-issuing cameras → **4** · `S2` surface stops activating → **3** (without it the
  running load is REFUSED, so the camera-identity case reddens too) · `S3` surface reports ids it never
  re-issued → **4**. Both files restored byte-identical after every arm.

- **Measured:** three-runtime **531 → 535** (23 files), Studio **474 → 483** (31 files), `tsc --noEmit` exit 0
  in both. No existing case moved — the re-point only ADDS a target that previously could not be named.

### Amendment 228 (M5 v228, three-runtime) — `createAnimation` was the one `create*` verb that did not refuse a scene the graph does not hold

_Numbering: 228 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment [0-9]*"` topped out at 227). Code and tests:
`threeRuntime.ts` and the new `test/animationSceneGuard.test.ts` (2 files)._

- **The defect, measured on the shipped bytes before the fix.** A survey of the registry seams after v225
  (which taught `createScene` and `createCamera` to refuse a taken id) went looking for the same family —
  a verb that answers a bad argument with a silent no-op dressed as a success. `attachNPC`, `attachPlayer`,
  `attachController` and `attachCombatant` all refuse a taken slot; `addComponent` replaces by design with a
  documented eviction cleanup (v208). The one hole was `createAnimation`: the scene was looked up AFTER the
  animation was built, and the registration was guarded with `if (scene)`. A probe called it twice on one
  bogus scene id and printed:

      returned: "anim-…/Ghost/clips=1"      — a live animation object, handed back as success
      scenesHoldingTheGhost: 0              — registered NOWHERE
      realSceneAnimationCount: 0            — and not in the real scene either
      scenesInGraph: 1                      — the graph did not grow
      animationCreatedFired: 2              — news about a record no scene holds
      reachableById: "no"                   — `playAnimation` could never find it again
      PROBE SIBLINGS { cameraOutcome: "Scene scene-that-does-not-exist not found",
                       entityOutcome: "Scene scene-that-does-not-exist not found" }

  So the caller was handed a success for work that did not happen, announced on the bus, under an id no
  scene's map holds.

- **The fix is the guard moved to the top**, which is also the order the siblings already use: `createEntity`
  and `createCamera` both answer `Scene X not found` before building anything. Two orderings are pinned
  because they are separate claims: the SCENE is asked before the CLIPS (a bogus scene with no clips reports
  the scene — the wider claim first), and the emit follows the registration (a listener reading
  `scene.animations` from inside `animationCreated` finds the record the news is about — the same rule v211
  established for the entity verbs and v218 for `setPixelRatio`).

- **The battery: 3 arms, 3 predictions, 3 reds, 3/3 MATCHED — after one re-derivation, recorded rather than
  smoothed.** The first A1 was mis-armed: it deleted the guard but left the registration unconditional, which
  produced a `TypeError` on `undefined.animations` instead of the pre-fix lenient path — and two cases that
  should have reddened went green for the wrong reason. The arm was rebuilt to restore the exact pre-fix shape
  (`if (scene)` around the registration) and its prediction re-derived to 5; re-run alone, 5/5. `A2` clip
  check before the scene guard → 1 · `A3` announce before the registration → 1. Source restored byte-identical
  after every arm, HEAD unchanged throughout.

- **Measured:** three-runtime **535 → 541** (23 → 24 files), `tsc --noEmit` exit 0, Studio **484/484**
  unchanged (no studio source moved, and no studio case calls `createAnimation`). No existing case moved:
  every caller in the corpus passes a real `scene.id`, which is why the hole could sit there for nine
  increments since v108 introduced the verb.

### Amendment 229 (M2 v229, agents/runtime tests) — the `FsWriteLike` disk every suite defined for itself, made ONE disk with a named listing policy

_Numbering: 229 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment 22[0-9]"` topped out at 228). Test-only: the new
`agents/runtime/test/memDisk.ts` and eleven migrated suites. No `src/` byte moved._

- **The defect.** Eleven suites in `agents/runtime/test` each defined their own `MemDisk`/`FakeDisk` for the
  runtime's `FsWriteLike` seam — and under that one name they answered `readdirSync` THREE different ways:
  **five threw** ("not implemented for this suite"), **two answered an empty listing**, and **three answered a
  real one** (byte-identical to each other), while `durability`'s `FakeDisk` carried a fourth shape (a `dirs`
  set, `withFileTypes`, a real directory listing). Same name, different disk — so "the mock" meant something
  different in every file, and a suite that NEEDED a listing had no way to say so. The bodies were otherwise
  identical (`readFileSync`/`statSync`/`mkdirSync`/`writeFileSync`), so only the LISTING was a real choice.
- **What landed.** `agents/runtime/test/memDisk.ts` — one `createMemDisk({ listing, seed })`. The listing
  policy is NAMED at each call site, never inferred:
  - `'refuse'` — this suite never lists, and a directory read here is a bug in the TEST; it THROWS, which is
    the answer v206 argued for ("a mock that reports 'no entries' for a disk that HAS entries is the kind of
    lie a future test would pass against"). Taken by **testRunner, ledger, vectordb, chain, evaluate**.
  - `'empty'` — the code path under test may ask and the honest answer for THIS suite is that it holds nothing.
    Deliberately the dangerous one; taken only where a case measured it. **memory, vectorStore**.
  - `'real'` — a true flat listing of the files (and any `dirs` a `mkdirSync` recorded). **durability,
    indexVectors, indexStore, pipeline**.
- **A defect the migration found in the helper's own first draft.** The seed loop wrote each seed path with
  `writeFileSync`, which does NOT derive parent directories — but `durability`'s `FakeDisk` CONSTRUCTOR did, and
  `disk.list` walks via `collectTextFiles`, which reads directories. So a migrated `durability` case that
  seeded `out/a/x.md` and listed would have found NOTHING: the walk reads `readdirSync('out')`, and with no
  `out` directory recorded it returns `[]`. The seed loop now derives the parent dirs (`out`, `out/a`); a later
  `writeFileSync` still does not, because a listing that reported a directory a later write never made would be
  inventing structure. This is the kind of thing a green suite cannot see — the case went red, and it did,
  before the fix.
- **Evidence.** `agents/runtime` **540/540** (36 files) green, `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json --noEmit` exit 0. No
  test added or removed — the count is unchanged, which is the proof the eleven migrations are
  behaviour-preserving (a suite that meant something different would have moved a case). `realfs`'s `FakeFs` is
  NOT migrated: it implements `FsLike` (not `FsWriteLike`) and carries a `root`-prefix `strip`, so it is a
  different seam with root-relative path handling, not the same disk under another name.
- **Bounds (§60).** The helper is test-only (`agents/runtime/test/`), so nothing in the shipped package moved.
  The listing policy is a per-suite DECLARATION, not an inference — a suite that needs a listing must now say
  which kind, which is the point. `mkdirSync` records directories (so a listing can report them) while
  `writeFileSync` does not; only the seed derives them. Two `MemDisk` type annotations (`chain`, `indexVectors`)
  now name the exported `MemDisk` interface rather than a local class.

### Amendment 230 (M2 v229 follow-on, agents/runtime tests) — the `'empty'` listing policy is REMOVED, and the shared disk gets its own cases

_Numbering: 230 was free (`grep -ao "^### Amendment [0-9]*"` topped out at 229). Test-only: `memDisk.ts`,
`memDisk.test.ts`, and the two suites that carried the policy._

- **What amendment 229 left open.** It made the eleven mocks one disk with a NAMED listing policy, which is the
  fix plan item 19 asked for. But two of the eleven still declared `'empty'` — `memory.test.ts` and
  `vectorStore.test.ts` — and `'empty'` answers `[]` for a disk that HAS entries. It was kept as "the
  dangerous one, deliberately, taken only where a case measured it", and no case had measured it: the two
  suites never reached a listing at all.
- **Measured, not assumed.** With the disk's own suite in place, the arms graded exactly that. `A1` (`'refuse'`
  answers `[]` instead of throwing) reddens **only the disk's own cases** and none of the five `'refuse'`
  suites — which is the measurement of v206's claim, stated in five copies of a comment and never once
  checked. `A2` reddens only the disk's own case, and tightening both `'empty'` suites to `'refuse'` moves
  **nothing**: 549/549 before and after.
- **So the policy is removed rather than kept for symmetry.** `'empty'` was strictly dominated: a disk that
  holds nothing answers `[]` truthfully under `'real'`, and a disk that holds something must not answer `[]` at
  all. `MemDiskListing` is now `'refuse' | 'real'`, the two policies that are actually about something.
  `memory.test.ts` and `vectorStore.test.ts` now say `'refuse'`, which is the true statement about them.
- **The disk gets cases of its own** (`test/memDisk.test.ts`, 9). A shared helper whose behaviour is nobody's
  assertion is the same hazard in a new place: the three policies were eleven unsynchronised copies, and one
  unpinned helper would have been a twelfth. The cases pin each policy, the difference between a SEED
  (which derives its directories, because it is a whole tree) and a WRITE (which does not, because a listing
  that reported a directory nobody made would be inventing structure), `mkdirSync`'s recording, and that the
  listing is sorted and deterministic so no case depends on `Map` order.
- **The battery: 5 arms, 5 predictions, 5 reds, 5/5 MATCHED — after two re-derivations, recorded rather than
  smoothed.** The first A1 predicted 10 and measured 2, because it assumed the ported suites would redden;
  the measurement said otherwise and the finding replaced the prediction. A2 was then re-armed to the lie the
  removal prevents (`'real'` answering `[]` for a directory that has entries), first predicted 7 and measured
  5, and corrected. Final: `A1` `'refuse'`→`[]` → 2 · `A2` `'real'`→`[]` → 5 · `A3` files-only listing → 3 ·
  `A4` `mkdirSync` stops recording → 1 · `A5` a write derives its parents again → 1. Each arm is graded on the
  disk's own suite AND on the whole package, and the second reading is what proved no other suite reaches a
  listing under `'refuse'`. The disk is restored byte-identical after every arm.
- **Measured:** `agents/runtime` **540 → 549** (36 → 37 files), `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json --noEmit` exit 0.
  The 9 new cases are the disk's own; the 540 existing ones did not move, which is the proof the policy
  removal changes nothing the corpus relies on.

### Amendment 231 (M1/v231, packages/design-model + apps/studio) — `InstanceNode['overrides']` could not express a text override; the `text` sibling is folded into the per-child patch

- **The defect (plan item 17, found by v204's widened gate).** `InstanceNode['overrides']` was
  `Record<NexusId, Partial<Pick<NodeBase, 'width'|'height'|'visible'|'x'|'y'|'rotation'|'fills'|'cornerRadius'>>> & { text?: Record<NexusId, string> }` — a reserved `text` SIBLING of the map. Two consequences, both real:
  1. **No correctly-typed code could write a text override.** An object literal's `text` key had to satisfy the
     index signature as well as the named field, so `{ 'cmp::label': 'Clicked' }` could not be typed; every
     writer (and `readOverrides` itself) cast around it — `instances.test.ts` carried the identical cast with a
     sentence explaining why, which is the smell the item was filed on.
  2. **A master child literally named `text` was unreachable for geometry patches.** `readOverrides` skipped the
     `text` key to avoid clobbering the sibling, so an override for a child whose id WAS `text` silently vanished.
- **The canonical decision (ADR 0004/0015 territory — an override IS a patch, so `text` is just another patchable field).** The reserved sibling is gone. `InstanceChildOverride` now carries `text?: string` alongside the geometry fields, and `InstanceNode.overrides` is `Record<NexusId, InstanceChildOverride>` — no index-signature trap, and `overrides['text']` now MEANS the child named `text`'s patch (its `text` field is that child's text), the exact shape that was unreachable before. The text is still applied only when the clone is a text node (`clone.type === 'text'`), preserving the original guard.
- **Legacy snapshots are a lossless ENCODING, not a schema.** A snapshot written before v231 carries the text overrides in `overrides.text = { [masterId]: 'words' }`. That is the same data under a different key, so `normalizeInstanceOverrides` folds it on READ (`overrides` → `Record<NexusId, InstanceChildOverride>`, remapping any `text` sibling into each child's `.text`) rather than orphaning every local snapshot behind a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump — `apps/studio/src/lib/persist.ts` REFUSES unknown versions, so a bump would throw away all of a user's saved documents. The one genuinely ambiguous shape — a child literally named `text` carrying a text-only patch — still folds correctly, because the NEW key is `text` and the guard (`id === 'text' && value-is-a-map`) only treats the legacy sibling as a text map when its values are all strings (a new-shape patch for `text` answers with numbers/booleans/arrays, never a string map).
- **Files:** `packages/design-model/src/types.ts` (`InstanceChildOverride.text?`, `InstanceNode.overrides`), `packages/design-model/src/instances.ts` (`normalizeInstanceOverrides` + `readOverrides` reduced to a one-line call, `applyOverrides` folds `geom.text`, `cloneTree` drops its separate `text` parameter), `packages/design-model/src/index.ts` (export `normalizeInstanceOverrides`), `apps/studio/src/lib/store.ts` (four writer sites call `normalizeInstanceOverrides` and write `geom.text` instead of `next.text[m]`) — `setInstanceOverride`'s `isEmpty` check now also honours `geom.text`. The cast is GONE from `packages/design-model/test/instances.test.ts` (the test that used to carry it now writes the override as a plain field and adds cases for both defects plus the legacy fold); `apps/studio/src/lib/store-variants.test.ts` asserts `inst(instId).overrides[textId]?.text`.
- **Measured:** `packages/design-model` **34/34** (instances.test.ts 15 → 16, the legacy fold case exercises the pre-v231 shape through `normalizeInstanceOverrides`), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0 (dist rebuilt, exported). `apps/studio` **484/484** (31 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0 (Studio reads the rebuilt dist). No production code path changed meaning — a text override that landed in the sibling before v231 now lands in the field, and a master child named `text` is patchable for the first time.

### Amendment 232 (gate/v232, docs/evidence/agents) — the doc gate's §4 could not tell a loaded box from a regression; it now measures each arm and names the cause (plan item 23)

- **The defect (plan item 23, measured 2026-10-10).** §4 asserts HEAD's suite is green by checking that no OWNED test case failed. On a loaded box that assertion can redden on a spawn-heavy case that is fine standalone — `execHost.test.ts > the process tree (v55): what a timeout kill stops` takes ~3.7 s alone and is **39/39 green** on a quiet box, yet a loaded run pushed an arm past its 240 s budget (`runtime: vitest exit -1`) and §4 reddened on it. So a red §4 had **two** possible causes — a real regression, or host load — and the gate named neither. That is the failure mode amendment 152 warned about for `--no-file-parallelism`, one layer up: a gate whose reds cannot be told from the host's noise.
- **The fix — measure, classify, name.** §4 now (a) times each arm (`Date.now()` around the vitest spawn) and prints the wall-clock per arm in §2 and in the §4 summary line; (b) routes each arm through a **pure** `classifyArm(run, allRuns)` that answers one of three `kind`s: `ok` (green), `regression` (an owned failing case with no sibling trouble), `incomplete` (a non-zero vitest exit OR fewer owned files reported than HEAD owns — a timeout / loaded box); and (c) when a `regression` coincides with a non-zero vitest exit on a sibling arm, its message NAMES the coincidence and says to re-run on a quiet box before treating it as real. An `incomplete` arm's "failing" cases are quoted only as **suspects the timeout may have stranded**, never as the verdict — a timeout can strand a case mid-flight and report it failed.
- **Box-safe by construction.** On a healthy box every arm exits 0 and reports exactly its owned files, so `incomplete` is false and `timedOutSibling` is false — neither guarded arm is ever taken, and §4's green is byte-identical to before. The completeness signal is a basename comparison (`casesOf` keys `byFile` by basename, matching the `owned` set), so it compares like with like.
- **Witnessed (§4b).** A gate that gained a new verdict must be shown to produce it (§32). §4b grades `classifyArm` on five synthetic arms with no vitest and no host: a healthy arm → `ok`; a failing owned case with a clean sibling → `regression` whose message says so and does NOT cry host noise; a non-zero exit with no files → `incomplete` naming the timeout cause; an exit-0 arm missing an owned file → `incomplete`; and a regression beside a timed-out arm → the message names the coincidence.
- **Measured (this run, gate exit 0):** `[§2] runtime: vitest exit 0 · 106102ms` · `exec-host: vitest exit 0 · 27946ms`; `[§4] arms: runtime 106102ms exit 0 37/34 files · exec-host 27946ms exit 0 10/9 files` (the extra files are untracked in-flight suites another lane owns, named and not graded); `[§4b] classifier witnessed: ok · regression · incomplete (non-zero exit) · incomplete (dropped file) · timed-out-sibling coincidence`. §7 still reads the newest grant 231 as titled; the table is unchanged (816 cases, 43 files, 4/4 mutations caught).

### Amendment 233 (M7/v233, packages/design-model + apps/studio) — a publication can be REMIXED: the Studio reads someone else's published document back in as a NEW project

- **The bound it closes.** M7's own record (v196) ends with: *"the Studio never reads a publication back in its own UI."* `publishLane.readPublished` existed since v194 and had **zero consumers** — the Studio could publish but never remix. Remix is the community's first cross-user primitive, and it is the one door that turns a published artifact back into an editable project.
- **The decision — a remix is a FORK, not a load.** `doc.id` IS the publish service's projectId (the Studio publishes `doc.id`). So a remix that loaded the source document under its own id would re-publish OVER the source's record — a remix would silently become an edit of someone else's publication. `forkDocument(doc, name?)` (new, `packages/design-model/src/nodes.ts`) therefore gives the document a **fresh DOCUMENT id** — `id`, `rootId`, and the `nodes` key holding the root node all move together — while the node graph is preserved (node ids are document-scoped, so reusing them collides with nothing; rewriting every node id would rewrite every `parentId`/`childIds` for no gain). Pure and total; it THROWS when the document names a `rootId` its own `nodes` do not hold, rather than inventing a root.
- **The lane — a pure validator that NAMES the field.** `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.ts` is a fetch adapter over `readPublished` plus a PURE `extractRemixDocument(answer)` returning `{ ok: true, document } | { ok: false, reason }`. It checks what the model requires (string `id`/`rootId`/`activePageId`, object `nodes`) and names the failing field — NOT a deep schema (the store and renderer are the real authorities; a lane that re-implemented the schema would be a second, drifting one). A service that is **DOWN** (`ok:false` with the service's reason) and a publication that carries **NO document** are reported as DIFFERENT facts. The `DesignDocument` import is TYPE-ONLY, so nothing new enters the browser bundle.
- **The product face.** The Published panel row (`Toolbar.tsx`) gains a `remix` control beside `open`/`take down`; `onRemix` calls the lane, and on success the store's new `remixDocument(doc, source)` forks the document and loads it (status `Remixed <id> — this is now your project`), closing the panel because the editor behind it is now a different project.
- **Files:** `packages/design-model/src/nodes.ts` (`forkDocument`, `NexusId` import; exported via the existing `export * from './nodes.js'`), `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/lib/store.ts` (`remixDocument` on the interface + implementation, `forkDocument` imported), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (import + selector + `onRemix` + the row control), `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.test.ts` (new), `packages/design-model/test/fork.test.ts` (new), `docs/evidence/m7/remix-proof.mjs` (new), `package.json` (`verify:remix`).
- **Measured:** `packages/design-model` **34 → 40** (fork.test.ts 6 cases), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0 (dist rebuilt, `forkDocument` exported). `apps/studio` **484 → 492** (31 → 32 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0. `docs/evidence/m7/remix-proof.mjs` **5/5 sections PASSED**: §1 the validator (well-formed passes; service-down ≠ no-document; 4 malformed fields each refused by name), §2 the lane over a STUBBED transport (a `{action:"read"}` request, the document passed through, a down service and a throwing transport both answer `ok:false`), §3 the fork (fresh document id, same graph, source unmutated), §4 the wiring (remix control per row; store forks before load), §5 the §60 dependency audit (lane holds no service address and no server import; model import type-only). One defect caught in the first draft: `remixLane.ts` imported `@/lib/publishLane`, an alias the Studio's vitest config does not resolve (lib files cross-import relatively) — fixed to `./publishLane`.

### Amendment 234 (M7/v234, apps/studio) — the artifact page offers a Remix link, so a VISITOR can take the work

- **The gap v233 left.** v233 wired remix into the Studio's own **Published panel** — a control only the PUBLISHER sees (it lists the service's publications inside their own editor). The community loop needs the other half: someone who has only the ARTIFACT URL (`/p/{id}`) must be able to remix. Without it, "remix" is a button in the author's own toolbar, which is not a community primitive at all.
- **The fix — one link and one intent.** `renderArtifactHtml` gains a `projectId` and, when it has one, injects a **remix bar** before `</body>`: an `<a href="/?remix=<id>">` (the id `encodeURIComponent`-encoded and the href HTML-escaped) — the drawing itself is untouched. `injectRemixBar(html, projectId)` is PURE and total: a preview that carries no `</body>` is returned unchanged rather than corrupted, and a caller that names no project gets no bar. On the Studio side, `remixIdFromSearch(search)` (PURE) reads the intent — a bare `?remix=` is `null`, not a project named `""` — and a mount effect in `Studio.tsx`, declared **after** the persistence-hydrate effect so an explicit remix wins over a stale local snapshot, fetches through the v233 lane, forks via `remixDocument`, and then **drops the query** (`history.replaceState(null, '', '/')`): the URL was a one-time intent, and a reload must not silently discard the edits the visitor makes.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/artifact.ts` (`renderArtifactHtml` takes `projectId`; new pure `injectRemixBar`), `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts` (passes `projectId`), `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.ts` (pure `remixIdFromSearch`), `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the remix-on-mount effect), `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.test.ts` (+3 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/artifact.test.ts` (+4 cases), `docs/evidence/m7/remix-proof.mjs` (§5 the visitor loop, graded against the SHIPPED artifact module type-stripped with its `./preview`/`./paint` dependencies).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **492 → 499** (32 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0. `remix-proof.mjs` **6/6 sections PASSED** — §5 asserts the REAL `renderArtifactHtml` output carries an encoded remix link and the stage, that no project id means no bar, that a body-less string is returned unchanged, and that the route and `Studio.tsx` carry the wiring. Bounds: the bar is a fixed-position overlay with no author, date or attribution (M7 still has no accounts), and a visitor who remixes and never publishes leaves no trace anywhere — there is no lineage recorded from a remix back to its source.

### Amendment 235 (M7/v235, apps/studio + docs/decisions) — the ACCOUNT MODEL lands, and ADR 0018 decides what it is allowed to mean

_Numbering: 235 was free (the ADR topped out at 234). Full decision record in `docs/decisions/0018-accounts-ownership-and-publication-identity.md`; this is the ledger entry._

- **The gap this closes.** Every M7 grant from v194 on has carried the same sentence, and v234 wrote it twice: *the remix bar has no author, date or attribution — **M7 still has no accounts***. Every publication is anonymous, every publication is anybody's to take down (`DELETE /projects/{id}` checks nothing), and a remix records no lineage. M7's remaining surfaces (profiles, follow, likes, comments) all depend on the missing fact *who is this*, and the plan had filed the item with an explicit precondition: it *"needs a canonical decision (an account model + how a publication names its owner + how the Studio authenticates) before any of those surfaces can be honest."* This increment is that decision plus the model's pure core; the service-side enforcement is deliberately not in it.
- **The decision is ADR 0018, and the boundary is in the TYPE SYSTEM rather than in a comment.** Four options were weighed; **C** — *a local, unsigned identity that produces a CLAIM* — was chosen over OAuth (needs an IdP, a client registration and a token store, and a half-wired one that never validates produces a badge), passwords (credential storage is a security surface this repo is not ready to own, and ADR 0013 is still Proposed), and doing nothing (which is the bound). What that choice buys is that the honesty is structural: `accounts.ts` contains **no password, no token, no session, no signature and no cryptography**, and the suite asserts that by **reading its own source** — a §60 claim measured rather than promised.
- **The model, as data.** `normalizeHandle` is the canonical rule and returns a VERDICT (a handle is data a person typed, so the caller must be able to show them what is wrong rather than catch an exception): TRIM → LOWERCASE, 3–24 characters, `[a-z0-9_-]`, must start and end alphanumeric. The regex is deliberately **not** length-aware — a two-character handle is a LENGTH failure, not a character failure, and one reason must not answer two questions; the suite pins that split. `createAccountId(handle, deviceSeed)` is FNV-1a over handle+seed, deterministic per device and testable, and it **refuses a seed that is only whitespace** — a defect the suite found in the first draft, which checked `!deviceSeed` and accepted `'   '`, so a host that persisted a padded empty string would get one id and a different one next time. `AccountRegistry` refuses a second registration of any handle that normalizes to one it holds (`Nexus` and `nexus` are ONE account), lists in handle order rather than registration order, and hands out COPIES so a caller cannot mutate the roster through a record it was given.
- **What an identity is worth is carried in the data, not in prose.** Every `AccountRecord` carries `assurance: 'unsigned-local'`; `ownerClaim(account, at)` names itself `kind: 'owner-claim'` and repeats the assurance, so a service receiving it can tell a claim from a verified identity without pattern-matching a sentence; and `isOwnerClaim` is the service-side shape check that refuses every near-miss (`kind: 'owner'`, `assurance: 'verified'`, a string `claimedAt`, a numeric `accountId`, a bare `{ kind }`, `null`, a string). The module **reserves no names**: a reserved list the client enforces and the service does not is a refusal nobody agreed to, and that is recorded as a bound rather than shipped as a feature.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/accounts.ts` (pure core), `apps/studio/src/lib/accounts.test.ts` (10 cases: the normalization matrix including every refusal reason, the seed rules, the roster's collision/copy/order rules, the claim shape, the near-miss table, and the source-level §60 audit), `docs/decisions/0018-…md` + its README index row.
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **499 → 509** (32 → 33 files, `npx vitest run` 33 files / 509 tests all passing), `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0. `accounts.test.ts` **10/10**. Two defects the suite caught before landing, both recorded above: the whitespace seed and the length/character split in the pattern.
- **Bounds (§60), stated.** A claim is forgeable by anyone who can call the API — that is why `assurance` exists. The device seed is per-browser, so one human on two devices gets two ids until the service merges them. **No publication carries a claim yet**: `publishDocument`, `readPublication` and `DELETE /projects/{id}` are unchanged, and no UI in this increment implies the service agrees. The service-side work — an owner field on a publication, an owner-checked unpublish, and a remix that records lineage — is the next increment, and until it lands nothing depends on a claim being true.

### Amendment 236 (gate/v236, docs/evidence/agents) — the doc gate's "240 s arm budget" was a NO-OP: the spawn option was `timeoutMs`, which `execFileSync` ignores

- **The defect, found while verifying v234.** The gate's vitest spawn carried `{ timeoutMs: 240_000 }` since v141, and item 23's fix (v232) even quoted "its 240 s arm budget exceeded" as a thing to name. But `child_process.execFileSync` takes **`timeout`**, not `timeoutMs` — an unknown option is silently ignored. Measured 2026-10-14: a 4 s child spawned with `timeoutMs: 1000` ran its full **4798 ms** (no throw), while the same child with `timeout: 1000` threw **ETIMEDOUT at 1144 ms**. So the arm had NO budget: it was killed only by whatever the host imposed, and here that was **~120 s** — the gate died with `vitest wrote no JSON for runtime (exit -1 after 120072ms)` and **`(exit -1 after 120019ms)`** on two consecutive runs, while the same suite run directly took **121.66 s** and finished green (37 files / 549 cases). The suite had simply crossed the host's 120 s line, which the missing budget could not report as a timeout because there was no timeout to report.
- **The fix — one word.** `timeoutMs: 240_000` → `timeout: 300_000`, with the measurement recorded in the comment so the next reader does not "restore" it. 300 s gives the now-REAL budget headroom over the runtime suite's ~100–122 s and exec-host's (measured this run) **162 s** — both of which the old no-op would have let the host kill.
- **Measured (gate exit 0 once 235 was titled):** `[§2] runtime: vitest exit 0 · 100907ms` · `exec-host: vitest exit 0 · 162040ms`; `[§4] arms: runtime 100907ms exit 0 37/34 files · exec-host 162040ms exit 0 10/9 files`. The 162 s exec-host arm is the witness: it would have been killed at 120 s under the old option, and now it completes and is REPORTED. `§4b` still witnesses the classifier; the table is unchanged (816 cases, 43 files).
- **Bounds (§60).** A real `timeout` makes the gate FAIL LOUDLY where it used to be killed silently — but a host whose own limit sits below 300 s will still kill the child first, and the gate will report that as `incomplete` (§4's new verdict) rather than as a regression, which is the honest answer: the budget is the gate's, the kill is the host's, and §4 now distinguishes them.

### Amendment 237 (M2/v237, docs/evidence/agents) — the mojibake repair gets an integrity gate: a writer model, a flank rule that protects real Chinese, and a 116-line digest ledger

- **The gap this closes.** Amendment 236 landed the 24 derived fixes over the 116 record
  lines the writer corrupted, and nothing in the repository could say whether the tree still carried that class
  of damage, or whether one of those repairs had been undone. The gate now answers both on every sweep.
- **The model is data, and its structural claims are measured.** Four writer mechanisms are declared as
  functions, not as prose, so the gate can ask them what they would produce. From that: M1 eats all 96
  printable ASCII followers of a 3-byte punctuation character while only 33 of them spell `?` — the rest
  are silently rewritten as CJK, which is why the repair had to append a character rather than replace one. The
  render registry (898 spellings) is DERIVED from the model rather than hand-listed, so a spelling cannot
  be added to charge a line without also being producible by the writer.
- **The rule, stated as a rule.** Chargeability is decided by the two tight neighbours, not by the character:
  the middle dot before a letter is rendered by M1 as the first character of `路径`, which is also the word for
  road. U+FFFD and C0 controls are chargeable unconditionally because no bilingual text explains them. Measured
  both ways at rest: a planted render charges, a planted CR charges, a planted `路径` line does NOT charge and
  moves the rejected count from 5 to 6.
- **The ledger keys on line bytes, and that choice is a witness.** A repaired-line digest pairs the rows; the
  arm that flips a digest reddens the pairing ("0 found at nothing"), while the arm that moves a recorded line
  number leaves the tree side green and reddens only the ref side — the tree must survive a record that grows,
  the pinned ref is positional by construction. The digest is a MULTISET: one damaged line occurs twice in
  `scene3dSurface.test.ts` and is repaired identically, so rows pair onto distinct tree lines and a row cannot
  claim the same line twice.
- **A repair must be earned.** For each of the 24 fixed sites the gate runs the UNFIXED producer and asks
  what it explains at the ref: measured 19 explain nothing, 5 explain the site only by consuming
  exactly the character the fix supplies, 0 are free. The alternative — a fix that restates a character the
  writer left in place — is named as a failure clause, not tolerated.
- **Files:** `docs/evidence/agents/record-encoding-proof.mjs` (new row, its own budget and repository
  confessions in the first column). No runtime module changed; no test case added.
- **Measured:** Studio 33 files / 509 tests, exit 0, three-runtime 24 files / 543 tests, exit 0, `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 in both; census 0 chargeable over
  464 graded files; ledger 116 rows / 58 sites / 24 fixes (17 GLUE +
  7 CONTROL) split 93-13-10; walk 116/116 image-exactly by M1/M2/M3/M4; arms
  9/9 HIT with the clause names predicted first.
- **Bounds (§60).** The gate grades tracked text plus its own file, and an untracked proof is invisible to
  `git ls-files` — SELF is added and disclosed. It cannot distinguish a corrupted CJK character whose neighbours
  are also CJK, which is the price of the flank rule that keeps `路径` legal; the ref-pinned ledger is the
  backstop for exactly those lines. On a NO-GIT plane the ref half is UNGRADED and the row says so.

### Amendment 238 (M2/v238, docs/evidence/agents) — the flank rule's rescued half becomes a pinned population: 10 bilingual-context lines named by file and line digest, with the writer model as their admission ticket

- **The gap this closes.** Amendment 237 kept the census at zero chargeable lines and disclosed
  10 render sites it refused to charge. The disclosure was a count. Nothing could say WHICH lines, so
  a new render that happened to sit next to real Chinese would have raised the count and changed no verdict —
  exactly the shape the flank rule exists to allow, and the shape this amendment makes auditable.
- **The rule, stated as a rule.** Every line the census sees a registered spelling in is pinned as
  (file, sha16 of the line's bytes, image codepoints, rescue reason), as a MULTISET. Joining the population and
  leaving it are both findings. A pinned image must be producible by the declared writer model, and a pinned
  reason must be a rescue — `REJECTED` — because charges are S2's to report.
- **Measured at rest.** 10 rows over 6 files, one image spelling (U+8def),
  3 of them rescued on both flanks; 0 chargeable lines stay at zero over 464 graded
  files, and the ledger's 116 rows and 17 GLUE + 7 CONTROL fixes are untouched by this change.
- **Why the plant is the witness.** v237's own arms planted this line and observed S2 stay green; the only red
  was the gate's ASCII self-claim. Re-running that plant against S2b turns the first red into
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: S2b no render-bearing line may join the tree unnamed by this pin, naming file and digest. The same battery keeps the old clause honest: an ASCII-flanked writer
  render still reddens S2 first (AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: S2 the tree must carry NO chargeable damage), so the new clause narrows nothing.
- **Files:** `docs/evidence/agents/record-encoding-proof.mjs` (the S2b section and the census carrying line
  bytes). No runtime module changed; no test case added; the sweep's row count is unchanged.
- **Measured:** Studio 33 files / 509 tests, exit 0, three-runtime 24 files / 543 tests, exit 0, `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 in both; arms 8/8 HIT with the
  clause names read from the battery log.
- **Bounds (§60).** The pin names the rescued lines; it does not judge them. A record that rewrites a pinned
  bilingual line must amend the pin in the same grant, and the gate refuses the difference rather than accepting
  a silent rewrite of a line whose bytes are the evidence. Because the pin admits only registry spellings, a
  damage class outside the four declared mechanisms stays invisible to both S2 and S2b — that ceiling belongs to
  the model, and amendment 237 states it.

### Amendment 242 (M7/v242, services/nexus-api) — the PUBLICATION gets an OWNER, and the service enforces CONSISTENCY of a claim without ever claiming to verify it

_Numbering: 242 was free (the ledger topped out at 241). v235 landed the account model and ADR 0018 and
recorded its own remaining half verbatim: _"No publication carries a claim yet:
`publishDocument`/`readPublication`/`DELETE` unchanged."_ This is that half. Full narrative in
`docs/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`; this is the ledger entry._

- **The gap this closes.** Every publication was anonymous, so `DELETE /projects/{id}` checked nothing and
  a remix recorded no lineage. v235 gave the Studio a pure account core (`accounts.ts`) and decided what
  an identity is worth (ADR 0018: option C, an UNSIGNED identity producing a CLAIM). This increment makes
  the service the thing that can finally hold one — as a claim, with the consistency rules a claim can
  support, and with no pretence of verification anywhere.
- **The column is NULLABLE, and that is the whole compatibility story.** `owner_account_id`,
  `owner_handle`, `owner_assurance`, `owner_claimed_at`. Every row written before v242 has no owner, and
  `hasOwner()` answering false is not a special case — it is the pre-v242 rule, deliberately kept:
  *locking an anonymous publication to nobody would make every publication ever written unpublishable by
  anybody*, which is a worse fault than the one this increment fixes. Two new cases pin both directions.
- **Four rules, and the takeover one is the point.** (1) A publish carrying a claim records it, and the
  claim's own instant — `ownerClaimedAt` is the AUTHOR's, not the publish's, and a case asserts they
  differ. (2) A re-publish under the SAME account is the ordinary path: owner kept, version bumped. (3) A
  re-publish under a DIFFERENT account is refused (`OwnerTaken`, 403) and **the row is not saved** — "the
  publication of project X" must have exactly one owner, exactly as it has one row and one current
  version, and letting a second caller quietly become the author of somebody else's work is the fault the
  whole bound was describing. (4) A re-publish naming NOBODY keeps the owner the row already has, because
  a client that stopped naming its author must not silently orphan a publication.
- **The unpublish rule is a comparison, and says so.** `unpublish(projectId, claimerAccountId)`: an owned
  row requires the matching account id (`NotTheOwner`, 403, nothing deleted); an ownerless row may be taken
  down by anyone including a caller who names nobody. `claimerAccountId == null` is the same as naming the
  wrong person for an owned publication. The claim arrives as a **query parameter** — a DELETE with no
  body is the conventional shape.
- **403, not 400, and deliberately not a subtype of `InvalidPublication`.** The request was well-formed, so
  a 400 would tell the caller to fix a field that is fine. `@ExceptionHandler({NotTheOwner.class,
  OwnerTaken.class})` answers 403 with an `error` code of `not-the-owner` or `owner-taken`, so a Studio can
  tell "you may not" from "you would move it" without matching on a sentence.

- **The claim's shape rule, and the ONE assurance this build accepts.** `requireClaimable` refuses by name:
  a blank account id, a blank handle, a handle over 24 characters (the Studio's `HANDLE_RULES.maxLength`),
  a null `claimedAt`, and — the load-bearing one — an assurance outside `{unsigned-local}`. A claim carrying
  `"verified"` would be a claim the client cannot honestly make, because **nothing verified it**, and
  recording it would let a future reader believe something that never happened. `KNOWN_ASSURANCES` is one
  constant: widening that set is what "the service now verifies claims" would MEAN.
- **A defect the suite found before landing.** `requireClaimable` first read
  `!KNOWN_ASSURANCES.contains(claim.assurance())`. `Set.of(...).contains(null)` **throws NPE** rather than
  answering false, so a null assurance crashed the request instead of refusing it — the test expected
  `InvalidPublication` and got `NullPointerException`. The null check now comes first, and the case that
  caught it stays. (The lesson is the repo's own: a membership test is not a null-safe test, and the
  sentence you wrote is not the behaviour you get.)
- **Files:** `PublishedProject.java` (4 nullable columns, `hasOwner`, `isOwnedBy`, package-private
  `claimOwner`), `PublishDtos.java` (`OwnerClaim` record; `Receipt`/`Publication`/`ListingEntry` each carry
  `owner`; `PublishRequest` gains `owner`), `PublishService.java` (`publish(…, OwnerClaim)`,
  `unpublish(…, String claimerAccountId)`, `requireClaimable`, `OwnerTaken`/`NotTheOwner`),
  `PublishController.java` (one `claimOf` mapper for all three answers — three copies would drift, and the
  field that must never drift is `assurance`), `NotTheOwner.java` + `OwnerTaken.java` (new).

- **Measured:** `mvn -o test` → **Tests run: 33, Failures: 0, Errors: 0** (21 existing + 12 new: claim
  recorded, no-claim ownerless, same-account re-publish, different-account refused with nothing saved,
  no-claim keeps the owner, owner may unpublish, stranger refused with nothing deleted, a caller naming
  nobody refused, ownerless unpublishable by anyone and by nobody, an absent project still `false`, every
  malformed-claim field refused by name, and the `"verified"`/null-assurance pair), **BUILD SUCCESS**.
- **Bounds (§60), stated.** A claim is forgeable by anyone who can call the API — the check is the equality
  of two ids, not an identity, and `assurance: 'unsigned-local'` is the field that says so on every answer.
  There are no accounts, sessions, tokens or credentials on the server, and ADR 0018 stays **Proposed**.
  The Studio does not yet SEND a claim: `publishDocument`/`unpublishProject` and the Published panel are
  unchanged in this increment, so the owner column is exercised by tests only until the next one wires the
  lane. Remix lineage is still not recorded. A service-side verification (what would widen
  `KNOWN_ASSURANCES`) is the step this record exists to make honest when it arrives.

### Amendment 243 (design-model/v243) — `validateDocument`: the internal-consistency check the normalized graph always CLAIMED but nothing checked

_Numbering: the ledger skipped 243 (242 was the owner grant, 244 the camera control). This is that record — the code landed first (`f422fc7`, `3c931f8`) and its evidence section is titled `## v243` in `docs/evidence/design-model/README.md`; this entry completes it._

- **The gap.** ADR 0004's normalized graph has INVARIANTS (one root, pages and masters under it, every `childId` resolving to a node that names the parent back), and until v243 **nothing checked them**. Every path that brings a document INTO the model from outside — a remix (v233), a local snapshot (`persist.ts`), an AI batch, hand-edited JSON — handed it straight to the store and the renderer. A malformed graph does not crash: it draws something subtly wrong, which is worse than a refusal.
- **The decision — a VERDICT, never a throw.** `validateDocument(doc: unknown): { ok: true } | { ok: false, problems: { code, detail }[] }` is PURE and TOTAL: it lists EVERY problem, names each by a stable `code`, and never throws — the same rule `normalizeHandle` follows in the account model (a caller shows a person what is wrong rather than catching an exception). It checks shape (id/rootId/activePageId/nodes), the root (`root-missing`/`root-not-document`/`root-has-parent`), every node's identity and parent (`node-id-key-mismatch`, `node-without-parent`, `parent-missing`), both directions of every child link (`child-missing`/`child-parent-disagrees`/`duplicate-child`/`self-child`/`parent-does-not-list-child`), the active page (`active-page-missing`/`active-not-page`), cycles, and reachability (`cycle`/`unreachable`).
- **Three conventions it PINS, one of which the probe caught in this file's own first draft.** (1) A document's children live on the **root NODE's `pageIds`** — a `DesignDocument` has no `pageIds` of its own; the first draft checked `doc.pageIds` and every real document failed `bad-page-ids` until the probe (built from the SHIPPED `ops`) exposed it. (2) A document's `childIds` is a REQUIRED-but-DEAD field that must stay empty (`document-child-ids-used`) — two representations of "the document's children" would be one too many. (3) **`pageIds` is MISNAMED: it holds PAGES and component MASTERS** — a master is added via `addSubtree(doc.rootId, …)`, so it lands in `pageIds` beside the pages (verified: `root.pageIds = ["pg_…", "cmp1"]` after `createComponent`'s op). Consumers filter by `type` (`PageTabs` does), which is why this was never visible — so "every entry of `pageIds` is a page" is FALSE, the check does NOT assert it, and the quirk is recorded as a bound rather than repaired here.
- **A consumer, not a library ornament.** `extractRemixDocument` (`apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.ts`) runs the deep check AFTER its shallow shape checks: a publication whose graph is inconsistent is now refused BY NAME instead of loading into the store and drawing wrong.
- **Measured:** `packages/design-model` **40 → 51** (`validate.test.ts` 11 cases), `tsc` 0 (dist rebuilt); `apps/studio` **516 → 517**, `tsc` 0; `docs/evidence/design-model/validate-proof.mjs` **4/4** — §1 accepts what the model PRODUCES (empty; a rect; a component master under the root — the quirk tolerated; a second page), §2 refuses 14 malformed shapes by code + `unreachable`, §3 total (garbage never throws) and non-mutating, §4 the consumer refuses a graph-inconsistent document.
- **Bounds (§60).** It checks GRAPH consistency, not schema completeness, geometry, tokens or assets — a document can pass and still be an empty design. The `pageIds`-holds-masters misnomer is recorded, not repaired (a rename would touch every reader for no behavioural gain). And only the remix path validates today: `persist.ts`'s snapshot hydrate does not yet call it, which is the natural next consumer.

### Amendment 244 (M5/v244, apps/studio) — the camera set becomes a CONTROL: `addCamera`/`removeCamera` on the surface, and ONE walk behind every figure

_Numbering: the ledger's last committed entry is 241 and the working copy carries **another lane's** entry after it, uncommitted; `v242`/`v243` were taken by those lanes' commits, and the newest of them deliberately deferred its ledger entry. This increment is v244 and takes 244 — version and ledger number agree, and this record claims nothing about entries it is not writing._

- **The gap.** Every camera figure the report carried was a READOUT. `scene.cameras` was walked three separate times to make a count, a name list and an active id, and none of the three is an ADDRESS: to take a camera out of a scene you must say WHICH one, and a name is not one (two cameras can be called the same thing, and `createCamera` happily makes a second). Meanwhile v239 had shipped a runtime `removeCamera` verb with no product caller, so the camera leg's third bus name — `cameraRemoved` — was a subscription to a silence.
- **One walk behind every figure.** `SceneCameraRow { id, name, active }` is the address, the label and the state in one row, and `buildSceneReport` now walks the camera `Map` **once**: `scene.cameraRows` is that walk and `cameras` / `cameraNames` / `activeCamera` are projections read off it. Two walks would be two answers to "what cameras does this scene hold", and only one of them could go stale — the arm that drops `active` from the walk now reddens eleven cases instead of hiding behind a second pass.
- **The authoring pair.** `SceneSurface` gained `addCamera(name)` and `removeCamera(cameraId)`. `addCamera` answers the id and the count the LIVE scene holds, and takes neither the active seat nor an aim: the runtime activates only a scene's FIRST camera, and that seat is what this surface's orbit aims. `removeCamera` answers `SceneCameraRemoval`, a union over `why: 'absent' | 'blocked' | 'unsupported'`.
- **The refusals are ordered, and the common one carries the host's own words.** `unsupported` when the registered host has no removal verb at all (the surface never deletes anything itself), `absent` when the subject is not in the scene the surface last read — decided BEFORE the runtime is asked — `blocked` when the runtime refuses, and `absent` again if a host answers `false` about a row the surface just saw. The runtime's two refusals arrive as THROWS (the active seat; a camera a registered sequence's shot names), so the seam catches and returns `error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)`: v239 wrote those sentences to name the call that unlocks the removal (`setActiveCamera`, `removeCinematic`), and a friendlier paraphrase would be a second, possibly wrong, answer to "why can't I delete this".
- **The product door.** `Scene3D.tsx` renders one row per camera with a `remove` control, a `+ camera` beside `− body`, and the refusal verbatim in `data-scene3d-camera-note` — the panel repeats the runtime's fact instead of inventing a hint.

### Amendment 256 (M5/v256, three-runtime lane) — the SAVE FILE'S ROWS are ordered by CREATION: the SORT was the claim, the random KEY was the defect

_Numbering: measured at HEAD `43f70ef` — this ledger carries 164 `### Amendment` headings with the highest at 255, `git log` over the last 400 subjects puts the highest committed grant LABEL at v255, and `docs/evidence` holds 89 `## v…` sections with the highest at v255, over 278 tracked files in `docs`, `apps/studio/src` and `tools`. So 256 was free in both spaces and this increment takes v256 AND 256 so the git label and the ledger number agree._

- **The job.** Amendment 255's own audit found the defect in this lane's runtime and wrote the mandate into its
  record: "decide whether the sort is the claim (then the key must stop being a random id, or creation order
  must be a filed field) or the pin is wrong, and pin the flip rate either way — 3/6 measured ONCE is not a
  baseline." This grant does all three: re-measures the rate, decides, and pins the rule where a user of the
  runtime is graded by it.
- **The flip rate, re-measured rather than inherited.** Ten runs of `docs/evidence/agents/scene-tools-proof.mjs`
  at rest on identical bytes: **5 red / 10**, one distinct first-red clause, `under the name the file carried`.
  v255 had quoted 3/6 from a single sitting; the two readings agree that the gate is a coin flip and disagree
  about the odds, which is exactly the reason a rate needs more than one sitting.
- **The defect, on the shipped bytes before the fix.** A probe built through the same seam the proofs use
  created 200 bodies in one loop: **183 of 199 adjacent pairs shared a millisecond**, **177 of 200 rows landed
  somewhere other than their creation position**, and the same construction in two processes produced two
  different row orders (`run-vs-run NAME order identical: false`).
- **The correction 255 owes, taken.** Its sentence "a save file for an UNCHANGED scene is not byte-stable
  across saves" is FALSE inside one process — measured, two saves of an unchanged scene from one runtime are
  byte-identical. The instability is ACROSS RUNS. The claim was the right shape with the wrong axis, and a
  later reader of this ledger should not have to discover that by probe.
- **The decision.** The sort IS the claim: a file whose rows arrive in mint order is a file a reader can cite
  as "the first body the author made". Filing creation order as a `SerializedEntity` field would move every
  file reader, the `Serialized*` name census and `SAVE_FILE_VERSION`, and pre-v256 files would still arrive
  random-ordered, so the schema would carry two rules at once. Instead the minted key now carries the order:
  `entity-<ms>-<8-digit per-runtime stamp>-<random tail>`, so lexicographic order IS creation order and the
  tail may never be the segment that decides a row. No schema, no version bump, no name-census churn, and old
  files keep the meaning their rows already had.
- **The shape of the mint.** The counter is per runtime and a restore does not consume it — a loaded body keeps
  the stamp it was born with, which is what makes a made-vs-arrived claim possible at all. Width 8 gives one
  runtime 100,000,000 mints before a stamp outgrows its padding; `Date.now()` at 13 digits holds until 2286;
  both bounds are documented, neither is enforced, and the Bounds row says so rather than leaving the reader
  to find the cliff.
- **The five cases** (`test/saveSnapshot.test.ts`, +112 lines, 161 → 166 in the file): the minted spelling,
  monotonic stamps and a DERIVED padding floor (`at least one same-millisecond pair crosses 9→10` — a zero
  census would grade no padding); 200 bodies filed in creation order by id and by name; two runtimes that
  never spoke producing the same row order; a body MADE first but RESTORED last still filed FIRST while the
  live map holds it last; and the NPC half ordered by the same rule over the same move. The fourth is the only
  case in the repository that separates "ordered by creation" from "left in map order", so the arms that
  delete the `.sort()` land on it and nothing else.
- **Witness arms: 7 predicted, 7 reddened, 3 MATCHED, 4 WIDER.** Every arm re-based from pristine bytes, every
  needle hit exactly once, `threeRuntime.ts` restored to digest `0bed37cffdd313a6` after each. A3/A4 (drop one
  `.sort()`) matched their single predicted case 4/4 and reddened nothing else. A7 (drop the tail) matched case
  1 4/4 — and its one collateral red, a v136 case that compares ids minted by two different runtimes, appeared
  in 1 of 4 observations, which is the collision the tail exists to prevent; the runner elided the refusal's
  own sentence, so this record does not claim which pair collided. **Four predictions missed, all WIDER, all
  from one fact the predictions got wrong:** cases 4 and 5 compare a body made early with bodies made late,
  and whether early and late fall in different milliseconds is decided by the machine, so a
  stamp-destroying arm reddens them at a rate. A1/A3/A6/A7 were therefore re-run three extra times each:

### Amendment 257 (v257, apps/studio) — the SNAPSHOT hydrate validates before it loads: v243's bound, closed

- **The bound v243 stated.** `validateDocument` (v243) shipped wired into the REMIX path only, and its record named the natural next consumer: *"`persist.ts`'s snapshot hydrate does not yet call it."* A local snapshot is the OTHER way a document enters the model from outside, and `deserializeApp`'s checks were SHALLOW — a foreign app, an unsupported version/schema, a missing root, no resolvable page — and said nothing about whether the graph was CONSISTENT. A snapshot whose `childIds` name nodes it does not hold, or whose parent disagrees with its child, passed those checks and loaded.
- **The fix — one call, after the shallow reasons.** `deserializeApp` now runs `validateDocument(doc)` after its existing checks and refuses with `snapshot graph is inconsistent: <first detail> (+N more)`. The shallow reasons stay FIRST, so a missing root or page is still reported in its friendlier words; only a document that passes them reaches the deep check.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/persist.ts` (the import + the call), `apps/studio/src/lib/persist.test.ts` (+1 case: a shape-valid snapshot with a dangling `childId` is refused by name).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **725 → 726** (43 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`), `persist.test.ts` **13/13**, `tsc -p tsconfig.json` exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** Only the SNAPSHOT path validates: the in-memory AI batch path (`generate`/`editSelection` → `history.dispatch`) does not, because an `OpBatch` is applied through the model's own ops (which refuse a malformed op) rather than a whole document being adopted. A refused snapshot starts the Studio FRESH — the user's broken document is not loaded, and the refusal names the problem rather than silently discarding it. And the doc gate's §7 title arm is currently THROWING on its own self-test precondition (`table-recount-proof.mjs`, the landmine the studio README records), so this record's title is verified by `grep`, not by that door.

### Amendment 258 (gate/v258, docs/evidence/agents) — the §7 title arm THREW on a heading style it assumed: it now asserts the CREDIT and says when the dash axis is unverified

- **The defect, met while verifying v243/v257.** §7's title arm picks the first record HOLE (`c.hole[0]`), builds a house-style title from that hole's OWN ledger heading, and asserted `!EXPLICIT.has(t4)` — that the EXPLICIT mention grammar REFUSES the phrase. That is true only for the OLD house style `## Amendment N — vN: …`, whose em dash the grammar's negative lookahead refuses. Newer headings are parenthesised (`### Amendment 242 (M7/v242, …)`), which EXPLICIT **accepts** — so when the hole's heading was 242 the assertion threw on a TRUE statement about a different door: `this arm's meaning depends on the mention grammar refusing the house-style dash after 242`. The studio README's v255 section had already measured this landmine ("the door now throws deterministically at line 535 instead of refusing at line 490"); this is its repair.
- **The fix — assert the CLAIM, not the mechanism.** The arm's real claim is that a house-style title **credits** the number (and so closes the hole). WHICH reader credits it depends on the heading's style, so the arm now asserts `credited.has(t4)` (version label OR amendment phrase — always true), and pins the dash rule ONLY when the heading is actually dash-ended (`if (dashEnded) assert RECORD.has(t4)`). When every hole is parenthesised it prints `DASH axis is UNVERIFIED this run` rather than pretending it measured it — the same "say so instead of claiming a caught mutation" rule the surrounding arms already follow.
- **Files:** `docs/evidence/agents/table-recount-proof.mjs` (the conditional mechanism + the console line).
- **Measured (gate exit 0):** `[§7] ledger headings 250 · dangling explicit citations 0 · the newest grant 257 IS titled`; `caught the ledger's own house-style title for 242 appears in the README → the title hole shrinks by exactly one, credited through the amendment phrase (this heading is parenthesised, so the DASH axis is UNVERIFIED this run)`; the prose arm, the sole-site scrub, the within-a-line arm and the newest-grant arm all still fire. `[§4] failing TRACKED cases: 0 · runtime 57903ms exit 0 · exec-host 31244ms exit 0`.
- **Bounds (§60).** The dash rule is NOT verified on a corpus whose holes are all parenthesised — the arm says so instead of inventing a subject. A future cycle with a dash-ended hole re-verifies it automatically. And the arm still depends on the hole's heading carrying a version label (`vN`); a heading with none would fail the `credited` assertion, which is the honest outcome (that heading would be untitleable by this door).

### Amendment 259 (M7 v259, apps/studio) — the ACCOUNT FACE: session verbs over the current-device record, and the panel that finally calls them

- **The gap.** Amendment 252 gave this device a persisted `AccountRecord` and the publish lane learned to send it as an owner CLAIM — but **nothing in the product could SET one**: `setCurrentAccount` had no caller anywhere in the app, so the claim the lane sends could only ever be built for an account no user could create. That is plan item 27's UI half, and this is it.
- **The session seam.** `apps/studio/src/lib/accountSession.ts` composes the two pieces that already exist — `accounts.ts`'s pure rules and `currentAccount.ts`'s storage boundary — into the four verbs a face needs: `register`, `rename`, `signOut`, `current`. The clock, the randomness and the store are injected (ADR 0002's testability), so an id and an instant in a test are known values. The refusals are the point: `register` **REFUSES when an account is already set** (`an account is already set on this device — sign out first`) rather than silently replacing someone's local identity; `rename` changes the display name ONLY (id, handle, `createdAt` and `assurance` are pinned, because the id was derived from the handle and a seed); and the DEVICE SEED is persisted under its own key and **kept across `signOut`**, so re-registering the same handle on the same device yields the SAME id — `signOut` forgets the name, not the device.
- **The panel.** `apps/studio/src/components/AccountPanel.tsx` holds NO storage logic of its own: every verb is a session call and every refusal is shown verbatim. It renders `assurance: 'unsigned-local'` from the record itself, because ADR 0018 records that a "signed in" badge would be a lie in this build. `Toolbar.tsx` gains one account control (👤) that toggles the panel, beside Publish/Published/Explore.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/accountSession.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/lib/accountSession.test.ts` (new, 13 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/AccountPanel.tsx` (new), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the control + the mounted panel).
- **The HEAD this grant repairs, measured before it landed.** The account-session SUITE was committed first (`0c30934 prep(stage identity): accountSession/currentAccount refusal and boundary edge tests`) and **the module it imports was not** — `git ls-tree HEAD --name-only apps/studio/src/lib/` carried `accountSession.test.ts` and no `accountSession.ts`. So the repository's HEAD did not typecheck and could not collect that suite: a fresh clone of HEAD was **red**, and the green 817/817 the working tree showed was the WORKING TREE's, not HEAD's. This is the same class the ledger records elsewhere (a test that landed before the thing it tests), and it is why the record names the module as part of its own files: the grant is only real once the module is IN the tree, and it is now.
- **Measured:** `accountSession.test.ts` **13/13**; `apps/studio` **817/817** (43 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`; the number is the SHARED working tree's, and this increment's own delta is the 13 account-session cases); `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**.
- **Bounds (§60).** No password, no token, no session, no signature, no cryptography (ADR 0018) — the record is a name this DEVICE chose, and the service still enforces nothing but claim CONSISTENCY. ONE account per device: a second `register` refuses, so there is no roster, no account switch and no import of an account from another device. The panel is **type-checked only** — this repository has no DOM test, so the wiring `Toolbar → AccountPanel → accountSession` is not exercised by a browser harness, and the storage boundary that IS exercised is the one behind the session. The display name is not unique and may be anything; the HANDLE is the identity.

### Amendment 260 (M5/v260, apps/studio) — the CAMERA SEAT is a CONTROL, and the orbit aims the camera the frame DRAWS

- **The gap, measured on the shipped bytes.** `aim()` resolved `built.cameraId` — the camera the surface COMPOSED — while `animate()` renders from `scene.cameras.find(c => c.active)`. With the seat moved to a second camera, one drag wrote the first: the probe printed `aimed camera-6, drawn camera-7`. And v244’s `removeCamera` refusal told the user to `call setActiveCamera first` when no control on the panel performed that call.
- **The mechanism.** `seatOf()` reads the live active row of the scene this surface owns; `aim()` resolves `seatOf() ?? built.cameraId`, so a single-camera scene changes by nothing and a scene with no seat at all keeps a view it can still orbit. `activateCamera(cameraId): SceneCameraActivation` is lookup-before-asking: `unsupported` when the host has no `setActiveCamera` verb (declared optional on the seam), `absent` when this surface’s registry does not hold the id — WITHOUT asking the host — and `absent` when the host answers `false`. On success it aims the NEW seat with the orbit already held (the handover, so the view does not jump to a fresh camera standing at the origin looking down -Z) and answers `{ ok: true, cameraId, activeCamera: seatOf() }`: the answer is the scene’s truth, not the request. `surface.cameraId` stays the address the surface was composed under.
- **The panel.** `onActivateCamera` and a `data-scene3d-camera-activate` button inside a `{!c.active && (` guard — offered on the rows that do not hold the seat and on no row that does — with the refusal shown as `${answer.why}: ${answer.reason}` in `data-scene3d-camera-note` and a `surface.report()` re-read after every row ask.
