The arm-A prediction first named 3 and the hand-run measured 4; the extra case is the idempotent one, which also aims the seat. Files restored byte-identical after every arm.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts` (the seam verb, `SceneCameraActivation`, `seatOf`, the re-pointed `aim`, the `activateCamera` implementation), `apps/studio/src/components/Scene3D.tsx` (handler + guarded row control + note), `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.test.ts`, `apps/studio/src/lib/surface.test.ts`, `docs/evidence/studio/scene-surface-proof.mjs` (§5b), `docs/evidence/studio/README.md` (this grant’s section).

- **Bounds (§60).** One active row per scene is the runtime’s invariant and this seam only reads it — a host that leaves a scene naming no seat is answered `activeCamera: null` and aimed at the composed row. `activateCamera` grants seats INSIDE the surface’s own scene; it is not a cross-scene switch and the surface has no verb that changes which scene the panel reads. ### Amendment 261 (M5/v261, apps/studio) — the SCENE SEAT is a CONTROL, and every write follows the world on screen

- **The gap, measured on the shipped bytes.** v260 closed this disagreement for the CAMERA: the surface resolved the row it aimed from the one it COMPOSED, while the runtime draws, picks and walks off the row the graph flags active. The SCENE was the same disagreement one level up, and it was still open — `buildSceneReport` read `graph.activeSceneId` (the world the frame draws) while every WRITE named `built.sceneId` (the world the surface composed). With the seat moved out of band, the shipped bytes answered: one drag aimed the composed world's camera while the frame drew a different world entirely; the camera rows the panel listed were refused by that panel's own remove button as `not in scene …`; `save()` wrote the four demo bodies while the person was looking at one other body; and `setLight` changed a light no report was reading. The count and the address were two reads of one Map as well, so a panel could print "2 scenes" and name an active one that was not in the list it drew.
- **The mechanism.** `liveSceneId()` reads the graph's active row and falls back to the composed world when the graph names none, and every write verb resolves through it — the light, the rename, the hide, the component toggle, the camera pair, the seat handover, the pick ray and the saved file. `aim()`'s composed-camera fallback became SCENE-CONDITIONAL, because `built.cameraId` is a camera of the composed world and aiming it while looking at another one is the same cross-scene bug one line deeper. `buildSceneReport` now walks the graph's Map ONCE: `sceneRows` is the single read behind the rows, the count (`scenes === sceneRows.length`) and the active address — the same shape v244 gave the camera set, so a count and an address that come from different reads can no longer disagree in front of the person being shown both.
- **The verb.** `activateScene(sceneId): SceneSceneActivation` is lookup-before-asking in the same shape as v260's `activateCamera`, and its refusals are DATA: `unsupported` when the host has no `setActiveScene` (the seam declares it optional), `absent` for an id the graph does not hold — WITHOUT asking the host — and `absent` for a host that answers `false`. There is no `blocked` arm, and the reason is stronger than it was for the camera seat: the runtime's `setActiveScene` refuses nothing that exists, so there is no invariant for a refusal to protect. On success it does three things beyond the runtime's write: it re-aims the new world's camera with the orbit the person ALREADY HOLDS (the handover, so the view does not jump to a fresh camera standing at the origin looking down -Z), it CLEARS the pick (a selection is a body in a scene, and the new world does not hold it), and it answers `{ ok: true, sceneId, activeSceneId, aimed }` — the graph's own answer after the ask, not the request.
- **The panel.** `Scene3D.tsx` adds `onActivateScene` and a `data-scene3d-scene-activate` button inside a `{!r.active && (` guard — offered on the rows that do not hold the seat and on no row that does, because a control that cannot change anything misreports itself. Each row names its world and how many bodies are in it, because two worlds otherwise differ on screen only by a name. The refusal is shown in the surface's own words in `data-scene3d-scene-note`, in its OWN slot: a scene refusal and a camera refusal can be on screen about different rows at the same time.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts` (the seam verb `activateScene`, the `SceneSceneRow`/`SceneSceneActivation` types, `liveSceneId()`, the re-pointed writes, the ONE walk behind `sceneRows`), `apps/studio/src/components/Scene3D.tsx` (handler + guarded row control + note), `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.test.ts` (+13), `apps/studio/src/lib/surface.test.ts` (+3), `docs/evidence/studio/scene-surface-proof.mjs` (a new §9 over the real runtime), `docs/evidence/studio/README.md` (this grant's section).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **817/817** (43 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`; the number is the SHARED working tree's, and this increment's own delta is the 16 new cases); `scene3d.test.ts` **138** (125 → 138); `surface.test.ts` **24** (21 → 24); `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json --noEmit` **exit 0**; `node docs/evidence/studio/scene-surface-proof.mjs` **exit 0**, with the new §9 printing `3 worlds in the graph, walked once, each row counting its own 4/5/0 bodies` and `switching aimed camera-… with the held view … and the very next frame carried THAT scene and THAT camera to the backend`.
- **Witness arms: 9/9 matched, 0 prediction misses, and arm D's arithmetic is recorded because it did not come out as predicted.** The battery sits OUTSIDE the working tree (`nexus-v261-arms/`) so no file-walking census counts it; baseline (proof exit 0, units exit 0, 0 failed test lines) then one spliced production expression per arm, BOTH planes run, the predicted red required, the file's own bytes restored and proved by sha256 (`3df9d6d3b460`, `41487ae64118`). A/B/E/F re-point one write (the pick ray, the saved file, `addCamera`, `setLight`) at `built.sceneId`, C deletes the handover's `aim();`, G deletes `selected = null;` — each reddened exactly 1 unit case plus the §9 clause named for that write, with §1..§7 still green: the older legs cannot see this defect. ### Amendment 262 (v262, apps/studio) — the reserved `_lineage` key reads through ONE guarded reader, and the studio's `tsc` RED is closed

- **The defect, measured.** v245/v247 taught EXPLORE and the artifact page to read the service-written `_lineage.sourceProjectId` back off a fetched document, each with its own hand-rolled guard chain — and **neither chain typechecked**. The key is not a member of `DesignDocument`, so `doc._lineage` is `TS2339`; and on the other route `typeof x === 'object'` narrows `unknown` to `object`, on which `.sourceProjectId` is also `TS2339`. `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json --noEmit` was **exit 2 with 14 errors** at HEAD (6 in the two routes, 8 in `scene3dSurface.test.ts`, which read `refused.why` / `refused.reason` on a union that `expect(refused.ok).toBe(false)` asserts about but does NOT narrow). A red type check had been assumed green because the suite was green — the suite runs the files anyway, because vitest does not typecheck.
- **The fix — one reader, and guards that NARROW.** `apps/studio/src/lib/lineage.ts` exports `readRemixedFrom(document: unknown): string | null`: it takes `unknown` because that is what a fetched document IS before anyone has proven it a `DesignDocument`, guards every property access, and answers `null` for a non-object, an absent/rotten `_lineage`, or a missing/non-string/empty `sourceProjectId` — never a throw, and never an empty string a card would render as `remixed from `. Both routes now call it (the explore route and the artifact route), so the rule exists once. In `scene3dSurface.test.ts` the four union reads now narrow with an explicit `if (refused.ok) throw new Error(...)` guard, which both proves the branch and teaches the compiler the type.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/lineage.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/lib/lineage.test.ts` (new, 7 cases), `apps/studio/src/app/explore/route.ts`, `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts`, `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3dSurface.test.ts` (4 narrowing guards).

The renumbering is a change of LABEL only: the grant, its files, its measurements and its bounds are the same ones the draft carried.

A lineage the service never wrote is simply `null`, which is the same answer a first publish gives — the card cannot tell "not a remix" from "remix whose source was deleted", and today neither can the service.

### Amendment 263 (M7/v263, apps/studio + services/nexus-api) — the ACCOUNT you set is the CLAIM you publish, and the claim's instant is read in the client's own unit

- **The gap, measured on the shipped bytes.** Amendment 252 gave this device a persisted account and 253 taught the publish lane to carry an owner claim — but **nothing in the product ever supplied one**: `Toolbar.tsx` called `publishProject(doc.id, doc.name, doc)` with no owner and `unpublish(projectId)` with no claimer, so the claim plumbing existed end to end and was fed nothing. Three consequences, all real: every publication the Studio made was **OWNERLESS**, so the byline that v245/v246 put on `/explore` and `/p/{id}` could never appear for a Studio's own work; anyone could take anyone's publication down (the service's pre-v242 rule for a row that names nobody); and the account face v259 landed — a panel that set a local identity and changed **nothing** about what you publish as. A control that cannot change the thing it names is the failure this repo keeps meeting.
- **The fix — the rule lives in ONE place, so no caller can forget it.** `publishLane.ts` gains a `ClaimSource` seam (`current()` + `now()`, injected per ADR 0002) and `claimOf(source?)`, which reads the **same** `currentAccount` record the account panel writes. `publishProject` attaches `owner ?? claimOf(source)` and `unpublish` attaches `claimer ?? claimOf(source)?.accountId`; an explicitly named claim still WINS, because a caller that names a claim means it. The Toolbar's two calls are **unchanged** — that is the point: the rule is no longer something a caller has to remember.
- **The consequence, measured over the REAL service** (a new §10 in `docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs`, over a throwaway PostgreSQL and the built jar): a publish carrying a claim is **OWNED** — the receipt and the listing both name the account, the handle and the assurance; a take-down by ANOTHER account is **403 `not-the-owner`**; a take-down naming **nobody** is 403 too (on an owned row, "named nobody" is "named the wrong person"); the **owner's** take-down is 200; a re-publish under a **different** account is **403 `owner-taken`** while the same account's re-publish is 200 at version 2; and a publish naming **nobody** stays ownerless and open to anybody — the pre-v242 rule, still in force, and this section exists partly to prove it was not quietly broken.
- **The defect the wiring exposed, measured before it was fixed.** The claim's **INSTANT** had never been exercised, because nothing had ever sent a claim. The client states `claimedAt` as epoch **MILLISECONDS**; the service's `OwnerClaim` record declared it an `Instant` while its own docstring said it mirrored the client's shape — and Jackson reads a bare JSON number as epoch **SECONDS**. So the Studio's `1700000000000` (2023-11-14) was deserialized as **`+55840-11-08T22:13:20Z`** and STORED that way: a fact the system of record held about when a claim was made, wrong by **53,817 years**, silently, because the unit was a comment nobody had checked against the wire. The service now reads the client's unit (`Long claimedAt`, documented in the record) and writes it back in the same unit, so **the claim that comes back is the claim that went in**. Measured before: `+55840-11-08T22:13:20Z`. Measured after: `1700000000000`.
- **A rule removed rather than kept — the range guard that could not fire.** The first draft refused a claimed instant that is not representable. It can never fire: every `long` number of milliseconds is inside `Instant`'s range (±292 million years against ±1 billion), so the guard was a comment pretending to be a check. It is gone, and the service does **not** compare the claimed instant against its own clock — the assurance rule says this service records claims and verifies nothing, and the instant is part of the claim. The suite pins the non-verification as a fact (`anInstantTheServiceCannotCheckIsStillRecordedBecauseAClaimIsAClaim`).
- **The panel.** The Published row names its owner and says **"yours"** when that owner is this device's account; a row that names nobody says "by nobody". The lane's listing entry carries the owner, which the service has always sent and the lane used to DROP. A take-down the service refuses is now explainable — and a refusal the user cannot explain is a refusal the user cannot act on.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/publishLane.ts` (the `ClaimSource` seam, `claimOf`, the two attachments, the listing's `owner`), `apps/studio/src/lib/publishClaim.test.ts` (new, 7 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the owner line), `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/publish/PublishDtos.java` (the record's unit), `.../PublishService.java` (the conversion at the storage boundary), `.../PublishController.java` (the answer in the same unit), `.../PublishServiceTest.java` (+2 cases), `docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs` (a new §10).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **801/801** (43 files under `--no-file-parallelism`; the number excludes `monetization.test.ts`, which is a CONCURRENT lane's in-flight file and was red and mid-edit throughout this increment — not this increment's); `publishClaim.test.ts` **7/7**; `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0** on every file this increment touched; `services/nexus-api` **43/43** (41 + 2), `BUILD SUCCESS`; `node docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs` **exit 0**, with §10 printing the measured instant `1700000000000` and the whole owner chain.
- **Landing note (v263).** This increment's bytes landed in a commit named for ANOTHER increment — `320e279 prep(stage monetization): subscriptionDaysLeftText N/A/Expired/critical tests` — because a concurrent lane staged with a broad `git add` and swept the already-staged files in with its own. The content is this record's: the lane, its cases, the panel line, the service's unit, the proof's §10 and this ledger entry are all in that commit, and nothing of the other increment's subject is mixed into the code. The commit MESSAGE is the thing that does not describe what it carries, so this note is here to make the ledger the authority — and the lesson is the one `docs/evidence/type-gate` already writes down: an unstaged foreign change is one broad `git add` away from an unrelated commit, which is why every increment here stages by NAME.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service still **verifies nothing**: `unsigned-local` is the only assurance it accepts, it does not check that the account exists, and a claim is forgeable by anyone who can call the API (ADR 0018). The claim is an **owner, not an identity** — it decides who may take a publication down and whose name is on it, and it does not authenticate anybody. A device with no account publishes **anonymously** and may take down only ownerless rows; that is the pre-v242 rule, unchanged and re-measured. The account is per-browser, so one human on two devices is two accounts and two owners. The listing carries the owner, but the **artifact page and `/explore` already read it** (v245/v246), so the byline is now real for the first time; the Studio's own Published panel is the one surface that had to learn to show it.

### Amendment 264 (M7/v264, apps/studio + tools/harness) — the ACCOUNT FACE is driven in a REAL browser, and the bound that said "type-checked only" is closed

- **The bound this grant closes, quoted.** Amendment 259's own record ended: *"The panel is **type-checked only** — this repository has no DOM test, so the wiring `Toolbar → AccountPanel → accountSession` is not exercised by a browser harness, and the storage boundary that IS exercised is the one behind the session."* A wiring that no browser ever ran is a wiring that has never been shown to work; the 13 unit cases grade the session and the store, and nothing graded the three of them **together**.
- **The harness.** `tools/harness/studio-account.mjs` drives the REAL bundle in a REAL Chrome over the CDP pipe (ADR 0017) against the REAL dev server, and adds `npm run verify:account` — the fourth surface harness, beside `verify:scene`, `verify:assets` and `verify:world`. It owns two localStorage keys and clears them itself, so a run starts from a known state and says so rather than assuming a fresh profile.
- **What it grades, and what each assertion is really about.** §1 the account control is on the toolbar and the panel opens (the wiring itself). §2 registering writes a **real record into this origin's storage** — an id, the handle, the display name, an instant and the assurance — and the panel shows the handle and the assurance. §3 the page carries **NO "signed in" badge**: ADR 0018 records that one would be a lie in this build, and a rule nobody checks is a rule that decays. §4 while an account is set the panel offers **NO create control** — one account per device is **structural** here, not a message, and the session's own refusal (`sign out first`) is therefore unreachable *through the panel*; it is still graded by the unit suite, and the panel's shape is what makes it unreachable. §5 a rename changes the **display name only**: the id, the handle and the instant are pinned. §6 signing out forgets the **name** and keeps the **device seed** — signing out is not a factory reset. §7 re-registering the same handle on the same device yields the **SAME id**, which is the whole promise of "this device publishes as". §8 the run raises no console errors.
- **Measured:** `node tools/harness/studio-account.mjs --url http://127.0.0.1:3210` — **14/14 assertions passed**, 1 console message and 0 errors, against the real dev server on port 3210.
- **The three failures the harness found in ITSELF, and what they were.** `countOf` passed an arrow function to `evaluate` instead of calling it, so the door's own count came back as `{}`; the device seed was read through a JSON parser that could not parse a plain string, so a present seed read as "unparsable"; and the re-register step tried to create an account with an empty handle, which the session **correctly refused** — the harness was wrong, not the product, and it now types the handle again, which is the path a person takes. The first of the three is the same class as the ledger's own "a test that asserts a behaviour the behaviour does not implement": a harness that grades nothing is worse than no harness, because it reads as coverage.
- **Bounds (§60).** The harness proves the CLIENT half: that the panel writes the record, shows the handle and the assurance, keeps the device seed, and offers no second account. It does **not** prove that the claim reaches the service — that is the publish proof's §10 (amendment 263), over the real service and a real database. It runs against a dev server, not a production build; it needs a Chrome and a running `next dev`; and it asserts on the DOM's own words, so a panel that reworded itself would fail the harness rather than pass it silently. There is still **no verification**: the record says `unsigned-local` and the service records claims without checking them (ADR 0018).

### Amendment 265 (M7/v265, apps/studio) — the BYLINE reaches the page: the service-answer → card mapping moves into the pure half, and the whole path is graded

- **The gap, found by looking for what was NOT tested.** The explore renderer had byline cases (`by ada · unsigned-local`, escaped, absent for an unowned row), so the byline was **renderable**. What had no test at all was the step that FEEDS it: the route turned the service's listing row into a card, and that mapping — which decides whether the owner survives the trip — lived in `app/explore/route.ts`, where nothing could assert it. A renderer that can draw a byline and a page that never receives one look identical from the outside. This is not hypothetical: v263 found the **publish lane** already dropping the listing's owner on its way to a page, and the same shape of drop was one line away here.
- **The fix — the mapping is the pure half's job, and there is exactly ONE.** `explore.ts` gains `toExploreItem(row, read, thumbnail)`: the whole service-answer → card mapping, with the owner's reduction stated where it happens (the service sends the WHOLE claim — account id, handle, assurance, instant — and the card shows two of those fields), the lineage read moved out of the route and into the same function, and the "why there is no thumbnail" note kept. The route is now a thin caller: list, read each row, draw, `toExploreItem(row, read, thumbnail)`, render.
- **Two guards that NARROW, in the repo's v262 pattern.** A **malformed** owner — a handle that is not a string, an assurance that is not one — is shown as **NO owner**, never as `by undefined`: a card that says "by undefined" is worse than a card that says nothing, and both are true. And a document that carries no `_lineage` yields no source, because the lineage reader (v262) already answers `null` for every shape that is not a lineage.
- **The route can no longer grow a second mapping.** The explore proof's §3 now asserts that the route calls `toExploreItem(row, read, thumbnail)` **and** that it does NOT map the owner itself (`owner: row.owner` is refused) — because a second mapping is a second chance to drop it, and a hand-written mapping in a handler is exactly what went unasserted.
- **A new §5 in the explore proof grades the WHOLE path**: the service's own answer shape in, the page's HTML out. An owned row shows `by ada · unsigned-local`; a row the service recorded **no** owner for shows **no** byline; a **malformed** owner shows none rather than a broken one; and a remixed publication still names its source. The proof's own module loader had to learn the new sibling import (`./lineage` is now stripped into the box beside it) — a missing sibling would have been an unresolved import rather than a graded failure, which is why the loader is part of the record.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.ts` (the `ExploreRow`/`ExploreDocumentRead` types and `toExploreItem`), `apps/studio/src/app/explore/route.ts` (the thin call), `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.test.ts` (+6 cases over the mapping), `docs/evidence/m7/explore-proof.mjs` (§3's two new assertions + a new §5).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **851/851** (44 files, accurate under `--no-file-parallelism`); `explore.test.ts` + `lineage.test.ts` **31/31**; `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**; `node docs/evidence/m7/explore-proof.mjs` **exit 0**, with §5 printing the byline path and §3 printing the pure mapping.
- **Bounds (§60).** This proves the CLIENT half of the byline: the service's answer becomes a card, and the card becomes a page that says who published it. It does **not** prove the service records an owner for a publication made in a browser — that is the publish proof's §10 (amendment 263), over the real service and a real database. The artifact page's own byline path was already in a testable module (`publishServer.ts` reduces the service's answer before the route sees it) and is not changed here. The byline is a **claim**, not a verified identity: it says `unsigned-local` next to the name, and the service verifies nothing (ADR 0018).

### Amendment 266 (M7/v266, tools/harness) — the OWNERSHIP chain in a REAL browser: a claim set by hand reaches the service, becomes a byline on the public page, and makes a take-down REFUSABLE

- **What this grant closes, and why it was still open.** The ownership story had been proven in three places and none of them was the product: the service recorded a claim (§10 of the publish proof, over a real database), the lane attached the device's claim (unit cases over the wire), and the page rendered a byline (the pure mapping, v265). **Nobody had driven the three together through a real browser**: set an account by hand, press Publish, and watch the service record an owner, the public gallery show the byline, and a take-down by a device with no account be refused. Each half being proven is not the whole being proven — the whole is the seam between them, and the seam is where the owner was already dropped once (v263's lane).
- **The harness now proves the chain, in the ORDER a person walks it.** §3.5 the account panel opens on the toolbar, a handle is typed, and the record lands in the origin's storage with `assurance: 'unsigned-local'` — and the page carries **no "signed in" badge** (ADR 0018: one would be a lie). The account is set **before** the publish, because a publication made with no account is ownerless, and an ownerless publication can show no byline, refuse no take-down and be taken over by anybody: the whole story is only reachable with an account in place. §4.5 the SERVICE, read independently of the browser, carries the **owner** — the account id, the handle and the assurance — and the claim's **instant** is the client's own millisecond value, not the same number read as seconds (the defect v263 measured and fixed). §7.5 the public gallery (`/explore`, the Studio's own route) answers 200 and the card for THIS project carries `by <handle> · unsigned-local`. §9 the published list names the owner on the row and says **"yours"**; then the device **signs out** and presses "take down", and the service **REFUSES** (`not-the-owner`, named in the panel's own note) and the publication is **still there** — a refused take-down takes nothing down; then the device **signs back in** and the owner takes their own publication down, which is the pre-v266 behaviour and the post-v266 behaviour at once.
- **The byline is read over HTTP, not asserted from the browser's memory.** The gallery is fetched from the Studio's route and the HTML is checked for the byline text and for `data-explore-card="<projectId>"` — so the card is the RIGHT card, not some other publication's byline on the same page.
- **What the first runs of this grant found in ITSELF, recorded rather than hidden.** Three of its own assumptions were wrong, and all three are the kind that a harness that never ran would have shipped. (1) The account record was read into a **block-scoped** `const`, so the later section that needed it threw `ReferenceError: record is not defined` — a harness that crashes on its own scoping is a harness that grades nothing. (2) The refusal assertion looked for the service's error **code** (`not-the-owner`), while the Studio's route deliberately keeps only the service's **message** — so the rule reaches the user as the service's own prose ("a caller that is not that account may not take it down"), which is the more useful of the two; the assertion now asks for the rule in the words the user actually sees. (3) The instant assertion compared the account's `createdAt` with the claim's `claimedAt` and called them the same fact — they are **two different instants** (when the account was made, and when the claim was made), and the first run failed on a true statement about the wrong thing. What the assertion should say is the UNIT: the value must be a number in the client's milliseconds and must read as a real instant. Read as epoch seconds it would carry the same digits and the year 55840, so the corrected assertion (a number, a year ≥ 2020, and within an hour of the browser's clock) still catches the defect v263 measured.
- **Files:** `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (§3.5 the account, §4.5 the recorded owner, §7.5 the byline, §9 the refused and the permitted take-down).
- **Measured:** `node tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` — the three layers stood up (a throwaway PostgreSQL, the built jar, and the real Studio on its own port), the whole chain driven in a REAL Chrome. The assertion count and the failures, if any, are printed by the run itself.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service still **verifies nothing**: `unsigned-local` is the only assurance it accepts and it does not check that the account exists, so the byline says what the claim is worth rather than pretending it is an identity (ADR 0018). The refusal is a **refusal of a take-down**, not an authentication: a caller that forged a claim naming the owner's account id could still take the publication down, and this grant does not claim otherwise. The device is a browser with a localStorage, so "the owner" is "the account id this browser holds" and nothing more. The account is **one per browser**: the harness signs out and back in rather than switching, because there is no roster and no switch (v259's stated bound).

### Amendment 267 (M7/v267, apps/studio + packages/design-model) — a REMIX records its LINEAGE: the writing half joins the reading half, and the reserved key becomes part of the format

- **The gap, found by asking what a remix actually IS in this product.** The lineage had a **reading** half (v245/v246 read `_lineage.sourceProjectId` back off a published document; v262 gave it ONE guarded reader) and a **writing** half on the SERVICE (its `remix` endpoint writes `_lineage { sourceProjectId, remixedAt }` into the document JSON). But **the Studio never called the service's remix endpoint** — the route speaks `publish | read | unpublish | list` and `publishServer.ts` has no remix function at all. The Studio's remix is a **FORK IN THE EDITOR**: it reads a publication back, forks the document, and the person publishes the fork. So a publication made the way a person actually remixes carried **no source at all**, and the "remixed from" link v251 made clickable could never appear on it. The reading half and the writing half existed, and the path a remix actually takes had neither.
- **The fix — ONE module owns both halves, and the key is part of the format.** `lineage.ts` gains `stampLineage(document, sourceProjectId, remixedAt)`: PURE (a new document; the caller's own is never touched), **OVERWRITING** any lineage the document carried, and **REFUSING** a blank source or a blank instant by throwing. The store's `remixDocument(doc, source, remixedAt)` stamps the fork, and **the caller names the instant** (the store owns no clock) — the panel and the visitor path both pass `new Date().toISOString()`. The reserved key is now declared in the **canonical model** (`DesignDocument._lineage` and `DocumentLineage`), so it stopped being a convention three parties kept separately and became part of the document format.
- **Why the stamp OVERWRITES, which is the subtle half.** `forkDocument` SPREADS the document, so a copy inherits the lineage of the copy it was made from — and that inherited value names the **wrong** source. A remix of a remix must name **its own** source; the copy it was made from keeps its own, and that is exactly what the new cases pin.
- **Why a blank source THROWS rather than being written.** A lineage that names nothing is a claim about a provenance that does not exist, and the reader would render it as `remixed from ` — the same reason `forkDocument` throws for a root it cannot find: a document that cannot say where it came from is a fact, not a blank.
- **Two proofs that were RED at HEAD, found by running the lane's own gate — and the loader lesson they carry.** `npm run verify:remix` — the remix lane's OWN gate — did not run, for two separate reasons: (1) the module loader stripped `artifact.ts` but never `pageShell.ts`, which `artifact.ts` imports, so the box could not resolve it — an **unresolved import**, not a graded failure; and (2) §6 asserted that the lane's *whole* model import was `import type`, which was never true, because the lane calls `validateDocument` as a **value**. The assertion now says what is true: the `DesignDocument` TYPE is imported type-only, and `validateDocument` is called as a value. Separately, v263 gave `publishLane.ts` a **value** import of `accounts.ts` and `currentAccount.ts`, which broke the loaders of the remix proof AND the validate proof the same way — and the lesson is an ORDER: `strip` writes a module and **imports it in the same step**, so a module's own siblings must already be in the box. A proof that cannot resolve an import is not a passing proof; it is a proof that stopped running, and the two of them had stopped running long before this grant.
- **Files:** `packages/design-model/src/types.ts` (`DocumentLineage` and the reserved `_lineage`), `apps/studio/src/lib/lineage.ts` (the writing half), `apps/studio/src/lib/store.ts` (the stamp on the fork, and the action's new argument), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` and `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the caller names the instant), `apps/studio/src/lib/lineage.test.ts` (+4 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/remixLane.test.ts` (+2 cases, and the two existing ones updated for the new argument), `docs/evidence/m7/remix-proof.mjs` (a new §3b, §4's stamp assertions, §5's visitor-loop assertion, and the two loader repairs), `docs/evidence/design-model/validate-proof.mjs` (its loader repair).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **857/857** (44 files, `--no-file-parallelism`); `@nexus/design-model` **51/51** (4 files); `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` and `tsc -p packages/design-model/tsconfig.test.json` both **exit 0** — after the model's `dist` was REBUILT, because the studio's type check reads the package's built types while its suite reads the sources, and the reserved key had to be in both; `node docs/evidence/m7/remix-proof.mjs` **ALL SECTIONS PASSED** (with the new §3b); `node docs/evidence/design-model/validate-proof.mjs` **ALL SECTIONS PASSED**.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service's own `remix` endpoint is still **unreachable from the Studio** — and that is deliberate, not an omission: the Studio's remix is an editor fork (a different flow), and the service's endpoint creates an **ownerless** row, which would contradict the ownership v263 established. The client-side stamp is what makes a Studio-made remix both **owned** and **sourced**. The `_lineage` key is a **reservation on top of the canonical graph**, not a node: it is a fact about the publication, not about the drawing, and `validateDocument` still judges the graph alone. `remixedAt` is an ISO-8601 string in the service's own format, and **nothing reads it** — it is there so a reader can say when, and no reader does yet. The lineage names a **project id, not a person**: it does not check that the source publication still exists, that it was ever published, or that the remixer had any right to it — the service verifies nothing (ADR 0018).

### Amendment 268 (M7/v268, tools/harness) — a REMIX's LINEAGE, end to end: the fork published, the SERVICE storing the source, and the public gallery linking back

- **What this grant closes.** v267 gave the remix a lineage: the fork is stamped with the reserved `_lineage`, the writing half joined the reading half in one module, and the key became part of the canonical model. What was still missing was the **whole path**: a person remixing a publication *in the real Studio*, the fork published, the service storing the lineage, and the public gallery naming the source. Half a story being proven is not the story being proven — the seam is where the owner was already dropped once (v263) and where the lineage was never written at all (v267).
- **The chain, driven in the real product.** §8.5a the published row offers a **remix control** — the community loop's second door. §8.5b clicking it forks the publication into a NEW project (the editor now holds a different document). §8.5c publishing the fork creates a **NEW publication under a NEW id**, read from the URL the service itself returned — `window.__nexus` deliberately exposes no document id, so the note is the authority. §8.5d the **SERVICE**, read independently of the browser, holds the fork's document with `_lineage.sourceProjectId` naming the publication it was remixed from, and the fork is **OWNED by the same device** — the claim rode on its publish too, so a remix is both sourced and signed. §8.5e the public gallery names the source **and links to it**, and the remix has its **own card** — the last clause matters, because a gallery that showed somebody else's byline next to the assertion would pass the weaker check.
- **The id is read from the SERVICE's URL, not from the editor.** The harness reads the fork's project id out of the publish note, exactly as it read the source's — because the bridge is a frozen read-only snapshot that deliberately exposes no document id, and an id invented from the editor would be an id the harness made up.
- **Files:** `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §8.5, between the artifact page and the take-down).
- **Measured:** `node tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` — the three layers stood up (a throwaway PostgreSQL, the built jar, and the real Studio on its own port), the whole chain driven in a REAL Chrome. The assertion count and any failure are printed by the run itself.
- **Landing note (v268).** This increment's bytes landed in a commit named for ANOTHER increment — `3e8374f prep(stage 861/861): full suite green - all pure models + UI helpers covered` — because a concurrent lane staged with a broad `git add` and swept the already-staged files in with its own. The content is this record's: the harness's §8.5, the README section, this ledger entry and the ROADMAP line are all in that commit. The commit MESSAGE is the thing that does not describe what it carries, so this note makes the ledger the authority — and the lesson is the one v263 already wrote down and v265 demonstrated in the other direction: an unstaged foreign change is one broad `git add` away from an unrelated commit, which is why every increment here commits by NAME (`git commit -- <paths>`, which bypasses the shared index).
- **Bounds (§60).** This proves that a remix **made the way a person makes one** is sourced, owned and linkable — it does not prove that the source still exists, that the remixer had any right to it, or that the service verified anything: the service **records claims and verifies nothing** (ADR 0018), and the lineage is a **project id, not a person**. The service's own `remix` endpoint is still unreachable from the Studio, and that remains deliberate: it creates an **ownerless** row, which would contradict the ownership v263 established. The gallery still caps at 24 rows with no paging and no search, so a source outside that window is simply not on the page. The `remixedAt` instant is stored in the service's own ISO format and **nothing reads it** yet.

### Amendment 269 (M7/v269, tools/harness + apps/studio) — the VISITOR's remix, in a REAL browser: a URL is enough, and the intent is dropped once honoured

- **The gap.** v234 gave the artifact page a remix bar so that someone who has only the URL can take the work, and the Studio reads that intent on mount. It had **never been driven in a real browser**: the remix proof grades the lane by running it and grades the WIRING by reading the shipped source — and a source can be perfectly correct while the mount effect does nothing. The panel path was proven end to end by v268; the **visitor's** path — the one that needs no account, no button and no published-panel — had no run at all.
- **The mechanism, and the two things it had to get right.** The Studio reads `?remix=<id>` on mount, fetches the publication, forks it, and **drops the query** with `history.replaceState`. Both halves are load-bearing and neither is obvious: a URL that kept its query would remix again on every reload (a remix nobody asked for twice), and a fork that did not happen would leave the visitor holding an empty Studio while the URL claimed otherwise. The harness therefore checks the query is **gone** and that the editor says so **in the Studio's own words** — `Remixed <id> — this is now your project` — before it publishes anything.
- **One small product change fell out of it: the status became ADDRESSABLE.** The Studio's status line had no `data-` attribute, so a harness could only find it by guessing at the toolbar's text. The publish note has had `data-toolbar-publish-note` since v194; the status now has `data-toolbar-status` beside it, which is the same idea: a piece of UI that a test must read should say where it is. Nothing about the Studio's behaviour changed.
- **What the proof grades.** §8.6a a second browser page opens `/?remix=<id>` and the intent is honoured with **no button pressed**. §8.6b the query is **dropped** once honoured. §8.6c the visitor **publishes their own NEW publication under a new id** — a remix must never overwrite its source, and the id comes from the URL the service returned. §8.6d the **SERVICE stored the lineage** for the visitor's remix too, so the community loop's front door produces a sourced publication and not just a fork in an editor.
- **Files:** `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §8.6), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the `data-toolbar-status` attribute).
- **Measured:** `node tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` — the three layers stood up (a throwaway PostgreSQL, the built jar, and the real Studio on its own port), the visitor path driven in a REAL Chrome. The assertion count and any failure are printed by the run itself.
- **Bounds (§60).** The visitor's remix is still only a **local fork**: the person edits it in their own Studio and publishing it is a separate, deliberate act — the URL does not publish anything on the visitor's behalf. The fork is owned by the visitor's device only once they publish it, and only if they have set an account (v263); without one it is an anonymous publication, which the service records as ownerless. The lineage still names a **project id, not a person**, the source may since have been deleted, and the service verifies nothing (ADR 0018).

### Amendment 270 (M7/v270, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the PROFILE page: the listing narrowed to one OWNER, and a byline that is an ADDRESS

- **The milestone item this closes.** M7's plan has carried "Profiles — an account's page and the publications it owns" as an open item since the community surface was designed, blocked behind a server that could not answer it. It is **not** blocked by ADR 0018: a profile is a public view of what an account published, and the service already stores the owner on every row (v242). What the service lacked was a way to ASK.
- **The service half — one query, and one rule that matters more than the query.** `GET /projects?owner=<accountId>` narrows the listing to one owner through a new finder (`findByOwnerAccountIdOrderByPublishedAtDesc`), for the same reason the newest-first finder exists: the cap has to reach the database, and a profile that read every publication and filtered in memory would be a table scan on every page load. The rule that matters: **a blank owner is the ABSENCE of one and answers an EMPTY list** — "the publications of nobody" is not the whole table, and that distinction is the difference between a profile and a leak. The owner is trimmed before it is asked for, and the limit rules are unchanged (clamped, never refused, non-positive refused by name). 4 new cases.
- **The Studio half — a profile that says what it cannot know.** `profile.ts` is PURE (the facts + the renderer), like `explore.ts` and `artifact.ts`. The facts come from the claims on the account's own publications, because **the service holds no account table**: an account exists in it only as far as publications NAME it. So the profile can show the handle and the assurance — the claims agree, because they are the same account — and it **cannot** show a display name, a bio, a follower count or a joined date, because the service never received them. And it cannot tell "this account has published nothing" from "there is no such account": both are an empty list. The page **says so**, rather than letting a reader discover it, and it says so in the empty state rather than in a comment.
- **The byline became an ADDRESS.** The gallery's card now renders `by <handle> · <assurance>` as a link to `/u/<accountId>`, and the card's owner carries the **account id** beside the name — a link needs an address, not a name. The account id is the key the service filters by, and the handle is a name the account chose; the page is careful about which of the two it treats as the address.
- **One builder, two pages.** The per-row read-and-draw (a listing carries no documents, so a card costs one extra read) moved into a shared `gallery.ts`, and BOTH the gallery route and the profile route build their cards with it. Two pages that draw the same card must draw it with the same code, or they drift — and the drift shows up as a card that looks right on the gallery and wrong on a profile.
- **The loader's ORDER, for the third time.** The profile module imports the gallery's renderer, and the proof's `strip` **writes a module and imports it in the same step**, so a module's own siblings must already be in the box. The same lesson appeared for the remix proof (`pageShell`), for the validate proof (`accounts`, `currentAccount`) and now here (`explore` before `profile`). A proof that cannot resolve an import is not a passing proof; it is a proof that stopped running — and the cost of getting the order wrong is a red gate that looks like a red assertion.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/.../PublishedProjectRepository.java` (the owner finder), `.../PublishService.java` (`list(limit, owner)`), `.../PublishController.java` (the `owner` parameter), `.../PublishServiceTest.java` (+4 cases); `apps/studio/src/lib/profile.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/lib/gallery.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.ts` (the account id on the owner, the byline link, the exported card grid), `apps/studio/src/app/u/[accountId]/route.ts` (new), `apps/studio/src/app/explore/route.ts` (the shared builder), `apps/studio/src/lib/publishServer.ts` and `publishLane.ts` (the owner), `apps/studio/src/app/api/publish/route.ts` (the list action's owner), `apps/studio/src/lib/profile.test.ts` (new, 8 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.test.ts` (the byline link), `docs/evidence/m7/explore-proof.mjs` (a new §5b and §3's wiring assertions).
- **Measured:** `services/nexus-api` **47/47** (43 + 4), `BUILD SUCCESS`; `apps/studio` **870/870** (45 files); `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**; `node docs/evidence/m7/explore-proof.mjs` **ALL SECTIONS PASSED** (with the new §5b); and the publish E2E **48/48** end-to-end (the profile page answers 200 over the real service and lists that account's publication).
- **Bounds (§60).** A profile is a **public list of what an account published** — it is not an identity page, and it carries no account of its own: no display name, no bio, no followers, no joined date, and no way to tell an unknown account from a silent one. The service **verifies nothing** (ADR 0018), so the assurance beside the name says what the claim is worth and no more. The listing still **caps** at 24 rows with no paging and no search, so an account with more publications than the cap shows only the newest 24 — and the page states the cap rather than implying the list is complete. There is no link from a profile to another profile, no follower count, and no way to REMIX from a profile: the two doors a card carries are still `open` and `remix`.

### Amendment 271 (M9/v271, services/nexus-api) — the AUDIT TRAIL: the service records what the publication verbs DID, and says so over HTTP

- **The milestone this opens.** The ROADMAP has carried **M9 — NEXUS Ops** as "⬜ planned" since the project began, and its first words are "observability". An audit trail is the piece of observability that needs no agent, no incident and no patch: a record of what each publication verb did, in the order it did it. This is M9's **server-side** beginning.
- **A second table, and the reason it is a second table.** The publication row says what **IS**; the audit row says what **WAS DONE**. They change for different reasons: a publication is **REPLACED** on every re-publish, so it cannot hold a history, while an audit entry is **APPENDED** and never replaced. Putting a history on a row that is overwritten would lose it.
- **Two rules, both stated rather than assumed.** (1) **Only SUCCESSFUL mutations are recorded.** A refused take-down throws before anything is written, and the refusal is already in the response the caller received — the trail says what happened, not what was attempted. (2) **An entry with no actor is a real entry, not a missing one.** An anonymous publish names nobody, and an audit trail that could not say "nobody" would have to invent an actor.
- **The write JOINS the caller's transaction, and that is what makes rule (1) true.** The first draft used `REQUIRES_NEW` so an entry would survive a rolled-back publish — which is exactly wrong for a trail that claims to record what happened: an entry in its own transaction would record a publication that **never happened**. The propagation is now the default, and the docstring says why.
- **The take-down names an account id and NOTHING else.** The request carried a **claimer**, not a claim, so the service never saw a handle or an assurance for it — and it records none rather than borrowing the publication's. The difference between "the claim said this" and "the caller named this" is the difference between a fact and an inference, and the trail keeps it.
- **The wire shape is the client's own `AuditEntry`, field for field** — the id is a string, the instant is epoch **MILLISECONDS** (the same unit the claim's own instant travels in, per v263, and the one the client's `createdAt: number` expects), and the assurance travels with the actor so a reader is told what the entry is worth instead of inferring it. **One honest difference:** the client's type says `actorId: AccountId` and `assurance: Assurance` — both non-null — while the service sends **null** for an anonymous action. The service will not fake an actor to fit a type; the client's model is the one that will have to widen, and it belongs to a concurrent lane.
- **The door.** `GET /audit` — newest first, capped (20 by default, 100 the most), the count and the cap both reported so "20" is never mistaken for "there are only 20".
- **What the suite found in ITSELF, recorded rather than hidden.** The first version of "a REFUSED take-down records nothing" built a row with **no owner** — and an ownerless row is open to anybody, so the take-down **succeeded** and the case went red. The refusal needs an **OWNED** row: that is the pre-v242 rule, and the case now says which row it meant instead of the rule passing by accident.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/ops/AuditEntry.java` (the entity), `.../ops/AuditEntryRepository.java`, `.../ops/AuditService.java` (the write and the read), `.../ops/AuditController.java` (the door and the wire shape), `.../publish/PublishService.java` (the three write points), `.../publish/PublishServiceTest.java` (+5 cases, and the mock the service now takes), `docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs` (a new §11).
- **Measured:** `services/nexus-api` **52/52** (47 + 5), `BUILD SUCCESS`; `node docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs` **exit 0**, with the new §11 reading the trail back over HTTP from the real service and the real database: **10 entries**, the owned publication has exactly **one** publish entry and exactly **one** unpublish entry — so the two **refused** take-downs recorded **nothing** — the anonymous publication has an entry that names **NOBODY**, the assurance travels with the actor, the instant is a real instant, and the trail reads newest first.
- **Bounds (§60).** The trail records what **happened**, not what was attempted: a refused verb is absent from it (it is in the response). The service **verifies nothing**, so the assurance beside an actor is the entry's own statement of what the claim was worth and not a check (ADR 0018). Only **`publish` and `unpublish`** are recorded: the service's remix endpoint is unreachable from the Studio (v267's bound), and `follow` / `like` / `comment` / `tip` — the other actions the client's model declares — **do not exist server-side at all**, so their absence from the trail is an absence from the product, not a gap in the recorder. There is **no Studio surface for the trail yet**: the door exists and the client's model already matches its shape, and the panel that reads it is the next increment. The trail is append-only but the service offers no way to TRUNCATE it, and it will grow forever.
### Amendment 272 (M9/v272, apps/studio) — the AUDIT TRAIL becomes READABLE: a panel that says what happened, to what, by whom, and both counts

- **The gap v271 left stated plainly.** The service records the trail and answers a door; the client's own model already declares its shape; and **nobody could see a single entry**. An audit trail nobody can read is a table nobody audits — v271 ended by saying the panel was the next increment, and this is it.
- **Two PURE halves, in the shape every lane here has.** `trail.ts` is the mapping (the action’s display verb, the actor’s text, the instant’s text, and the rule for what cannot be shown); `auditLane.ts` is the browser half (it GETs this Studio’s own `/api/audit` and answers with a **reason**, never a thrown error, because a panel that says “could not read: service unreachable” is an honest panel and one that throws into React is not a panel at all). The route is server-side for the same reason `/api/publish` is: the service’s address is not the browser’s business.
- **The route forwards the SERVICE'S OWN answer** — `{ ok, entries, count, limit }`, order included — rather than re-shaping it. The trail's order, its count and its cap are the service's facts, and a route that re-sorted or re-counted them would be reporting something the service never said. The panel is `force-dynamic`: caching a database read in a place the next write cannot invalidate would be storing a system of record somewhere it is not.
- **BOTH numbers are on screen, always.** The panel states `rendered of count entry(ies) shown · the service caps at limit` beside the rows. The reading half **drops** a row it cannot display honestly (no id, no action, no target, no finite instant) instead of rendering it with invented columns — and a panel that only reported the rows it managed to render would make that drop invisible. The two numbers are kept side by side so a discrepancy is visible out loud.
- **An unknown action is passed through, never relabelled.** `follow` / `like` / `comment` / `tip` are in the client's model and do not exist server-side (v271's bound); if one ever arrives, the panel shows it as it is. A trail that could not recognise `follow` and printed `published` instead would be worse than no trail.
- **The trail names ACCOUNT IDS, not handles — and the panel says so instead of papering over it.** The service holds no account table (v270's finding), and the actor of a take-down never published anything, so **no row anywhere carries a handle for it**: borrowing the publication's owner as the actor's name would attribute an action to somebody who did not do it. The actor is therefore rendered `acct-ada · unsigned-local` from the entry's own fields, and `nobody (anonymous)` when the entry names no one — the one place the client's `ops.ts` type is wrong (`actorId` declared non-null), and the reason the service refuses to fake an actor (v271).
- **A stale trail would lie, so the panel re-reads after every verb.** A publish writes an entry and a take-down writes an entry; the open panel re-reads both times, exactly as the Published panel re-probes its rows. And the two panels are **mutually exclusive**: two fixed panels at the same corner is not two panels a person can read at once, it is one hiding behind the other.
- **What the real-browser proof asserts, and why the last two are the point.** §9.5 opens the panel and reads the rows out of Chrome, then finds the entries for the publication §9 **took down** — which the service answers **404** for. The entries are still there: a publication table is REPLACED while an audit table is APPENDED, and **a trail that lost the row it witnessed would witness nothing**. It then asserts the take-down names the account that did it, with the assurance its claim carried, that every row **links** to the thing its entry happened to (an audit row naming a publication nobody could reach would be a row you could only take on trust), and that the footer states the service’s count beside what was rendered.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.ts` and `trail.test.ts` (new — the pure mapping, 17 cases across both new files), `apps/studio/src/lib/auditLane.ts` and `auditLane.test.ts` (new — the browser lane), `apps/studio/src/app/api/audit/route.ts` (new — the server-side door onto the service), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the `data-toolbar-trail-toggle` control, the panel, and the re-read after each verb), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §9.5).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **887/887 (47 files)** (870 + 17), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**; `node docs/evidence/m7/publish-proof.mjs` **exit 0** (the §11 trail section still passes with the reading half in place). The real-browser assertion count for §9.5 is printed by the run itself.
- **Bounds (§60).** The panel reads what **happened**, and a refused verb is not there (it is in the response, per v271). It names **account ids, not people**, and cannot resolve them to handles because the service has no account table to resolve them with — a handle here would be borrowed from a publication, and a take-down’s actor never published anything. The trail is `publish` / `unpublish` only: the other actions in the client’s model **do not exist server-side**, so their absence is an absence from the product rather than a gap in the recorder. The service **verifies nothing** (ADR 0018), so the assurance beside an actor is the entry’s own statement of what the claim was worth. The panel shows **20** entries by default with no paging control, so a trail longer than the cap shows only the newest 20 — the footer states the cap so “20” is never mistaken for “there are only 20”. The service still offers **no truncation**, and the trail grows forever.

### Amendment 273 (M9/v273, apps/studio + docs/evidence/m9) — the client's ops model stops disagreeing with the service's wire, and a PROOF holds them together

- **The disagreement this closes.** v271 built the service's audit door and shipped a client model beside it that did not fit. The service sends `actorId: null` and `assurance: null` for an anonymous action; the client's `AuditEntry` declared both **non-null**. The service said, in its own record, that it "will not fake an actor to fit a type" — and the client's own docstring had to admit the mismatch in prose: "the one place the client's `ops.ts` type is wrong (`actorId` declared non-null)". **A type that is wrong in a comment is still wrong.** So the type gave: `actorId: AccountId | null` and `assurance: Assurance | null`.
- **Why the two fields are nullable together, and not separately.** An assurance travels *with* an actor — it is the claim's own statement of what the claim was worth. An entry with no actor has no claim, and so has no assurance to state. Widening one without the other would produce a type that could say "somebody acted, and here is what their claim was worth" for an entry the service recorded as having **nobody** at all.
- **Widening two fields is not widening six.** The other four (`id`, `action`, `targetId`, `createdAt`) stay **required and non-null**: the service always sends them, and a client that treated the id as optional would have to invent one — and an invented id is a row nobody can address. The proof asserts this in the negative (§4), because "everything is nullable" would be just as wrong as "everything is required".
- **A verb this build has never heard of must still FIT.** `AuditAction` keeps its known seven and adds a `string & Record<never, never>` arm (not `string & {}` — the `ban-types` rule forbids the empty object, and the intersection behaves the same). The service is a **separate deployable**: it can add a verb before this client is rebuilt, and a client that rejected the answer would show a *gap* where the event was.
- **An anonymous entry belongs to NO account — and the type alone does not make that true.** A type that can say "nobody" is not the same as a grouping that keeps a nobody out of somebody's bucket. `auditEntriesByActor` now routes actorless entries to a **reserved** bucket key, `ANONYMOUS_ACTOR = '__anonymous__'`, which no real account id can ever be: account ids are `acct-<base36>` (`createAccountId`), so they never begin with `__`. A key that could collide would be a bug that only shows up on a device with no account — the exact device whose entries would land in the wrong bucket.
- **The PROOF, and why it is a file and not a test.** The claim is a claim about **two source files**, so the two source files are the fixture: `docs/evidence/m9/audit-contract-proof.mjs` reads the Java `record` out of `AuditController.java` and asks the **TypeScript compiler** what `ops.ts`'s interface means, and asserts they agree — field for field, order for order, nullability for nullability. It needs nothing but Node: no Java, no Maven, no Docker, no database, no running service. Restating the field list inside the proof would have made it assert the thing it is supposed to check, so the field list is **parsed out of both sources** instead.
- **§5 asks the COMPILER, and that is the part that is not a hand-written imitation.** The proof compiles a probe that imports the **shipped** `ops.ts` and assigns the service's real anonymous entry to it. A re-narrowing of the type makes `tsc` fail; the proof is red. The other sections compare the two sources; this one asks the language itself.
- **It has been shown to FAIL — three mutations, three different sections.** Re-narrowing `actorId` is caught by **§3** ("a type that refuses null is a type the service has to lie to satisfy"); re-narrowing `assurance` likewise; and removing the open arm of `AuditAction` is caught by **§5** (`Type '"stake"' is not assignable to type 'AuditAction'`). Neither section would catch the other's mutation, and a green proof nobody has seen go red is decoration.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/ops.ts` (the widened model, the open action union, the reserved anonymous bucket and the ownership rule that keeps a nobody out of somebody's), `apps/studio/src/lib/ops.test.ts` (+7 cases: the nullable wire shape, an unknown verb, anonymous grouping, and the reserved key), `docs/evidence/m9/audit-contract-proof.mjs` (new — the contract proof, 6 sections), `docs/evidence/m9/README.md` (new — what the proof grades, and the mutations that were run against it).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **900/900 (47 files)** (870 + the reading lane's 17 + these 7), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**; `node docs/evidence/m9/audit-contract-proof.mjs` **exit 0**; `mvn -B test -f services/nexus-api/pom.xml` **52/52, BUILD SUCCESS** (the service is unchanged by this increment — the whole point is that it did not have to change).
- **Bounds (§60).** This is a **type-level** alignment: it proves the client can HOLD what the service sends, and it does not make the service verify anything (ADR 0018). The assurance beside an actor is still the entry's own statement of what the claim was worth, and `unsigned-local` is still the only value in play. The client's seven known verbs are a **design**, not a fact: only `publish` and `unpublish` exist server-side today (v271), and the open arm is there so a verb added to the service before the client is rebuilt arrives as an **event** rather than as a gap. The `__anonymous__` bucket is a **client-side grouping key**, not an identity: nothing in it can be owned, signed in to, or verified — it says "nobody was named", and it says nothing about who that nobody was.
- **Landing note (v273).** The ledger is ONE file, so this commit carries **amendment 272's record as well as this one** — 272 is the parallel lane's reading half (`trail.ts` / `auditLane.ts` / `app/api/audit`), whose CODE lands in that lane's own commit, while 273's bytes (`ops.ts`, `ops.test.ts`, `docs/evidence/m9/`) land here. The commit message names only 273, so **the ledger is the authority** about which bytes are whose — the same lesson v263 wrote down, v265 demonstrated in the other direction, and v268 repeated.

### Amendment 277 (M5/v277, apps/studio) — the BODY LANE moves WITH the seat: the frame writer is HANDED the world it animates

- **The bound this closes, and the fact it was measured from.** Amendment 261 moved every read and every write onto the world on screen and then named the one pair it had NOT moved: `addBody` / `removeBody` stayed on the COMPOSED scene because the host resolved the frame writer and the document send against `surface.sceneId`. Re-measuring that on the shipped bytes: with a sibling world live, `step()` handed the writer the composed world's bodies, so the world the person was looking at stood still while an off-screen one spun; `addBody` filed a body nobody could see and reported a count from the wrong world; `removeBody` took out a body of another world and answered `false` about the one under the cursor; and one Save press wrote TWO worlds, because `save()`'s file carried the live one while the store write beside it named the composed one.
- **A list per world, not one list read as if it belonged to the world on screen.** `bodiesByScene` is a `Map<sceneId, string[]>` seeded with the composed lane, `authoredByScene` the same, and `bodyIds` / `authoredBodyIds` are getters over the world the seat names. The seat is the only address a caller can ask for, and `liveSceneId` hands it out.
- **The frame writer is HANDED its subject.** `writeFrame(sceneId, bodyIds, motion)` replaces a callback that took ids alone and resolved a scene on the far side. This is the load-bearing change, because the defect was never the list — it was that two places independently decided WHICH world a frame belongs to. With the pair handed as one value, a host cannot express "animate this world's bodies in that world" by accident, and the proof's writer can refuse such a pair on the spot.
- **A broken seat is a refusal, not a crash.** `addBody` looks the live world up before asking; the runtime's `insertEntity` answers an unknown scene by THROWING (`packages/three-runtime/src/threeRuntime.ts:1416`), so pre-v277 a seat naming a world the runtime does not hold turned the Add-a-body button into an exception. It now answers `null`. `removeBody`'s domain is the live world's entity membership — an id that world does not hold is `false`, whichever other world holds it — and both tracked lists are cleaned up on the way out.
- **The asymmetry is kept on purpose, and it is stated twice rather than once.** `removeBody`'s domain is the WORLD; `step`'s is the LANE. A body the host placed in the world on screen is reportable and removable by this surface and is NEVER spun by it, because a surface animates what it composed or authored. A second surface composed while another world holds the seat likewise starts with an empty lane.
- **The panel stops carrying an address.** `Scene3D.tsx` resolves the scene from the id it was handed, and both store writes and the document send use `surface.liveSceneId`; `surface.sceneId` does not appear in the component's comment-stripped bytes, and `surface.test.ts` reads those bytes for the handed pair, the three `liveSceneId` reads and the two `writeSaveFile` addresses. This is the third grant in a row to pin a wiring claim from shipped bytes rather than from a renderer, for the reason v142 recorded: the Studio has no DOM test environment, and "this branch renders that surface" is not worth two dependencies — but "the toggle writes the world it was handed" is worth one regex, because typechecking cannot see it.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.ts` (+98/-42), `apps/studio/src/components/Scene3D.tsx` (+15/-5), `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3d.test.ts` (+138/-17, 138 to 142 cases: six added, two removed — v261's `THE BOUND` case is the one this grant closes and one frame-write case was renamed, which counts on both sides), `apps/studio/src/lib/scene3dSurface.test.ts` (+5/-2, same 70 cases, writer re-signed), `apps/studio/src/lib/surface.test.ts` (+32/-0, 24 to 25), `docs/evidence/studio/scene-surface-proof.mjs` (+98/-17), `docs/evidence/studio/README.md`.
- **Witness arms: 9/9 matched, 20 unit reds, two predictions corrected by reading rather than by widening.** Each arm splices ONE production line, runs the headless proof and the three suites (237 collected tests), requires the exact red set predicted before it ran, and restores its file byte-for-byte in a `finally`; the harness lives outside the repository so no file census counts it. CONTROL green/0. A composed-world frame loop (2 reds + §9's `it is HANDED the world on screen`), B one lane for every world (5), C authoring into the built world (4), D no ghost-seat guard (1), E the removal domain on the composed world (2), F `surface.sceneId` back in the component (1, proof GREEN — the proof never reads the panel), G a global authored list (2), H one address with every world's bodies (3). Two misses were recorded instead of smoothed over: A's first prediction named the harness's handed-pair guard, which that mutation cannot reach because it moves scene and ids together, and H's first prediction named 1 case where the run measured 3 — every one of them a true positive, including an IDENTITY comparison on the handed array and the fresh-restore surface whose `bodyIds` is empty while its own lane holds 4. Arm H exists precisely because A through G could not pull that belt.
- **Two findings about the tool, kept because they will bite the next grant.** The battery's preflight counts every needle against the pristine bytes BEFORE the first write, and it saved this run: arm E's two-line needle matched THREE sites (`removeBody`, `removeCamera` and the camera-seat verb all open with `const subject = liveSceneId();` above a `getScene` lookup), so the battery aborted at zero mutations rather than splice an ambiguous line; the needle gained `removeBody`'s own `entities.has(bodyId)`. And the battery no longer claims the whole tree is unchanged: a concurrent lane deleted its own scratch files mid-run and the old assertion charged that to this harness. The claim is now scoped to the files the battery owns and anything else prints as INTERFERED.
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` vitest **47 files / 900 tests, exit 0** (this increment's own files re-read by name: 142 / 25 / 70); `tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json --noEmit` **exit 0**; `eslint --max-warnings=0` over the five touched sources **exit 0** — the first invocation from the repository root exited 2 because ESLint 9 finds no config there, an invocation artifact corrected by re-running with the acting reader; `@nexus/three-runtime` **25 files / 577 tests exit 0** with `distSync` green and no rebuild, because no `packages/three-runtime/src` byte moved; `node docs/evidence/studio/scene-surface-proof.mjs` **exit 0**; the §7 ledger door **exit 0**.
- **Bounds (§60).** The lane is per world and per surface, so a body authored through this surface in a world it later leaves is remembered, while a body the host placed is not animated by anybody until a surface composes or authors it. Lanes are never reclaimed, because the runtime has no scene-deletion verb: one Map entry per world this surface has written into, for the life of the surface. A lane and the runtime's entity Map can still disagree — `removeBody` accepts the runtime's answer as authority and repairs the lane, so the lane follows the world, not the other way round. No browser harness ran (`next dev` plus a Chrome); the component is graded from its bytes and the runtime from `dist`. The save FILE and the save STORE now name the same world; the document send does too; what still names the composed scene is nothing in the stripped bytes of `Scene3D.tsx`, and that absence is the pin.

### Amendment 275 (M7/v275, apps/studio + services/nexus-api) — GALLERY PAGING: the window that reaches every row

- **The gap.** The service's listing had `limit` but no `offset` — so a gallery capped at 24 could never show row 25. The parallel lane's `OffsetPageRequest` adds the server half: a `Pageable` that carries an exact offset (not page-aligned), so `offset=25, limit=24` reaches the 25th row. The client half already supported `offset` in `listPublications` (v274); what was missing was the UI.
- **The explore route now parses `?offset=` and passes it through.** The route reads the query, clamps negative to 0, and calls `listPublications(24, undefined, undefined, offset)`. The service answers with the window it was asked for, and the response carries `skip` (the offset the service actually used) so the page knows where it is.
- **Paging controls in the pure renderer.** `renderExploreHtml` now receives `{ count, limit, offset }` and emits Prev/Next links with the correct offsets. The controls are disabled (opacity, pointer-events) when there is no previous/next page. The header states "showing X–Y of Z" so a person knows the window they are looking at.
- **Empty state keeps paging.** Even when the window is empty (e.g., offset beyond count), the paging bar still renders so a person can navigate back — a gallery that hid the controls on an empty page would trap them.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/app/explore/route.ts` (parses offset, passes to lane), `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.ts` (renderExploreHtml + paging controls), `apps/studio/src/lib/explore.test.ts` (25 cases updated with offset). Service side (parallel lane): `OffsetPageRequest.java`, `PublishController.java` `offset` param, `PublishService.list(limit, owner, skip)`.
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **931/931 (49 files)**, `tsc` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**. The parallel lane's service tests cover the offset logic.
- **Bounds (§60).** The offset is NOT page-aligned — that is the whole point of `OffsetPageRequest`. A page size of 24 with offset 25 is "page 1" (the page that CONTAINS it) and the offset says 25. The sort belongs to the finder (newest-first), not the window. The UI states the window explicitly so "page 2" is never mistaken for "rows 25–48".
