### Amendment 280 (M9/v280, apps/studio) — the AUDIT TRAIL, read at the THING it records

- **The gap.** v272 put the trail in the Studio’s toolbar: every entry, newest first, for the author to read. But the toolbar answers "what happened to the publications" and the ARTIFACT PAGE answers "what is this" — and a reader who opens a publication had no way to ask "what happened to THIS one?". The trail’s whole value is that it outlives the row it witnessed (v272’s proof: the publication answers 404 and its entries remain), and the place where that matters most is the publication’s own page.
- **Two new modules, both in the shape every lane here has.** `history.ts` is PURE: `historyRowsOf(entries, targetId)` filters the trail to ONE publication (exact match on the target, order preserved — the trail’s order is part of what it asserts) and `renderHistoryHtml(rows, carried)` renders the section. `auditServer.ts` is the server-side half: it reads the service’s `GET /audit` and answers with a REASON rather than a thrown error, because an artifact page that says "the history could not be read" is an honest page and one that throws into a route handler is a 500.
- **A failed read does NOT take the page down.** The artifact page reads the publication and the trail independently, and a trail that could not be read leaves the artifact intact with no history section at all. An artifact that 500s because the TRAIL was unreachable would make the publication unreachable for a reason that has nothing to do with it — and an EMPTY history is not inserted, because a heading with nothing under it would read as "this publication has no history", which a failed read knows nothing about.
- **The count of the WHOLE answer is stated beside the rows.** The trail is capped, so an old publication’s entries can be past the cap — and a reader must be able to tell "this publication has one entry" from "the answer was cut short before this publication’s entries appeared". The section says both numbers, and says the cap when the two disagree.
- **The page says what "no history" does not mean.** A publication published before the trail existed has no entries at all, and the empty state says that — "no audit entries name this publication. That is not the same as ‘nothing happened’". A page that implied nothing happened would be making a claim the service never made.
- **The styles travel with the section.** The artifact page’s shell belongs to the PREVIEW renderer; the history is a guest in it, and a guest that assumed it could restyle the host would be a guest that could break the drawing. The section carries its own scoped styles.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/history.ts` and `history.test.ts` (new — the pure filter and the section, 13 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/auditServer.ts` and `auditServer.test.ts` (new — the server-side reader, 6 cases), `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts` (reads the trail server-side and injects the section).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **951/951 (51 files)** (932 + 19), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**.
- **Bounds (§60).** The trail records what **happened**, and a refused verb is not in it. The page shows only the entries that NAME this publication — an entry names one project id, and a row that named none belongs to no publication. The trail is capped, so an old publication’s entries can be past the cap; the page says so rather than presenting a partial history as complete. The service **verifies nothing** (ADR 0018), so the assurance beside an actor is the entry’s own statement of what the claim was worth. The service offers **no truncation**, and the trail grows forever.
### Amendment 281 (M9/v281, apps/studio) — the trail’s FILTERS and its TALLY: the panel answers questions, not just lists

- **The gap.** The trail panel (v272) showed every entry, newest first, in one list. That is the honest and complete thing to show — but a reader with a question ("what was taken down?", "how many times was this published?") had to read the whole list and count it themselves. A list that cannot be narrowed is a list that makes the reader do the work the system already did.
- **The TALLY, counted from the rows the answer carried.** `trailSummaryOf(rows)` counts publishes, take-downs, and — importantly — an `other` bucket for any action this build does not know. A verb this build does not recognise is NEVER folded into a verb it does: if a `follow` ever arrived (it is in the client’s model, not in the service), a summary that said "3 published" when one was a follow would be a lie. The tally is over ALL the rows, not the filtered ones — the filter narrows the LIST, so a reader can always see what the filter is hiding.
- **The FILTERS, in the trail’s own language.** `filterTrailRows(rows, action)` matches on the service’s word (`publish` / `unpublish`), NOT on the display verb ("published" / "took down"): the display verb is a rendering choice, and a filter that matched on it would break the day the wording changed. The panel carries three controls — All, Published, Taken down — and a filter that matches nothing says "no entries of that action" rather than falling back to the whole list.
- **THREE numbers in the footer, because there are THREE questions.** What is SHOWN (the filter admits), what could be RENDERED (the reading half accepted), and what the SERVICE says it carried. The last two are the v272 drop-check, unchanged: renderable can never exceed the service’s count, and a smaller number is exactly the discrepancy the footer exists to expose. The first differs from the second whenever a filter is on — which is the filter working, not a discrepancy.
- **The proof grades the filter, not just the list.** §9.6 in the real-browser harness: the panel states the tally; the take-down filter shows ONLY take-downs and FEWER rows than the whole trail; the publish filter shows ONLY publishes; and ‘All’ puts every row back — because a filter that could not be undone would be a trap.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.ts` and `trail.test.ts` (the tally and the filter, +6 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the filter controls, the tally line, the three-number footer, and the `data-trail-action` attribute on each row), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §9.6).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **957/957 (51 files)** (951 + 6), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**. The real-browser assertion count for §9.6 is printed by the run itself.
- **Bounds (§60).** The filters narrow the LIST; they do not re-ask the service. The trail the panel holds is the newest window the service returned, and a filter over a window cannot reach past it. The tally counts what the answer carried, not the whole trail — the service’s own count is stated beside it. The service **verifies nothing** (ADR 0018), so the assurance beside an actor is the entry’s own statement of what the claim was worth.
### Amendment 283 (M7/v283, services/nexus-api) — LIKES: the smallest social act, and the easiest to get wrong

- **The milestone item this opens.** The ROADMAP’s M7 row has carried **likes** (with comments and follow) since the community surface was designed. This is the first of the three, and it is the one that needs the LEAST: a like is a fact about a publication and an account, and both of those already exist — the publication as a row, the account as the CLAIM that v263 established. The parallel lane’s `community.ts` already declares the client’s own `Like` shape (`accountId`, `projectId`, `createdAt`), and the service’s wire shape is that shape field for field, plus the two fields the service knows and the client does not need.
- **A NEW package, and that is deliberate.** The service lives in `dev.nexus.api.social` — five new files, none of them touched by the concurrent lane’s work in `publish` and `ops`. A like is its own aggregate with its own table, its own rules and its own tests; folding it into the publication package would have made a publication’s rules and a like’s rules one file, and the two have nothing to say to each other.
- **Rule 1: a like needs an ACCOUNT, and the refusal SAYS WHY.** An anonymous like cannot be DE-DUPLICATED — two likes from one device and two likes from two devices are the same row as far as the service can tell — so the count would be a number nobody could defend. The service refuses such a like BY NAME, and the name says the real reason: the service cannot tell one anonymous like from the same one twice. A message that said “unverified” would send the caller looking for a signature instead of an account.
- **Rule 2: liking twice is liking ONCE, and the count is ASKED for, not incremented.** The second like finds the row the first one wrote and answers with it; the count does not grow. The UNIQUE constraint on (publication, account) is what makes that a fact the DATABASE enforces rather than a fact the service hopes for — and the count is read from the table rather than added to, so a lost update cannot inflate it.
- **Rule 3: only the account that liked can take the like back, and a refusal is NOT a silent ‘fine’.** Somebody else’s un-like is refused, because a caller that asked to remove something and was told “fine” would believe the like is gone. And there is no 404: a like that is already gone is “already gone”, the same rule the publication’s take-down follows.
- **A row, not a counter — and that is what makes the rules enforceable.** A counter on the publication row would answer “how many” and nothing else: it could not say WHO liked, WHEN, or whether the same person liked twice. The row answers all three, and it is the row that the unique constraint protects.
- **The instants are the service’s own.** The like records `clock.instant()` (truncated to milliseconds, like the publication’s), never a value the client sent: a client that sent its own instant would be asking the service to believe a number it never checked. The wire shape sends the instant in epoch MILLISECONDS, which is the client’s own unit and the unit v263 settled.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/LikeEntry.java` (the entity and its unique constraint), `.../social/LikeRepository.java` (the finders, every windowed one carrying a `Pageable`), `.../social/LikeService.java` (the three rules), `.../social/LikeController.java` (`POST /likes`, `DELETE /likes/{projectId}?claimer=`, `GET /likes?projectId=`), `.../social/LikeDtos.java` (the wire shapes), `.../social/InvalidLike.java`, `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/LikeServiceTest.java` (14 cases).
- **Measured:** `services/nexus-api` **LikeServiceTest 14/14** (the rest of the service suite is the concurrent lane’s in-flight work and is measured by them), `mvn -o -B test -Dtest=LikeServiceTest` **exit 0**, and the module COMPILES with the new package. The real-browser proof of the like surface is the next increment.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service does NOT check that the publication exists, and it does NOT verify the account: both are the same posture the publish service takes (it records a claim and verifies nothing — ADR 0018), and both are bounds rather than bugs — the service records THAT a like happened, and a like of a project id that was never published is still a like that happened. A take-down does NOT take the likes with it: the likes are facts that happened, and the trail’s rule (a publication is REPLACED while an audit entry is APPENDED) applies here too. The service offers **no count-of-everything** and no leaderboard, because a leaderboard is a feature with no rules yet. Likes are **not in the audit trail yet** — the trail records the publication verbs, and a like is a social verb. The account is a CLAIM: the assurance travels with every like so a reader is told what it is worth, and nothing here makes it worth more than that.
### Amendment 284 (M7/v284, apps/studio) — the LIKES surface: the page shows the count, the Studio does the like

- **The shape of the feature, and why it is split.** The artifact page is SERVER-RENDERED, and the account lives in the BROWSER’s storage (ADR 0018 is why there is no session). So the page can report the COUNT — a fact that does not depend on who is asking — but it CANNOT act, and it cannot say whether YOU liked it. The like therefore happens in the Studio, which is where the account is — exactly the way the remix works: the page carries a bar, the bar links to `/?like=<id>`, and the Studio reads the intent on mount. The page does not pretend to know more than it knows.
- **A failed read is NOT zero likes.** The bar is left out ENTIRELY when the count could not be read, because “0 likes” and “the likes could not be read” are different facts, and a page that showed the first when it knew the second would be lying in the way that matters most: a reader would conclude nobody cared. A count of ZERO, on the other hand, IS something to say — nobody has liked this yet — and the two are told apart.
- **The page does not claim YOU liked it.** A bar that said “Liked” to a reader who had not would be a claim the page cannot support, so it offers the like and lets the Studio, where the account lives, answer the question that only the Studio can.
- **The client never invents an actor.** The claim is built from the device’s OWN account; a device with no account has NO claim, and the Studio says so in its own words (“this device has no account, and a like needs one”) rather than making one up. An invented account id would be a like nobody made, and the service would record it as a fact. The service refuses an accountless like BY NAME (v283), and the client refuses to pretend otherwise.
- **The intent is DROPPED once honoured**, exactly like the remix: a URL that kept its query would like again on every reload, and a like is idempotent (liking twice is liking once) but a reader reloading a page should not re-trigger the action they already took.
- **Three modules, in the shape every lane here has.** `likeServer.ts` is the server-side half (it reads and writes the service over the server-side hop, and answers with a REASON rather than throwing); `likeLane.ts` is the browser half (it talks to this Studio’s own `/api/likes`); `likeBar.ts` is the PURE renderer (the count, the link, and the injection). The Studio’s `/api/likes` route forwards to the service’s `/likes` — three verbs, three shapes: GET reads, POST likes with the claim in the body, DELETE takes back with the claimer as a query parameter (a DELETE with no body is the conventional shape, and the publication’s take-down does the same).
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** §10: the artifact page carries the bar and states a count of ZERO for a publication nobody has liked; the bar offers the like as a link to the Studio; the Studio likes it when the URL asks and says so in its own words WITH the count; the intent is dropped; the SERVICE recorded the like (read independently of the browser, from the real database) and the like names the ACCOUNT with its assurance; the artifact page now says ONE like — the count moved because the SERVICE moved it, not because the page was told; a device with NO account is refused and the refused like changed NOTHING.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/likeServer.ts` (the server-side read and the two writes), `apps/studio/src/lib/likeLane.ts` and `likeLane.test.ts` (the browser lane, 9 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/likeIntent.ts` (the URL intent and the claim builder), `apps/studio/src/lib/likeBar.ts` and `likeBar.test.ts` (the pure bar, 17 cases), `apps/studio/src/app/api/likes/route.ts` (the Studio’s door), `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts` (the page reads the count and injects the bar), `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the mount intent).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **983/983 (53 files)** (957 + 26), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**. The real-browser E2E **75/75** with the new §10 (the whole like loop: the bar, the intent, the row, the accountless refusal).
- **Bounds (§60).** The page shows the COUNT and nothing about the viewer. The like happens in the Studio, so it costs a trip to the Studio — the price of not having a session, and the reason the bar is a LINK rather than a button. A device with no account cannot like at all, and the refusal is by name. The service does NOT verify the account (ADR 0018): the assurance travels with the like so a reader is told what it is worth, and nothing here makes it worth more. A take-down does NOT take the likes with it — the likes are facts that happened. Likes are **not in the audit trail yet** (the trail records the publication verbs, and a like is a social verb). There is no “who liked this’s publication’ page, and no list of one account’s likes, yet.
### Amendment 285 (M7/v285, services/nexus-api) — COMMENTS: the first social act that says something

- **The milestone item.** The ROADMAP’s M7 row has carried **comments** beside likes and follow since the community surface was designed. This is the second of the three, and it is the first one that says something — and saying something is where the rules get sharp: a comment with no author is unattributable, a comment with an unbounded body is a way to fill the table, a comment anybody can delete is a comment nobody can stand behind, and a comment that vanishes when it is removed is a comment nobody can audit.
- **Rule 1: a comment needs an ACCOUNT**, refused BY NAME with the reason that matters — “a comment with no author has nobody to take it back and nobody to answer to”. The client’s own `community.ts` says the same thing in its type: `Comment.accountId` is NOT nullable, while `Like.accountId` and `Tip.recipientId` are separate concerns.
- **Rule 2: the body must be a BODY.** A blank body is refused (“a comment must say something”), and an absurdly long one is refused with the limit NAMED — “as much as you will give me” is a legitimate thing to say about a like and not about a paragraph. The body is stored VERBATIM: the client’s own model says the body arrives already escaped, and a service that escaped on the way IN would store something a reader sees twice-escaped, while a service that escaped on the way OUT would be trusting every future reader to remember.
- **Rule 3: only the author takes their comment back, and the take-back is SOFT.** Somebody else’s take-back is REFUSED (403, not 400 — the request was well-formed, so a 400 would tell the caller to fix a field that is fine). The row STAYS with `deleted = true`, because “this comment was removed” and “this comment never existed” are different facts, and a hard delete would make the first indistinguishable from the second. The client’s own model has the same `deleted` flag.
- **Rule 4: the list says how many are VISIBLE.** Deleted comments come back with their flag set — a reader who can see that a comment was removed is better served than a reader who cannot tell a quiet thread from a deleted one — and the visible count is stated beside the rows, so a list of three of which one was removed cannot be read as “there are three comments”.
- **The comment id is the SERVICE’s own.** A caller that named its own comment id could overwrite another account’s comment, and a comment is a thing that happened once. The instant is the service’s own too (the injected `Clock`, truncated to milliseconds like the publication’s) — a client that sent its own instant would be asking the service to believe a number it never checked.

- **Bounds (§60).** The service does NOT check that the publication exists, and it does NOT verify the account — the same posture the publish service takes (it records a claim and verifies nothing — ADR 0018). The body is stored as it arrived, so the ESCAPING is the caller’s responsibility and the page’s is to escape it again on the way out; the service does not pretend to be a sanitizer. There is no comment EDIT — a comment is appended or taken back, never rewritten, because a rewritten comment is a different comment and the reader cannot tell them apart. No moderation, no rate limit, and no profanity filter: a service that filtered words would be making editorial decisions with no policy behind them. The account is a CLAIM: the assurance travels with every comment so a reader is told what it is worth, and nothing here makes it worth more.
### Amendment 286 (M7/v286, apps/studio) — the COMMENTS surface: the page lists them, the Studio writes them

- **The shape, and why it is split the way the like was.** The artifact page is SERVER-RENDERED and cannot act: it does not know who the device is (ADR 0018 is why there is no session). So the page LISTS the comments — read through the same server-side hop the publication, the history and the like count came through — and offers a link to `/?comment=<id>`, where the Studio opens a composer over it. The comment is written in the Studio, because the Studio is where the account lives.
- **The body is ESCAPED AGAIN on the way out.** The service stored it verbatim (the client escaped it on the way in, per the community model), and a page that trusted the stored bytes would render whatever was in them. Escaping twice is not a bug: the first escape is the caller’s promise, and the second is the page’s own.
- **A REMOVED comment is shown as removed — not hidden, and not as its text.** “This comment was removed” and “this comment never existed” are different facts, and a reader who can see the first is better served than a reader who cannot tell it from the second. The section states the VISIBLE count beside the rows, so a list of three of which one was removed cannot read as “there are three comments”.
- **The query is NOT dropped, unlike the remix’s.** A remix is a one-time intent — a URL that kept its query would remix again on every reload, and a remix nobody asked for twice is a bug. A comment is not a one-time intent: the composer is a place the reader is, and a reader who reloads should still find it open over the publication it is for. The difference is not a detail; it is the difference between an intent and a destination.
- **The composer never INVENTS an author.** A device with no account has no claim, and the composer says so by name (“this device has no account, and a comment needs one”) rather than posting a comment nobody made. The service refuses an authorless comment BY NAME (v285), and the client refuses to pretend otherwise.
- **Four modules, in the shape every lane here has.** `commentServer.ts` is the server-side half (the read for the page and the write for the route); `commentLane.ts` is the browser half; `commentBar.ts` is the PURE renderer (the row, the section, the escaping); `CommentComposer.tsx` is the one piece of UI. The Studio’s `/api/comments` route forwards to the service’s `/comments`.
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** §11: the artifact page carries a COMMENTS section and says the thread is empty (and why it is not a one-click thing); it offers the composer as a link to the Studio; the Studio opens a composer over the intent; posting says so in the Studio’s own words; the SERVICE recorded the comment (read independently of the browser, from the real database), naming the ACCOUNT with its assurance and the body as it was typed; the artifact page now lists the comment with its author; a device with NO account is refused and the refused comment changed NOTHING.

The setter now comes from the element\u2019s OWN prototype. (2) The `until` helper returns **null** when it gives up, and several checks \u2014 including ones written in earlier increments \u2014 compared the result against `false`, so a TIMEOUT **PASSED** the check. Every such check now compares against `null`. A proof that cannot fail is not a proof, and both of these were a proof that could not fail.

A comment is written in the Studio, so it costs a trip there — the price of not having a session. The body is escaped by the client on the way in and by the page on the way out; the SERVICE stores it verbatim and is not a sanitizer. There is no comment EDIT, no moderation, and no rate limit. The comment id and the instant are the service’s own. The account is a CLAIM (ADR 0018): the assurance travels with every comment so a reader is told what it is worth, and nothing here makes it worth more.
### Amendment 287 (M7/v287, services/nexus-api) — FOLLOWS: the one social act that is about a PERSON

- **The milestone item.** The ROADMAP’s M7 row has carried **follow** beside likes and comments since the community surface was designed. This is the third of the three, and it is the first one whose subject is an ACCOUNT rather than a publication — which is exactly where its rules come from: the two ends of the edge are different things.
- **The two ends are DIFFERENT COLUMNS, and the model says so.** `followerId` and `followeeId` are separate columns, and the repository’s finders for the two directions are separate too. A model that stored “a and b” would have to guess which end was which, and a social graph with ambiguous edges is a graph nobody can count. The UNIQUE constraint on (follower, followee) is what makes “the same account cannot follow the same account twice” a fact the DATABASE enforces.
- **Rule 1: a follow needs an ACCOUNT.** The follower is the account the claim names; a follow with no follower has no edge to draw. The service refuses it BY NAME.
- **Rule 2: an account cannot follow ITSELF.** A self-follow is not a relation — it is a no-op dressed as one — and it would put one account in its own follower count. The service refuses it by name, and the refusal says what the rule is for (“that is not a relation, it is a no-op”).
- **Rule 3: following twice is following once.** The second follow finds the edge the first one wrote and answers with it; the counts do not move. And the counts are ASKED FOR, never incremented, so a lost update cannot inflate either — the same discipline the like uses.
- **Rule 4: only the follower takes the edge back**, and somebody else’s un-follow is REFUSED rather than silently ignored: a caller that asked to remove something and was told “fine” would believe the edge is gone.
- **What the service CANNOT know, stated rather than implied: whether either account EXISTS.** The service holds no account table (an account exists in it only as far as publications NAME it), so a follow of an account id nobody has ever published is a follow the service records faithfully — and the PROFILE page, which is the place where a reader would learn the truth, is the place that can say it. The service does not verify the account either (ADR 0018).
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/FollowEntry.java` (the edge and its unique constraint), `.../social/FollowRepository.java` (the finders, one per direction), `.../social/FollowService.java` (the four rules), `.../social/FollowController.java` (`POST /follows`, `DELETE /follows/{accountId}?claimer=`, `GET /follows?accountId=`), `.../social/FollowDtos.java` (the wire shapes), `.../social/InvalidFollow.java`, `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/FollowServiceTest.java` (12 cases).
- **Measured:** `services/nexus-api` **the social package 43/43** (12 follow + 17 comment + 14 like), `mvn -o -B test -Dtest="dev.nexus.api.social.*Test"` **exit 0**, and the module COMPILES. The real-browser proof of the follow surface is the next increment.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service does NOT check that either account exists, and it does NOT verify the account — the same posture the publish service takes (it records a claim and verifies nothing — ADR 0018). A follow of an account id nobody has ever published is recorded faithfully, and the profile page is where that would be visible. There is no MUTUAL follow, no follow request to approve, and no unfollow-everything: a follow is a one-way edge and the service does not invent rules it has no policy for. The follower and followee are account ids — CLAIMS, not verified identities — and the assurance travels with the claim so a reader is told what it is worth.
### Amendment 288 (M7/v288, apps/studio) — the FOLLOW surface: the profile shows the followers, the Studio does the follow

### Amendment 289 (M9/v289, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the SOCIAL verbs join the AUDIT TRAIL

- **The gap.** The trail recorded what happened to the PUBLICATIONS — a publish, a take-down — and the three social actions (like, comment, follow) happened to publications too, without a word in the trail. A reader asking “what did people DO with this publication?” had to read the like bar and the comment thread separately, and neither of them was a record: a panel is a view of NOW, and the trail is a record of WHAT HAPPENED.
- **The service writes, and the trail’s OWN rules hold for the social verbs.** (1) **Only a SUCCESSFUL mutation is recorded**: a refused like (no account) and a refused comment (blank body) write nothing, and the cases say so. (2) **A mutation that changed NOTHING is not recorded**: a SECOND like finds the row the first one wrote and changes nothing, so it writes nothing — the trail records what HAPPENED, not what was attempted, and a trail that recorded the second like would be recording an attempt. (3) **The write joins the caller’s transaction** (the default propagation, as in v271), so a rolled-back like leaves no entry claiming a like happened.
- **The un-verbs are recorded too, and they are NOT folded into the verbs.** A like that is taken back is something that happened, exactly as a publication that is taken down is: the service writes `unlike` and `uncomment`, and the trail’s words are “took the like back” and “removed the comment”. Merging them into the verbs would lose one of the two facts, and a reader asking “did they take it back?” deserves an answer.
- **A FOLLOW is NOT in the trail, and the reason is the trail’s own.** The trail’s target is what the event happened TO, and for a publication that is a project id — the panel links it to `/p/<target>`, and the artifact page’s HISTORY filters by it. A follow’s target is an ACCOUNT, and a target field that meant two things would break both readers. The follow is left out and said so, rather than squeezed in where it would lie.
- **The client LEARNS the verbs.** The trail’s display words, its tally buckets (`liked`, `unliked`, `commented`, `uncommented`) and its FILTERS all grow with the service: a like has its own bucket rather than falling into “other”, because a tally that called a like “other” would be hiding the very thing the panel is for. And the tally says only the buckets that are NOT zero — a line that always carried every bucket would grow a dozen “0 took down”s and a reader would learn to skip it.

The real-browser E2E **102/102** with the new §13 (the trail re-read and carrying the social verbs: the tally names them, the rows carry them, and the Liked filter narrows to them).
- **Bounds (§60).** A follow is NOT in the trail (its target is an account, and the trail’s target is a publication). The trail records the SOCIAL verbs but not every verb the product has: a moderation action, a report, or a tip would each need a target and a rule before they could be written down, and the service does not invent rules it has no policy for. The trail is still capped and still append-only, and the service still offers **no truncation**. The assurance beside an actor is the entry’s own statement of what the claim was worth (ADR 0018), and nothing here makes it worth more.
### Amendment 290 (M7/v290, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the SEARCH door: the client’s `?q=` finally means something

- **The gap.** The explore and profile pages have carried a search box since v278 and v279, and the client has been sending `?q=` to a service that **ignored it** — the gallery showed the same unfiltered listing whatever you typed. A search box that does not search is worse than no search box: it tells a reader their words were understood.
- **A NEW package, and why it is its own.** The publish package’s own comment said why it had no finder: "a search is a different feature with different rules (ranking, paging, what it does with a blank query)". So the search is its own door (`GET /search`), its own service, its own window and its own answer shapes — and the package is **self-contained on purpose**: it defines its own DTOs and its own claim record rather than reusing the publish package’s, because those DTOs are in flight in a concurrent lane and a search that would break when a record grew a field is a search that would break the build. The two doors answer the SAME shape, so the client parses them with the same code.
- **The search reaches into the DOCUMENT, not only the title.** A word that names a node in the work is a word the reader typed, and a search that only matched titles would answer a different question than the one that was asked. The cost is stated rather than hidden: a `LIKE` over a text column cannot use an index, so this is a **SEQUENTIAL SCAN** — at this table’s size that is the price of searching what is actually IN the work, and a table big enough for that to matter wants an index (or a full-text one).
- **A BLANK term is the plain listing, not an error.** “Show me everything” is a legitimate thing to mean, and a 400 would make the caller guess which word the service wanted. And a blank OWNER is the ABSENCE of one — the same rule the profile’s listing follows, and for the same reason: “the publications of nobody” is not a filter.
- **The window is EXACT, and the cap is the listing’s.** The search is the same listing with a filter, and a filter that changed the rules would make the two disagree — so the cap is CLAMPED the same way and the window skips an exact number of rows. The window is a `SearchWindow` of the search package’s own, and the record says plainly that it duplicates a window the publish package carries in a concurrent lane: two copies of one idea is a wart, and the search could not wait for a file another lane has not finished, and a search that silently paged by whole pages would show a reader results that do not exist.
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** §14: a term that appears in NO title — the source’s own id, which the forks carry in their lineage — finds exactly the forks (a title-only search would find nothing); the publication that does NOT mention the term is EXCLUDED (the filter really filters); and a term that matches nothing gives an EMPTY gallery rather than the whole one.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/search/SearchService.java`, `.../search/SearchController.java`, `.../search/SearchDtos.java`, `.../search/SearchWindow.java` (new), `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/publish/PublishedProjectRepository.java` (the two finders), `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/search/SearchServiceTest.java` (8 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/publishServer.ts` (a query goes to `/search`, a plain listing to `/projects`), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §14).
- **Measured:** `services/nexus-api` **the search package 8/8**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, `apps/studio` **1019/1019 (55 files)**, doc gate **exit 0**. The real-browser E2E **105/105** with the new §14 (a term that is only in the DOCUMENT finds the forks, the publication that does not mention it is EXCLUDED, and a term that matches nothing gives an EMPTY gallery).
- **Bounds (§60).** The search is a SUBSTRING match, case-insensitive, over the title and the document text — not a word match, not a phrase match, not a ranking: the results are newest-first like the listing, because a relevance ranking would need rules this feature does not have yet. It is a SEQUENTIAL SCAN, stated above. The search does not verify the owner and does not check that the publication exists (the same posture the publish service takes — ADR 0018). There is no fuzzy matching, no stemming, no stop-word list and no spell correction: a search that guessed would be a search that answered a different question than the one that was asked.
### Amendment 291 (M9/v291, docs/evidence/m9) — the TRAIL’s contract proof: the shapes that read the wire, checked against the wire

- **The gap, and it is not academic.** The v273 contract proof grades the client’s `ops.ts` against the service’s wire record. It does NOT grade the modules the TRAIL actually reads through — and the trail’s mapping **DROPS a row it cannot validate**: `toTrailRow` returns null for a row missing an id, an action, a target or a finite instant. So if the service RENAMED a wire field, the trail would not crash and would not complain: it would quietly render FEWER rows, and a rename of `assurance` would leave the trail showing rows with no assurance beside them — which reads as a fact rather than as a bug. A promise nobody checks is a comment, and a DROPPED ROW is the quietest kind of promise broken.
- **What the proof reads, and why it reads the SOURCE.** The service’s wire record is parsed out of the Java (a hand-written field list would make the proof assert the thing it is supposed to check), and the client’s two shapes are parsed with the **TypeScript compiler’s own parser** — the trail’s input shape in `trail.ts` and the server lane’s declared shape in `auditServer.ts`. Three source files, and the claim being graded is a claim about three source files, so the source files ARE the fixture: no service and no database are needed.
- **What it asserts, in order.** §1 the wire record’s six fields, in order, with the instant a `long` (epoch milliseconds) and the two nullable ones Strings. §2 every field the TRAIL reads is a field the service SENDS, AND every field the service sends is read by the trail — the second half is the one that matters: a field that arrives and is never looked at is a field the trail silently drops. §3 the same for the server lane. §4 the two client shapes name the SAME fields, because two client types for one wire shape is one more place for them to drift apart. §5 the reader is shown to FAIL: renaming a wire field in a COPY of the service’s source leaves the trail reading a field the service no longer sends, and the proof says so.
- **Files:** `docs/evidence/m9/trail-contract-proof.mjs` (new — the proof), `package.json` (the `verify:trail-contract` script).
- **Measured:** `node docs/evidence/m9/trail-contract-proof.mjs` **exit 0** (all five sections, and the mutation caught), and `npm run verify:trail-contract` runs the same thing.
- **Bounds (§60).** The proof checks the FIELD NAMES and the nullability of the two nullable ones — it does not check the VALUES, because a value’s correctness is the service’s business and its own tests. It checks the shapes the trail READS; a module that reached the wire through some other path would need its own check, and the proof says which files it grades so that a new reader knows what it is covering. The proof does not replace the v273 contract proof — the two grade different files, and both are needed: one for the client’s declared model, one for the code that actually reads the answer.

### Amendment 293 (M9/v293, docs/evidence/m9) — the SOCIAL verbs’ contract proof, on ONE reader

- **The gap.** The v273 proof grades the client’s declared `ops.ts` model; the v291 proof grades the TRAIL’s shapes. The three social verbs had no cover: the like, the comment and the follow each have a client shape that the service’s wire record does not check — and the failure mode is the same quiet one. The social mappings DROP rows they cannot validate (a comment with no body, a follower with no id), so a renamed wire field would not crash anything: the client would quietly show FEWER rows, and a renamed `handle` would leave the follower list showing account ids with no names — which reads as a fact rather than as a bug.
- **ONE reader, shared.** The proof’s reading machinery now lives in `docs/evidence/m9/wire-fields.mjs`: a Java `record’s field list parsed from the Java, and a TypeScript interface’s field list parsed with the **TypeScript compiler’s own parser** — because a proof that compares a hand-written list with a hand-written list proves only that two people typed the same thing. Two copies of a reader is two places for a reader to be wrong, and the whole point of these proofs is that a reader is CHECKED: the v291 proof was refactored onto the shared reader, and the new social proof sits beside it.
- **What it asserts.** §1 the three verbs’ client shapes and the service’s wire records name the SAME fields — symmetrically: a client that reads a field the service does not send reads nothing, and a field the service sends that the client never reads is a field that arrives and is thrown away. §2 the instant is a `long` of epoch MILLISECONDS on the wire and a number on the client — the same unit on both sides, which is the check that would catch a service sending SECONDS (the v263 incident). §3 the reader is shown to FAIL: renaming the follow’s `handle` leaves the client reading a field the service no longer sends.
- **Files:** `docs/evidence/m9/wire-fields.mjs` (new — the shared reader), `docs/evidence/m9/social-contract-proof.mjs` (new — the proof), `docs/evidence/m9/trail-contract-proof.mjs` (refactored onto the shared reader), `package.json` (the `verify:social-contract` script).
- **Measured:** `node docs/evidence/m9/social-contract-proof.mjs` **exit 0** (all three verbs agree, the instants are the same unit, and the mutation is caught), `node docs/evidence/m9/trail-contract-proof.mjs` **exit 0** after the refactor, and `npm run verify:social-contract` runs the same thing.
- **Bounds (§60).** The proof checks the FIELD NAMES and the instant’s unit — it does not check the VALUES, because a value’s correctness is the service’s business and its own tests. It grades the shapes the social lanes DECLARE; the loose input shapes the mappings validate (the ones that drop rows) are a second surface, and the mapping’s own dropping is graded by the unit tests rather than by this proof. The proof does not replace the v273 or v291 proofs — the three grade different files, and all three are needed.

### Amendment 294 (M7/v294, apps/studio) — the type checker found what no proof had: the un-verbs were routed to nowhere

- **The bug, and who found it.** The Studio’s un-like and un-follow call `/api/likes/<id>` and `/api/follows/<id>` — but both routes were FLAT (`/api/likes/route.ts`), with a DELETE handler that read `params.projectId` / `params.accountId` from a route that had no dynamic segment. The URLs the client called matched nothing, and the un-verbs would have answered **404**. The reads and the writes worked, which is why every proof passed: **nothing in six sections ever un-liked or un-followed.**
- **What found it was the TYPE CHECKER, not a proof.** Next’s typed-routes check reads the generated route types and asserts that each route module satisfies the config for its path — and a handler that reads a path parameter from a route that is not one does not satisfy it. The check had been RED in the studio’s `tsc` since the routes were added, and the red was being cleared by DELETING the generated types — which is the worst possible response to a red check: it made the type checker stop looking. (The fix for the clearing: `next typegen` regenerates the types instead of removing them, and the studio’s `tsc` is now red-free with the types PRESENT — which is the only way the check is worth having.)
- **The fix is the STRUCTURE, not a workaround.** The parent routes keep GET and POST; the DELETE handlers move into `api/likes/[projectId]/route.ts` and `api/follows/[accountId]/route.ts`. A route that reads a path parameter has to BE a path parameter.
- **And now a proof covers it.** §15 of the real-browser harness un-does both, for real: the device that liked the publication takes the like back (the Studio’s `?unlike=` intent), the service’s count goes to ZERO, the SECOND account takes the follow back (the `?unfollow=` intent), and the service’s follower count goes to zero. The section exists because the bug was found by a type checker and NO PROOF had exercised the path — a proof that only ever does the happy path is a proof that cannot find this.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/app/api/likes/[projectId]/route.ts` and `apps/studio/src/app/api/follows/[accountId]/route.ts` (new — the DELETE doors), `apps/studio/src/app/api/likes/route.ts` and `.../api/follows/route.ts` (the DELETE handlers removed), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §15).
- **Measured:** `npx next typegen` (the generated types are regenerated, not deleted) and `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0** with the types present; the real-browser E2E **110/110**, with §15 grading the un-verbs (the un-like takes the like back and the service’s count goes to zero; the un-follow takes the edge back and the follower count goes to zero).
- **The harness learned three things while this section was being written, and each one is a fix in the shipped file.** (1) A failing run now prints the **servers’ own output** — a check that fails because the Studio threw a TypeError is a check whose cause is in the Studio’s log, and a harness that swallows it makes the reader go and guess. (2) The waits budget for a **cold `next dev` compile**: the CDP’s 30-second default, the `waitForFunction`’s 10-second default and the lanes’ 10-second write timeout all outlasted a first route compile and reported the wrong fault — a timeout shorter than the work it waits for names the wrong culprit. (3) The harness waits for the page to **hydrate** before it clicks (`window.__nexus` is installed from a mount effect, and the server-rendered HTML is there long before React attaches its handlers \u2014 a click into a half-hydrated page does nothing, silently).
- **Bounds (§60).** The un-like and the un-follow are now REACHABLE, and that is a new surface rather than a fixed one: the service has always refused a stranger’s un-like and a stranger’s un-follow (v283, v287), and the Studio’s intents build the claim from the device’s own account — so the un-verbs can only ever remove the viewer’s OWN. The trails record the un-verbs (v289), so a taken-back like is a fact the trail keeps.
### Amendment 295 (M7/v295, services/nexus-api) — REPORTS: the M8 social act that asks for help

- **The milestone item.** The ROADMAP’s M8 row has carried **reports** beside subscriptions and tips since the creator economy was designed. The parallel lane’s `ops.ts` already declares the client’s own `Report` shape (`id`, `reporterId`, `targetId`, `reason`, `detail`, `status`, `createdAt`), and the service’s wire shape is that shape field for field, plus the reporter’s handle and assurance.
- **Rule 1: a report needs an ACCOUNT**, refused BY NAME with the reason that matters — “a report with no reporter cannot be followed up”. A report nobody can ask about is a report nobody can act on.
- **Rule 2: the reason is one of FOUR, and the refusal NAMES them** — `spam`, `harassment`, `illegal`, `other`. A closed set means a reader can COUNT by reason, and a caller that is told only “no” has to guess. The four are the client’s own, so the service and the client agree on the set rather than each having one.
- **Rule 3: the detail is bounded, and an EMPTY detail is allowed.** The reason alone is a report; the detail is the reporter’s words, and words have a length. The cap is named in the refusal.
- **Rule 4: the same account cannot report the same publication for the same reason twice.** The UNIQUE constraint on (reporter, target, reason) is the DATABASE’s rule, and the service asks the repository first so the refusal can be a NAMED refusal rather than a constraint violation. A DIFFERENT reason is not a duplicate — a report that says “spam” and a report that says “illegal” are two different facts about the same publication.
- **The withdrawal, and the statuses this build can and cannot reach.** The only move this build supports is the REPORTER withdrawing their own OPEN report, which answers `rejected` — and the service says so plainly. The other two statuses (`reviewed`, `resolved`) belong to a **moderator, and there is no moderator in this build**: the service does not invent a role it has no policy for. The row STAYS when it is withdrawn, because a report that was withdrawn is a fact that happened — the same rule the publication’s take-down and the trail’s entries keep.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/ReportEntry.java` (the entity and its unique constraint), `.../social/ReportRepository.java`, `.../social/ReportService.java` (the four rules), `.../social/ReportController.java` (`POST /reports`, `DELETE /reports/{reportId}?claimer=`, `GET /reports?target=`), `.../social/ReportDtos.java` (the wire shapes), `.../social/InvalidReport.java`, `.../social/NotYourReport.java` (the 403 that is deliberately not a 400), `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/ReportServiceTest.java` (16 cases).
- **Measured:** the service’s social package **64/64** (16 report + 19 comment + 17 like + 12 follow), `mvn -o -B test -Dtest="dev.nexus.api.social.*Test"` **exit 0**, and the module COMPILES. The real-browser proof of the report surface is the next increment.
- **Bounds (§60).** The service does NOT check that the publication exists, and it does NOT verify the account (the same posture the publish service takes — ADR 0018). The detail is stored AS IT ARRIVED: the client escapes it and the page escapes it again, and the service is not a sanitizer. There is no moderation QUEUE, no priority, no assignment and no notification — a moderation workflow needs rules this build does not have. The account is a CLAIM: the assurance travels with every report so a reader is told what it is worth, and nothing here makes it worth more.
### Amendment 296 (M7/v296, apps/studio) — the REPORTS surface: the page shows the count, the Studio files the report

- **The shape of the feature, and why the page cannot file one.** The artifact page is SERVER-RENDERED and does not know who the device is (ADR 0018 is why there is no session), so it shows the COUNT and links to `/?report=<id>`, where the Studio opens a composer — the same arrangement the like, the comment and the follow use. The composer asks for a REASON from a closed set of four (the client’s own) and takes an optional detail.
- **The bar does NOT name the REPORTER, and that is the load-bearing decision.** The service records the reporter’s account id and the name the claim carried, and a page that printed them would turn a report into a PUBLIC ACCUSATION with no moderation behind it — the count is the fact, and the identity is a moderator’s business. The page shows the reasons and the count; the reporter’s name is nowhere on it.
- **A failed read is NOT zero reports.** The bar is left out ENTIRELY when the count could not be read, because “0 reports” and “the reports could not be read” are different facts — and a reader misled into thinking nobody complained is the ONE reader a report page must not mislead.
- **A withdrawn report is shown as withdrawn**, not hidden and not shown as its reason alone: “spam (withdrawn)” says what happened and that the reporter no longer stands by it.
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** §16: the artifact page carries a REPORTS bar with a count of zero and offers the report as a link to the Studio; the Studio opens a composer over the intent; posting says so in the Studio’s own words WITH the reason; the SERVICE recorded the report (read independently of the browser, from the real database) naming the reason, the body and the ACCOUNT that filed it; the artifact page now says ONE report and does NOT name the reporter; a device with NO account is refused by name and the refused report changed NOTHING.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/reportServer.ts` (the server-side read and write), `apps/studio/src/lib/reportLane.ts` (the browser half, with the 45s write timeout v294 introduced), `apps/studio/src/lib/reportBar.ts` and `reportBar.test.ts` (the pure bar, 16 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/reportIntent.ts` (the URL intent), `apps/studio/src/app/api/reports/route.ts` (the Studio’s door), `apps/studio/src/components/ReportComposer.tsx` (the composer), `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the intent), `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts` (the page reads the count and injects the bar), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §16).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1050/1051 (57 files)** — this increment’s own **16** cases pass; the one failure is a concurrent lane’s in-flight `probe293`, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, the service’s social package **64/64**, doc gate **exit 0**; the real-browser E2E **121/121** with the new §16.
- **Bounds (§60).** The composer is a Studio overlay, so filing a report costs a trip to the Studio — the price of not having a session. The page shows the COUNT and the reasons, never the reporter. There is no moderation queue, no assignment, no notification and no way for the reporter to change the reason after filing (a report is appended, and a second report for the same reason is refused by the service) — a moderation workflow needs rules this build does not have. The detail is stored as it arrived: the client escapes it and the page escapes it again.
### Amendment 297 (M7/v297, services/nexus-api) — TIPS: the first social act that carries an AMOUNT

- **The milestone item.** The ROADMAP’s M8 row has carried **tips** beside subscriptions since the creator economy was designed, and the parallel lane’s `monetization.ts` already declares the client’s own `Tip` shape (`recipientId`, `amountCents`, `message`, `anonymous`). The service’s wire shape is that shape field for field, plus the payer’s account, handle, assurance, the currency, the id and the instant.
- **Rule 1: a tip needs a RECIPIENT and a PAYER.** The recipient is who the tip is for; the payer is the account that gave it. Both are the claim’s account. A tip with neither is not a fact anyone can act on.
- **Rule 2: the amount is POSITIVE and CAPPED, and each refusal says WHICH.** A tip of **zero** is not a tip. A **negative** amount is money moving the wrong way round, and the service refuses it by name rather than storing a number that reads like a payment in reverse. The **cap** (a million yuan) is named in the refusal: a tip that large is a typo or an attack, and this build has no payment rail that would make it meaningful.
- **Rule 3: the MESSAGE is bounded** and may be empty — an amount with no note is still a tip.
- **Rule 4: the amount is recorded AS IT WAS.** A price that changes later does not rewrite what was given, because “they gave 500 cents” is a fact about the past and a fact about the past does not move. The tip is APPENDED and never edited.
- **The total is summed by the DATABASE**, not by the service: a service that counted in memory would drift the moment two tips arrived together, and a total that drifts is a total nobody can defend.
- **What the service does NOT do: move money.** This service holds no payment token and moves no funds (ADR 0018). A tip here is a RECORD of a gesture — “this account gave that amount to that account” — and never a statement that a payment happened. The service verifies nothing: the accounts are claims, and the assurance travels with every tip so a reader is told what it is worth.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/TipEntry.java` (the entity), `.../social/TipRepository.java` (the finders and the DATABASE-side sum), `.../social/TipService.java` (the four rules), `.../social/TipController.java` (`POST /tips`, `GET /tips?recipient=`), `.../social/TipDtos.java` (the wire shapes), `.../social/InvalidTip.java`, `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/TipServiceTest.java` (12 cases).
- **Measured:** the service’s social package **76/76** (12 tip + 16 report + 19 comment + 17 like + 12 follow), `mvn -o -B test -Dtest="dev.nexus.api.social.*Test"` **exit 0**, and the module COMPILES. The real-browser proof of the tip surface is the next increment.
- **Bounds (§60).** The currency is **CNY** in this build — and the client says the same — so the amount is never a bare number. There is no currency conversion, no refund, no payout, and no way to see what a recipient has been paid out: this build records gestures, it does not move money. The tip is not tied to a publication (the client’s `Tip` names a RECIPIENT, not a work) — and saying so is the point, because tying a tip to a work would be a claim the service cannot check. A spammer can tip many times: the rules here are about honesty, not about moderation, and moderation is the same missing piece the reports have.
### Amendment 298 (M7/v298, apps/studio) — the TIPS surface: a tip is for an ACCOUNT, so the bar is on the profile

- **Where the bar belongs, and why.** A tip is for an ACCOUNT, not for a work — the client’s own `Tip` names a `recipientId`, not a publication — so the bar belongs on the **PROFILE**, the page a reader lands on when they want to know about a person. The explore page and the artifact page carry the things that happen to works; the profile carries the things that happen to people.
- **The page shows the NUMBERS and the MESSAGES, and never the PAYER.** The service records who gave what, and a page that printed the payer’s name would turn a small gesture into a public list of who supports whom. The count and the total are the facts; the identities are the reader’s business.
- **A failed read is NOT zero tips.** The bar is left out ENTIRELY when the count could not be read, because “no tips” and “the tips could not be read” are different facts — and a creator’s page must not say the first when it knows the second.
- **The composer asks for YUAN and sends CENTS.** The currency is CNY in this build (the client says the same), and the composer converts before it sends: a decimal amount is a thing a client and a service can disagree about, and the service’s unit is cents.
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** §17: the profile page carries a TIPS bar with a count of zero and offers the tip as a link to the Studio; the Studio opens a composer over the intent; posting says so in the Studio’s own words with the amount; the SERVICE recorded the tip (read independently of the browser, from the real database) naming the amount, the message and the account that gave it; the TOTAL is what the DATABASE summed; the profile page now says ONE tip and carries ¥5.00; and a device with NO account is refused by name, with the refused tip changing NOTHING.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/tipServer.ts` (the server-side read and write), `apps/studio/src/lib/tipLane.ts` (the browser half, with the 45s write timeout), `apps/studio/src/lib/tipBar.ts` and `tipBar.test.ts` (the pure bar, 13 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/tipIntent.ts` (the URL intent), `apps/studio/src/app/api/tips/route.ts` (the Studio’s door), `apps/studio/src/components/TipComposer.tsx` (the composer), `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the intent), `apps/studio/src/app/u/[accountId]/route.ts` (the profile reads the tips and injects the bar), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §17, and the harness’s own fixes).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1063/1064 (58 files)** — this increment’s own **13** cases pass; the one failure is a concurrent lane’s in-flight `probe293`; `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**; the real-browser E2E **133/133** with the new §17.
- **The harness learned three more things, and each is a fix in the shipped file.** (1) The servers’ logs were declared INSIDE the harness’s `try`, so the failure path — which lives after it — could not see them: the feature that prints the servers’ own output printed nothing, and the run said “the tip did not land” without saying why. (2) The harness’s checks that waited for a page’s own text now print the PAGE’s text when the wait gives up — a lane that refused says why, and the reason is the fact worth printing. (3) The tipper signs in FIRST, because the previous section ends by clearing the account — a tip with no payer is refused by name, so a tipper with no account would have been testing the refusal instead of the tip.
- **Bounds (§60).** The composer is a Studio overlay, so giving a tip costs a trip to the Studio. The amount is CNY and there is no conversion. The total is the DATABASE’s sum over the WHOLE history (not just the window the page read), so the number on the page and the number in the answer can differ when the window is shorter than the history — and the page shows the count it read beside the total the service knows. A tip is a RECORD of a gesture and never a payment (ADR 0018), and the page says the count and the total without ever saying that money moved.
### Amendment 299 (M9/v299, apps/studio) — the ECONOMY panel becomes REAL: the tips this account was given

- **What changed, and why it took five increments to get here.** v274 added the panel and found that there was nothing behind it: no economy endpoints existed, so the panel said ‘the economy door is not built’. That was honest, and it stayed honest for five increments — until v297 gave the service a tips table and v298 gave the profile its bar. Now the panel shows the REAL numbers: the tips the device’s account was given and the total they came to.
- **The total is the SERVICE’s number** (the DATABASE’s sum over the whole history), reported unchanged. A panel that added to the count would be showing a number the service never said — and the count it read (the window) and the total it knows are DIFFERENT numbers when the history is longer than the window, so the panel says both.
- **The panel asks WHO IT IS WHEN IT OPENS, not at render time.** The account can be set (or changed) after the toolbar last rendered, and a panel that asked ‘who am I’ when it mounted would answer for an account that no longer exists. This was found by the real-browser proof: the panel said ‘this device has no account’ for a device that had one.
- **And it says what has NOT been built.** The SUBSCRIPTIONS still need a PLAN CATALOG — who sets the price and the period — and that is a product decision this build has not made. The panel says so in words instead of showing a fake ‘no subscriptions’ as though the feature were there and empty: a reader who saw ‘no subscriptions’ would conclude that nobody subscribes, which is a different claim from ‘subscriptions are not built’.
