- **Bounds (§60).** Retiring is not cancelling: the subscriptions keep standing and the supporter is not refunded, charged, or told anything (there is no billing and no mail in this build — ADR 0018). A plan can be retired and it cannot be un-retired — the row’s `active` flag is a one-way fact, and offering the same plan id again is refused by the plan id’s own uniqueness. The creator’s claim is a CLAIM (the same posture as the take-down’s): the service compares the account id it was given with the row’s, and the account id is public — so a caller who knows a creator’s id can retire that creator’s plan, and the build says so rather than pretending otherwise. There is no grace period and no `unretire`: a creator who wants the offer back offers a NEW plan id.
### Amendment 317 (M7/v315, apps/studio) — the holder can END a subscription

- **The gap.** The service has had the ending since v300 (`DELETE /subscriptions/{id}?claimer=`, and it refuses somebody else’s subscription by name) and the panel had **no button** for it. So a supporter who wanted to stop backing a plan had no way to say so from the product — the promise simply stood, and the only way to be rid of it was to end the DEVICE’s account and lose everything else with it.
- **Ending is not deleting.** The row STAYS and its standing becomes `cancelled`, because a promise that was ended is a fact that happened — the same rule the taken-down publication and the withdrawn report keep. The panel’s button appears only on the rows that are still STANDING: an expired or an ended subscription has nothing left to end, and a button that would do nothing is a button that lies.
- **The button names the SUBSCRIPTION, not the plan.** Two subscriptions of the same plan are two promises, and a panel that could only name the plan could not end one of them — so the row carries the subscription’s own id (the wire already had it ✓) and the button carries that.
- **The panel says whether the call MOVED anything.** "ended" and "was already ended" are different facts, and a panel that said "ended" either way would claim a change that did not happen — the same rule the report’s withdrawal and the plan’s retirement follow ✓.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§29).** The creator offers a FRESH plan (§27 ended the only subscription there was and §28 retired the plan it was made against — so the section builds its own) → a supporter backs it → the panel offers the holder the ending → the subscription shows as ended, with the row still there → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser (the row’s status is `cancelled`).
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/planServer.ts` (`cancelSubscription`), `apps/studio/src/lib/planLane.ts` (`cancelSubscription`), `apps/studio/src/lib/planLane.test.ts` (+3 cases), `apps/studio/src/app/api/subscriptions/route.ts` (a DELETE beside the POST), `apps/studio/src/lib/economy.ts` (the row carries the subscription’s own id), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the button, the note), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §29).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1147/1147 (63 files)**, the service’s social package **106/106** (unchanged — this increment is the client’s half of a door the service already had), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **196/196** with the new §29.
- **Bounds (§60).** Ending a subscription does not refund, charge, or notify anybody — there is no billing and no mail in this build (ADR 0018), and the service’s `cancel` refuses with a 400 rather than a 403 (a well-formed request that names somebody else’s subscription) — which is the package’s own older shape ✓, and it is named here rather than quietly changed. The panel’s button is on the SUBSCRIPTIONS THIS DEVICE HOLDS — the ones the account paid for with a claim — and the service’s comparison is the same claim-posture as everywhere else: the account id is named, and the id is public. There is no `un-end`: a subscription that was ended stays ended, and backing the plan again is the database’s one-per-plan rule (v313’s bound ✓).
### Amendment 318 (M7/v311, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the trail records the REPORT verbs

- **The gap.** v289 put the like and the comment into the audit trail, and the report — the one social act that asks somebody ELSE to do something — had never been there. So a complaint left **no entry at all**: no record that it was filed, and no record that the reporter withdrew it. A complaint nobody can audit is a complaint nobody can answer, and the trail is where a reader looks for what happened.
- **The service writes both halves down.** `report` when a report is filed and `withdraw-report` when the reporter takes it back — INSIDE the transaction, like the like and the comment: a rolled-back report leaves no entry claiming a report happened. And only a report that was actually filed is written down: a refused duplicate is an ATTEMPT, and a trail that recorded attempts would be a trail of things that did not happen. The service’s own cases grade both (2 new in the report package): the filing writes, the withdrawal writes, and a REFUSED filing writes nothing.
- **The panel learns the words.** "reported", "withdrew the report", and — the one the service has recorded since v304 — "acknowledged the report". Until now that last one appeared as the raw action, which is honest but reads like a machine; the raw word was the right answer for a verb this build had no word for, and now there IS a word.
- **The tally gets its own buckets** (`reported` / `withdrew the report` / `acknowledged`), for the same reason the social verbs have their own (v289): a tally that called a complaint "other" would be hiding the very thing a reader of the trail is looking for. The tally still says only the buckets that are NOT ZERO, so it does not grow a line of zeroes as the verbs arrive.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§25).** The trail panel carries the filing, the withdrawal and the acknowledgement → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser (`GET /audit` carries all three actions) — because the panel could be showing its own copy.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/ReportService.java` (the trail, and the two records), `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/ReportServiceTest.java` (+2 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.ts` (the three words, the three buckets), `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.test.ts` (+2 cases), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §25).
- **Measured:** the service’s social package **112/112** (the report package 23/23), `apps/studio` **1128/1128 (61 files)**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **200/200** with the new §25.
- **Bounds (§60).** **The verbs whose target is NOT a publication are still out of the trail** — the follow and the tip (both about an ACCOUNT) and the plan and the subscription (about a PLAN) — and the reason is the same one the report’s identity is kept out of the wire (v307): the trail’s target column means "the publication this happened to", so a row saying "followed acct-ada" in that column would be a small lie. They would need the trail to say what KIND of thing the target is — a column the audit’s table does not have — which is a schema change, and this build has no migration tool (its own configuration says so). So the trail is named here as a bound and left for an increment that can carry a migration. The trail still names ACCOUNT IDS and not handles (v270’s finding: the service has no account table to resolve them with), so a reader of a report’s entry sees who filed it and not what they are called.
### Amendment 319 (M7/v316, apps/studio) — YOU FOLLOW: and the one way to take a follow back

- **The gap.** The un-follow has existed since v288 — the intent (`/?unfollow={accountId}`), the lane, the Studio’s door and the service’s own door (which refuses somebody else’s edge by name). **Nothing in the product pointed at it.** A capability with no door is a capability nobody can reach, and a reader who cannot undo a follow has a page that only ever grows: every follow is permanent, and the graph’s edge count is a number you can only increase.
- **The desk’s third section: YOU FOLLOW.** The accounts THIS device follows, each a link to that account’s profile, and beside each one an **Unfollow** button. The desk is where the device’s own social facts live — what came to you (the reports), what you sent (the complaints you filed) and, now, who you follow — and the follow is the only one of the three a reader can take back. The button appears on the device’s OWN list, because the Studio knows who the device is; the server-rendered profile page does not, and a page that showed an "Unfollow" button on somebody else’s follows would be offering a button that always fails.
- **The read, and the rule it keeps.** The Studio’s `/api/follows` grew a GET beside its POST (`?follower=`), and the browser half (`readMyFollowing`) answers with a REASON and never a thrown error. **A failed read is NOT an empty list**: "this device follows nobody" and "the list could not be read" are different facts, and a panel that showed the first when it knew the second would tell a reader their follows had gone — the same rule the desk’s tally keeps (v312) and the same rule the rest of the studio keeps.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§30).** The desk shows who this device follows → the Unfollow button takes it back → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: the edge is GONE (`?follower=` answers with an empty list).
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/app/api/follows/route.ts` (a GET beside the POST), `apps/studio/src/lib/followLane.ts` (`readMyFollowing`), `apps/studio/src/lib/followLane.test.ts` (new — 3 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the `YOU FOLLOW` section, the un-follow, the note’s hook), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §30, and the duplicate §25 a re-run had left behind removed).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1150/1150 (64 files)**, the service’s social package **112/112** (unchanged — this increment is the client’s half of doors the service already had), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **199/199** with the new §30.
- **Bounds (§60).** The un-follow is a CLAIM, exactly like every other write here: the studio sends the account id the device holds and the service compares it with the row’s follower — which is why the button is on the device’s OWN list and why the service refuses somebody else’s edge by name (a 403, `not-your-follow`). The PROFILE page still cannot offer the button: it is server-rendered and does not know who the reader is (ADR 0018), so the un-follow lives in the desk rather than on the profile. And the desk is now three sections wide (what came to you, what you sent, who you follow) with the tally above them — a panel that keeps growing is a panel that stops being read, and if a fourth section ever arrives it should be a new panel rather than a fourth block here.
### Amendment 320 (M7/v317, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the creator can CHANGE the price of a plan

- **The gap.** A creator could OFFER a plan (v301) and RETIRE it (v314) — and there was no way to change its price. So a plan’s price was fixed for ever, and a creator whose work got more (or less) valuable had no way to say so: the only honest move was to offer a NEW plan id, and the old one sat in the catalogue beside it for ever. The price is a SNAPSHOT precisely so that a change can be made (v300) — and this is the door that makes it.
- **The rule, and the thing it does NOT do.** `PUT /plans/{planId}?claimer=&price=&period=` — and only the creator’s own plan (a 403, `not-your-plan`, by name). **A price change does not touch the subscriptions already made**: each one holds the price as a snapshot, so a supporter who agreed to ¥15 a month still agreed to ¥15 a month, and the new price is what the NEXT subscriber agrees to. The service’s own case says so by asserting that the subscriptions repository is never written — a case that would fail the moment someone made a price change cascade.
- **The surface.** The account panel’s plan form grows a second button — **Change the price** — beside **Offer**, on the same three fields (the plan id, the price in yuan, the period). One form, two verbs, and the form says which is which: a creator typing a plan id they already offer and pressing "Change the price" is changing the price, and pressing "Offer" is offering a new plan (which the service refuses if the id is taken). The panel’s note says what happened, including the part that matters: "the subscriptions already made keep the price they were agreed at".
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§31).** The creator changes the price of a plan they offer → the panel says the new price and says that the old subscriptions did not move → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: the plan now costs the new price. (The snapshot itself is graded by the service’s own case — the proof’s subscriptions had all been ended by the sections before it, so there was no standing one to watch stay put.)
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/PlanEntry.java` (`reprice`), `.../social/SubscriptionService.java` (`reprice`), `.../social/SubscriptionController.java` (the `PUT` door), `services/nexus-api/src/test/java/dev/nexus/api/social/SubscriptionServiceTest.java` (+5 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/planServer.ts` (`repricePlan`), `apps/studio/src/lib/planLane.ts` (`repricePlan`), `apps/studio/src/lib/planLane.test.ts` (+2 cases), `apps/studio/src/app/api/plans/route.ts` (a PUT beside the POST and the DELETE), `apps/studio/src/components/AccountPanel.tsx` (the second button), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §31).
- **Measured:** the service’s social package **117/117** (the subscription package 37/37), `apps/studio` **1152/1152 (64 files)**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **201/201** with the new §31.
- **Bounds (§60).** A price change is the creator’s word about what their work costs from now on, and it is still a CLAIM (there is no session in this build — ADR 0018): the service compares the account id it was given with the plan’s creator, which is exactly as strong as the take-down’s owner check, and exactly as weak. The currency does not change (a plan’s currency is set when it is offered), a RETIRED plan may be repriced but stays retired (retiring is one-way), and there is no history of prices: the plan carries the price it has NOW, and the subscriptions carry the prices they were agreed at — which is where a price’s history lives, as a fact per subscription.
### Amendment 321 (M7/v318, apps/studio) — the desk filters by REASON

- **The gap.** The reasons are a closed set of four (v295) and the desk’s tally counts them (v312) — so the panel could already say "two spam and one harassment" — but a creator who wanted to LOOK at the spam ones had to read every row to find them. A count that cannot be turned into a list is a number, not a door: the tally made the reasons legible and then stopped there.
- **The filter.** One button per reason, and **only for the reasons that OCCUR**: a button for a reason with no reports is noise, and a reader who has learned to skip the whole row will not look again. The filter asks in the **service’s own word** (the raw reason — `spam`, `harassment`, `illegal`, `other`), not in the display word, the same rule the trail’s filter follows: a filter that matched on the translation would break the moment the translation changed, and the display word is a translation.
- **The tally is NOT filtered.** The tally keeps counting the whole answer, so the filter never hides anything without a number saying it is there — v281’s rule, the one the trail’s tally already keeps. Both are on screen at once, and the proof grades exactly that: filtering narrows the list, and the tally still names the reasons that are now off screen.
- **A filter that matches nothing says so.** "no reports with this reason" — because an empty list under a full tally reads as "the rows are still loading", and a reader who asked for one reason and saw nothing deserves to be told that the desk HAS reports, just not of that one.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§32).** The desk offers a filter for each reason that occurs → filtering by a reason narrows the LIST → the TALLY still counts the whole answer → and "All" brings every row back.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/moderation.ts` (`filterDeskRows` — pure, and it hands back a COPY so a caller cannot narrow the desk in place), `apps/studio/src/lib/moderation.test.ts` (+4 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the filter row, the narrowed rows, the empty note), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §32).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1156/1156 (64 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **136/136** (unchanged — this increment is the client’s half of a view the data already supported), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **207/207** with the new §32.
- **Bounds (§60).** **The filter is a VIEW, not a filter in the service**: the whole desk still comes over the wire and the rows are narrowed in the browser, so a desk with a thousand reports would still read a thousand — and the service’s desk door takes no reason parameter. Moving the narrowing to the service is a door that does not exist yet (it would be a query parameter the service would have to validate against its own closed set), and it is named here as the next step rather than done. The buttons wear the service’s own words on purpose: a paraphrased label would need a second mapping table, and the mapping a reader needs is the tally’s. And the filter is **not remembered**: the panel holds it in the component’9s state, so a reader who filtered yesterday and comes back finds the whole desk — deliberately, because a filter remembered from last week, applied to a desk that has changed since, answers a question nobody asked.
### Amendment 322 (M7/v319, apps/studio) — the trail filters by the REPORT verbs

- **The gap.** The trail has recorded the report verbs since v311 — the filing, the withdrawal and the owner’s acknowledgement — and the panel has counted them in its own summary since the same increment. But the trail’s FILTER stopped at the comment (v289’s social verbs): the three report actions were visible only under "All". So a reader asking the question the trail exists to answer — "was my work complained about?" — had to read the whole trail to find out, and the one action an owner ACTS on (the acknowledgement) was the hardest to find of the three.
- **Three more buttons: Reported / Withdrew / Acknowledged.** Each asks in the trail’s own **action** (`report`, `withdraw-report`, `acknowledge`), the same raw word every other button on that row has used since v281. The row now **wraps**: eight buttons do not fit in one line of a 400px panel, and a filter row that overflows its panel pushes its own summary out of sight — the summary is the part that says what the filter is hiding.
- **The label wears the display word; the filter asks in the raw action.** The buttons read "Reported" (the display word is "reported") and the filter takes `report` (the service’s action). Those are two different strings on purpose, and a unit case now pins the difference: **filtering by "reported" matches nothing**. If the two were the same string, a rename of the display word would silently change what the filter means — and a filter that suddenly matched nothing would look like a trail that suddenly went empty.
- **The summary still counts the whole trail** (v281’s rule, the one the desk keeps too): the filter narrows the list, the summary keeps the total, and both are on screen at once.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§33).** The trail offers a filter for every action it records, and the report verbs are among them → filtering by an action shows ONLY that action → the summary still counts the whole trail → and "All" brings every row back.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (three buttons, and the row wraps), `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.test.ts` (+2 cases), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §33).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1158/1158 (64 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **136/136** (unchanged — the service has recorded these actions since v311; this increment gives them a door in the panel), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **212/212** with the new §33.
- **Bounds (§60).** **The trail’s filter still has no buttons for the two undoings the service records** — `unlike` and `uncomment` — so "who took their like back?" is still an "All" question; the row is already two lines deep and the undoings are the least-asked-for pair, so they are named here and left for the increment that can afford them. The filter is a VIEW over the whole trail: the service’s `/audit` takes no action parameter, so the narrowing happens in the browser over a page the service already sent — the same shape as the desk’s reason filter (v318), and the same next step for both (a parameter the service would have to validate against its own set of actions). And the buttons are stable rather than dynamic: unlike the desk’s reason filter, which offers only the reasons that OCCUR, the trail offers every action it knows, so a reader can press a button before anything of that kind has happened — and the panel says "no entries of that action" rather than pretending the button was always there.
### Amendment 323 (M7/v320, apps/studio) — the UN-LIKE gets a door in the product

- **The gap.** The un-like’s chain was already whole: the intent (`/?unlike={id}` ✓), the lane ✓, the Studio’s own door ✓, the service’s door ✓, and the service’s own rule that somebody else’s like cannot be taken back ✓. **Nothing in the product pointed at it.** The artifact page’s bar offered exactly one link — "Like" — so a reader who had liked a publication could never take the like back: the count was a number only the reader could increase, and the trail’s `unlike` verb (recorded by the service since v289) was a fact that no reader could ever cause. A capability with no door is a capability nobody can reach — the same shape the un-follow had before v316.
- **The bar offers the taking-back.** A second link, `/?unlike={id}`, beside the like — the same arrangement (a link to the Studio, where the account lives) and the same wording discipline: the page still **cannot say whether YOU liked it**, so the link is an OFFER and not a claim. The bar’s own rule — "a button that says ‘Liked’ when the liker is unknown would be a claim the page cannot support" — is graded: the bar’s HTML carries no "liked" at all, and a case says so.
- **The Studio’s words were the liar, and now they are not.** The service answers the same way whether there was a like to take back or not — "a like that is already gone is already gone" is its own rule — so the old message, "took the like back on X", said something untrue for a reader who had never liked it. The message is now "**the like on X is gone — N like(s) now**", which is true in both cases. The existing proof’s check was updated to grade the new words, and it grades the SHAPE of them, not a phrase that can drift.
- **The trail can now ask for it by name.** The filter row gains a **Like taken back** button (`unlike`), because the service has recorded that fact since v289 and the product can now cause it: a filter that could not name a recorded verb would leave it in the "All" bucket with no way to say "just the takings-back".
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§34).** The bar offers the taking-back → the device likes the publication again → the SERVICE counts it → the device takes it back → the SERVICE agrees the like is gone → the trail offers a filter for the taking-back → and filtering by it shows ONLY the taking-backs. The section runs a whole cycle of its own, so the counts and the trail are graded on this section’s facts and not on the ones the earlier section happened to leave behind.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/likeBar.ts` (the second link, its style, and the bar’s rule), `apps/studio/src/lib/likeBar.test.ts` (+2 cases), `apps/studio/src/components/Studio.tsx` (the honest words), `apps/studio/src/components/Toolbar.tsx` (the trail’s new button), `apps/studio/src/lib/trail.test.ts` (+1 case), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §34, and the existing un-like check’s words updated).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1161/1161 (64 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **136/136** (unchanged — the service already had the door and the rule), `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **219/219** with the new §34.
- **Bounds (§60).** The bar offers the taking-back to EVERY reader, including one who never liked the publication — the page cannot know, and the service’s answer (and the Studio’s new words) are what tell the truth about it; the alternative — a bar that only offered the taking-back to somebody who had liked it — would need the page to know who is asking, which is ADR 0018’s session, not this build. The service’s idempotency is untouched: taking a like that is already gone is not an error, and no trail entry is written for it, because a thing that did not happen is not a fact to record. And **the other undoing is still shut**: the service records `uncomment` (v289) and the studio has no door, no intent and no link for it — a comment its author cannot take back is the same gap this increment closed for the like, and it is named here as the next one.
### Amendment 324 (M7/v321, apps/studio) — the UN-COMMENT gets a door in the product

- **The gap.** The service has had the take-back of a comment since v289 — `DELETE /comments/{id}`, the author’s own rule, the trail’s `uncomment` verb — and the STUDIO had **no door at all**: no server half, no lane, no route, no intent, no link. So a comment its author could not take back was a comment that could only be lived with, and the trail’s `uncomment` verb was a fact no reader could ever cause. This is the same shape the un-like had one increment ago (v320), and the same shape the un-follow had before v316: a capability with no door is a capability nobody can reach.
- **The chain, built end to end.** The server half (`removeCommentOnService`) → the browser half (`removeComment`) → the Studio’s own door (`DELETE /api/comments/{commentId}?claimer=`, a DYNAMIC SEGMENT, because a route that reads a path parameter has to BE a path parameter — v294’s lesson) → the intent (`/?uncomment={id}`) → the Studio’s handling → and the artifact page’s comments section, which now carries a **Take it back** link on every comment that is still standing.
- **The link is an OFFER, not a claim.** The page is server-rendered and cannot know who is reading (ADR 0018), so it does not say "your comment" and it does not hide the link from somebody else’s comment: every standing comment carries the link, and the SERVICE is the one that refuses somebody else’s comment by name. A comment that is ALREADY removed carries no link — there is nothing to take back, and offering it would be offering a thing that does not exist.
- **The words are the service’s own truth.** The service answers 200 whether a comment was taken back or was already gone, and it says which: `removed` is true when a row was taken back. So the Studio says **two different sentences**: "took the comment back — the thread now says it was removed by its author", and "that comment was already gone". A client that dropped the flag would say "took it back" about a comment nobody took back — the same lie the un-like’s message used to tell (v320).
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§35).** The artifact page’s comments section offers the taking-back → the Studio takes the comment back → the SERVICE agrees: the comment comes back marked as removed and the VISIBLE count drops → and the trail carries the `uncomment` → and the service’s own two answers are the two the client words differently.

### Amendment 329 (M7/v326, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the desk’s filter is the SERVICE’s

- **The gap.** v318 gave the desk a reason filter, and it was a VIEW: the whole desk came over the wire and the browser narrowed it. A creator with a thousand reports would download a thousand rows to see the spam ones — and the narrowing was in the wrong place, because the one that knows the reasons is the service. The v318 record named this as the next step ("moving the narrowing to the service is a door that does not exist yet"), and this increment is that door.
- **The service narrows, in its QUERY.** `GET /moderation/reports?owner=&reason=` — and the narrowing happens in the finder (`findByTargetProjectIdInAndReasonOrderByCreatedAtDesc`), not after it. That distinction is the whole increment: the desk’s rows are a WINDOW (the most recent N), and a window taken BEFORE the narrowing would answer a different question than the one asked — "the most recent hundred reports, of which these are the spam ones" rather than "the most recent hundred spam reports". The cap has to reach the database either way, and the two questions must not be confused.
- **A reason this build does not know is REFUSED BY NAME.** The reasons are a closed set of four (the social package’s own set — v295), and an unknown reason is a 400 that names them — not a reason that is quietly ignored. A caller that asked for a reason the service does not have and was answered with the whole desk would read the answer as "there was nothing of that reason", which is a different fact, and the one that matters.
- **The TALLY is not narrowed.** It is a door of its own (v312) and it counts EVERY report against the work — which is exactly what lets a reader see what the filter is hiding. The panel’s filter buttons now come from the tally’s own keys, because the rows on screen are narrowed and reading the reasons off them would offer only the reason already chosen.
- **The browser’s copy of the narrowing is GONE.** `filterDeskRows` and its four cases were removed: two mechanisms doing one job is how a filter starts disagreeing with itself, and the service’s answer is the truth. The panel asks again when a button is pressed, and renders what the service answered.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§40).** The desk offers the reason filter → the panel shows ONLY that reason → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: its own answer for that reason carries that reason and nothing else → and the TALLY still counts the whole.

The desk’s narrowing changed one thing a reader can see: the window is now the most recent N **of that reason** (v318’s browser-side filter narrowed the most recent N of all reasons) — which is the better answer to the question actually asked, and it is stated here because it is a change in what "the desk" means. ### Amendment 330 (M7/v327, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the creator sees WHO backs their plan

- **The gap.** v310 gave the creator the other side of the relation — the subscriptions they RECEIVED — and the rows showed a plan, a price and a standing. **They did not show who.** A creator reading that list was reading a list of plans, and the question a creator actually has ("who is backing this, and who stopped?") had no answer on the page. The name was not missing from the data: the supporter’s CLAIM carried it, and the service threw it away on the way in.

The wire’s `handle` and `assurance` slots have existed since v300 and were filled with **null** by the controller; they are filled with the row’s values now. Nothing about the wire’s SHAPE changed: a slot that was there and empty is now there and carries what it was always meant to carry.

The panel never invents a name, and it never shows a blank: the service’s own case says a claim without a handle produces a row without one.

### Amendment 331 (M7/v328, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the creator sees WHEN a subscription was taken back

- **The gap.** v327 gave the creator the supporter’s NAME, and the standing said whether the subscription was still up. But a row said **that** it ended and never **when**: the `active` flag was a fact about the past, and an expired subscription knew its period’s end, while a CANCELLED one knew only that it was over. So a creator asking the question a creator actually asks — "who stopped backing me, and when" — had half an answer, and the missing half was the date.
- **The row keeps the instant.** `SubscriptionEntry` gains `ended_at`, and the service writes the instant of the cancellation (`markCancelled(clock.instant())`) — the service’s own clock, because "when the supporter took it back" is a fact about a machine and not about a browser. The wire’s `Subscription` gains the matching `endedAt`.
- **The ending is the CANCELLATION’s, and the column is nullable for that reason.** A standing subscription has no ending; one that merely ran out of its period ended on its `expiresAt`, which is a different date and a different fact. The service’s own cases pin both halves: a cancelled row carries an instant, and a row that was never taken back carries none. The panel shows the line only when there is one — a row that says nothing rather than guessing.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§42).** The creator’s received row says WHEN the subscription was taken back → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: it sends the same instant it wrote down, and the panel’s date is that very date.

The column is **added** by `ddl-auto: update` (which adds columns but never drops constraints — the schema-bound work that genuinely needs a migration tool is the trail’s target kind and the subscription’s renewal, not this), and a subscription made BEFORE this increment has no name on its row: its supporter sees the creator’s account id, which is the truth about that row. And the supporter’s row still does not say what the plan BUYS — a plan is a promise of support, and this build has no billing to keep it (v313’s bound), so the row says what was agreed and not what was delivered.
### Amendment 334 (M7/v331, apps/studio) — the recipient of a tip sees WHO sent it

- **The gap.** The tip’s service has kept the payer’s handle since v298 (the row’s `payer_handle`, the payer’s own claim) and the wire has carried it since then too. The **panel** was calling every payer "a supporter" and throwing the name away — a category where a person was available. So a creator reading the money that came to them could see the amount and the message and not who gave it.
- **The lane stops dropping it.** The tips lane narrowed every tip to an amount, a message and a flag; it now keeps the payer’s name and the payer’s account id. The panel asks the same pure helper the economy module uses (`tipPayerText`), so the wording lives in one place: the name when the claim carried one, the account id when it did not, and "nobody" when neither is there — an address is better than a hole, and the panel never invents a name.
- **An ANONYMOUS tip says "Anonymous" and shows no name at all.** That is the payer’s own choice about their own money, and the recipient is told the tip is anonymous rather than being shown a name the payer withheld. The unit cases pin all three branches, because the anonymous branch is the one that must never leak: a tip that is anonymous with a name on the wire still reads "Anonymous".
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§45).** The recipient’s tip row names WHO sent it → and it is the tipper’s name and not a category → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: it sends the payer’s name on the wire, and the panel shows that very name.

- **Bounds (§60).** This increment is the CLIENT’s half of a fact the service has been sending since the tip’s own beginning — the name was never missing from the wire, only from the panel — and the record says so, because "the panel was not saying it" and "the data was not there" are different gaps. The name is a CLAIM (the service records it and verifies nothing — ADR 0018), exactly like the follower’s name on the follow row and the supporter’s name on the subscription row. A payer who changes their handle afterwards is still shown under the name they tipped with — a fact about the past. And **the tip’s amount and message are still the substance**: the panel names the person because the service knows who, and it does not say the money bought anything — a tip is a gift, and this build has no fulfilment to promise (v298’s bound).
### Amendment 335 (M7/v332, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the tipper sees what THEY gave

- **The gap.** A tip is a relation, and the product had only one side of it: the RECIPIENT could see the money that came to them (v298) — and the PAYER could see nothing. A reader who gave money and could not see what they gave had a receipt with no place to read it. The service’s repository has had the finder for the payer’s side since v298 (`findByPayerAccountIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc`) — with no service method, no door and no panel to reach it. That is the same gap the subscription had before v310, and the same shape of fix.
- **The same door, the other direction.** `GET /tips?payer=` — beside `?recipient=` — the way the subscriptions door answers both "what do I back" and "who backs me" (v310). The service gains `tipsGiven` and `totalGiven`, and the total is summed by the DATABASE (`sumAmountCentsByPayerAccountId`), not by the service: a total the service added up in memory would be the sum of a WINDOW, and a window’s sum is not a total.
- **The panel grows a section, not a row.** The economy panel gains **Tips you gave** under the tips it received — a receipt, in the reader’s own account. It says whether the tip was given in the open or anonymously (the payer’s own choice, shown to the payer), and it does not name the recipient: the recipient is a public identity, but the PAYER is the one reading, and the tip’s own amount and message are the substance of what they gave.

### Amendment 338 (M7/v335, services/nexus-api + apps/studio) — the commenter sees what THEY wrote, and can take it back

- **The gap.** A comment is a relation, and like the tip (v332) the product had only one side of it: the publication’s page LISTS the comments — and the commenter could not see what they had written there, nor take it back. The service’s repository has had the finder for the author’s side since v285 (`findByAuthorAccountIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc`) — with no service method, no door and no way to reach it. A comment is a thing a person might want to find again, or unsay.
- **The service grows the other direction.** `GET /comments?author=` — beside `?projectId=` — the way the tips and the subscriptions doors answer both sides of a relation. The service gains `commentsWritten`, and a question that names neither side is REFUSED BY NAME (a comment list with nobody on either side of it is nobody’s list).
- **The composer is where it belongs.** The **YOUR COMMENTS HERE** list lives in the comment composer — the place a commenter already goes to say something — and it carries a **Take it back** button on each comment that is still standing. The take-back itself is the chain v321 built (the service’s door, the studio’s door, the lane) — v321 left it with no door in the PRODUCT, and this is that door.
- **Two small truths the section had to get right.** A comment that was already taken back is shown as **"this comment was removed by its author"** — the same wording the artifact page uses — and it carries no button, because there is nothing to take back. And the take-back says WHICH of the two things happened: the service answers "removed: true" when a row was taken back and "removed: false" when there was nothing to take back, so the composer says "took the comment back" or "that comment was already gone" — never one word for both (the same rule the un-like keeps, v320).
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§49).** The commenter posts a comment of its own → the composer shows it under YOUR COMMENTS HERE → the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: the author’s own door answers with the comments they wrote → the commenter takes it back → and the SERVICE agrees the comment is marked as removed, and it STAYS on the record (a taken-back comment is a fact that happened, not a row that was never there).

The take-back is a CLAIM (the service compares the claimer with the comment’s author — exactly as strong as the like’s owner check, and exactly as weak: ADR 0018). And the list is the commenter’s own — nobody else’s comments are shown here, because a thread’s comments are on the publication’s page already, and this is the half that was missing.
### Amendment 339 (M7/v336, apps/studio + tools/harness) — the artifact page names WHO liked it

- **The gap.** The follow bar has named its followers since v288, and the like bar said only a count — so a reader could see WHO follows a creator and not WHO liked their work, which is the smaller of the two facts and the one a creator would want to see most. The wire had carried the likers’ names all along (the like row keeps `like_handle` and the wire has the slot); the artifact page simply dropped them when it rendered the bar.
- **The bar names them, in the follow bar’s shape.** `LikeBarFacts` gains `likers` and `renderLikeBar` renders a list beside the count — the same `<ul class="nexus-likes-list">` with one `<li data-liker="...">` per liker that the follow bar has used since v288, and the same shape of text: the name when the wire carried one, the account id when it did not, and the assurance beside it when there is one. The artifact page passes the likers it read; nothing about the wire’s SHAPE changed.
- **The proof of this increment had to wait for two repairs, and both are named here.** (1) **The Studio’s publish door called a slow answer "unreachable".** Its budget was 5 seconds, and the Studio’s own door is a `next dev` server whose FIRST call to a route pays that route’s compile — so a publish that timed out while the compiler was busy was answered as "nexus-api unreachable at …: The operation was aborted due to timeout". That is a FALSE sentence about a service that was there, answering a moment later, and the tip lane’s door made exactly this fix in v294 (45 seconds, not 10) for exactly this reason. This door had never caught up; it does now (`PUBLISH_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS = 45_000`, and a case that grades the budget). (2) **The harness gave up before the product was real.** Its budgets (the Studio’s start-up, the hydration, the publish, the comment, the trail) were sized for an idle machine, and a proof that measures the machine is not a proof — so they are bigger now, and the publish step says what the page held when it fails, because a timeout that says nothing about what the page held leaves the reader guessing.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§50).** A device with an account likes the publication again (the earlier section took its like back — that is what the taking-back is for) → the artifact page’s like bar names the people who liked it → and the SERVICE agrees, read independently of the browser: it sends the likers’ names on the wire, and the bar shows those very names.

- **Bounds (§60).** The names are CLAIMS — the service records them and verifies nothing (ADR 0018), exactly like the follower’s name in the follow bar. The bar names the likers the service sent, in the order it sent them, and it names only as many as the service’s window holds: the list is a WINDOW, not the whole history of who ever liked the publication. A liker whose claim carried no handle is shown by their account id — an address is better than a hole, and the bar never invents a name. The publish door’s bigger budget makes a slow answer wait rather than be misreported as a missing one; it does not make a HUNG service answer (a service that never answers still times out, and says so). And the harness’s bigger budgets make the proof wait for a real answer; they do not make a broken product pass — a check that fails for any other reason still fails.
### Amendment 340 (M7/v337, apps/studio) — every Studio door to the service is bounded, and a timeout is not called "unreachable"

- **The gap.** Seven doors in the Studio’s own lib folder — the comments, the likes, the follows, the economy, the moderation desk, the plans and the tips — fetched the service with **no budget at all**. A service that never answered left the Studio’s route waiting forever, and for a SERVER-RENDERED page (the artifact page, the explore page, the profile page) that is a reader waiting forever, with no sentence and no reason. The house’s rule — "a failed read is NOT an empty list" — has nothing to say about a read that never fails, so the read has to be BOUNDED and the bound has to be NAMED.
- **One budget, named once.** A new `serviceCall.ts` holds the budget (15 seconds — long enough for a cold first write on a busy machine, short enough that a reader is not left waiting) and the signal that stops a call that is not answered in time. Every one of the seven doors now passes that signal, and the publish door keeps its own 45 seconds (a WRITE, and the one door v294 already gave a budget to).
- **A timeout is not an unreachable service.** The catch in every door said "nexus-api unreachable at …", which is a FALSE sentence for a service that is merely slow: a reader who is told the thing is gone when it is only late stops looking for it. The shared helper now says "the service at … did not answer within 15 seconds" for a timeout, and keeps "nexus-api unreachable at …" for a service that really is not there.
- **A correction to amendment 339.** That record explained the publish door’s old 5-second budget by the route compile — and the compile is in the BROWSER→Studio hop, not in the Studio→service hop where that budget lives. The honest explanation is the one this amendment makes: the service was SLOW (a cold first write, or a busy machine) and a 5-second budget turned a slow answer into a false "unreachable". The fix is the same either way; the reason was wrong, and it is corrected here rather than left standing.
- **What the real-browser proof grades.** The whole E2E runs against the real service in a real database, and every one of the doors it drives — the artifact page’s comments and likes, the desk’s reports, the economy’s plans, the tips — now answers with a bounded call. The proof’s own numbers are unchanged: 264/264.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/serviceCall.ts` (new — the budget, the signal, and the reason a timeout is not an unreachable service), `apps/studio/src/lib/serviceCall.test.ts` (new — 4 cases), `apps/studio/src/lib/commentServer.ts`, `.../likeServer.ts`, `.../followServer.ts`, `.../economyServer.ts`, `.../moderationServer.ts`, `.../planServer.ts`, `.../tipServer.ts` (every call is bounded, and every catch names a timeout for what it is), `apps/studio/src/lib/planServer.test.ts` (+1 case — a door’s call carries a signal).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1206/1206 (67 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **148/148**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **264/264**.
- **Bounds (§60).** The budget is a BOUND, not a promise: a service that answers in 16 seconds is still a service that answers, and this change makes the Studio say "did not answer" for it — which is a true sentence about the answer, and a false sentence about the service. A door that refuses a slow answer is better than a page that never renders, and better than a page that renders "nothing" — but the honest version of a slow service is a faster one, and this is a bound, not a fix. The doors of the AUDIT trail are not in this change: the trail belongs to the other lane, and its door is edited there. And the browser’s own half of each lane keeps its own budget (the tip lane’s 45 seconds, v294) — the two hops are separate waits, and a call can be bounded at both ends.
### Amendment 341 (M7/v338, apps/studio) — the publish and economy lanes get a budget, and a slow compile is not an unreachable Studio

- **The gap.** v294 gave the tip lane a budget and explained why: the Studio’s own door is a `next dev` server, and the FIRST call to a route pays that route’s COMPILE, so a lane with no budget could be killed by a slow compile and report it as a failure of the thing it was asking for. Seven lanes took that lesson (the comments, the follows, the likes, the moderation desk, the plans, the reports, the tips) — and **two did not**: the publish lane and the economy lane, which is to say the two lanes the Studio uses most. A publish that was slow to compile was answered "studio server unreachable", which is a FALSE sentence about a Studio that was there.
- **The same budget, the same reason.** `publishLane.ts` and `economyLane.ts` now carry the 45-second budget v294 chose — the compile is the cost, and a compile is not a hung service — and every call passes a signal that can stop it. The remix lane rides on the publish lane (it reads the publication through it), so it is covered by the same change.
- **A timeout says what it is.** The publish lane’s catch said "studio server unreachable: …"; a timeout now says "the Studio did not answer within 45 seconds", and a Studio that really is not there still says "unreachable" and says where it looked. A reader who is told the thing is gone when it is only late stops looking for it — the same lie the house’s rule about failed reads is about, one hop earlier.
- **What the proof grades.** The unit case in `publishLane.test.ts` grades the wiring: the call to the Studio carries a signal, so a Studio that never answers cannot hold the lane forever. The real-browser E2E still passes end to end (264/264) against the real service in a real database — and the publish it drives is one of the calls this change bounds.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/publishLane.ts` (the budget, the signal on every call, and the honest reason), `apps/studio/src/lib/economyLane.ts` (the budget and the signal), `apps/studio/src/lib/publishLane.test.ts` (+1 case).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1207/1207 (67 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **148/148**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **264/264**.
- **Bounds (§60).** The AUDIT lane is not in this change: the trail belongs to the other lane, and its door is edited there — so the trail’s browser half is still unbudgeted, and that is named here rather than quietly left out of the sentence "every lane". The lanes that talk to a CONTAINER (the build, the deploy, the save, the world-save) are not in this change either: they have their own budget inside the container runner, and a container that never answers is a different fact from a Studio that never answers. And the budget is a BOUND, not a promise: a Studio that takes 46 seconds to compile is a slow Studio, and this change makes the lane say so — it does not make the compile faster.
### Amendment 342 (M7/v339, apps/studio + tools/harness) — the artifact page reads its four sources at once

- **The gap.** The artifact page read its four side sources — the reports, the trail, the likes and the comments — one after another. They are four INDEPENDENT facts about the same publication, so reading them in sequence made the page wait for their SUM: a service that was slow by a second made the reader wait four. The page’s own rule (v280, v284, v286) is that each source is read independently and a failed read leaves its section out — and it was independent in the failure and serial in the waiting, which is the worst of both.
- **One wait, not four.** The four reads now go out together (`Promise.all`), so the page waits for the SLOWEST of them and not for their sum. Nothing else about the page changes: the same reads, the same bars, the same "a failed read leaves its section out" rule, the same order of sections in the HTML.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§51).** The artifact page carries ALL FOUR of its sources — the likes bar, the comments section, the reports bar and the history section. A concurrent read is exactly the kind of change that can quietly drop one of the four, so the proof says so in one sentence: the page still has every one of them.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/app/p/[projectId]/route.ts` (the four reads go out together), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §51).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1207/1207 (67 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **148/148**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **265/265** with the new §51.
- **Bounds (§60).** The page’s own read — the PUBLICATION itself — still comes first and still decides the 404: a page for a publication that does not exist is not a page with four empty sections, and reading the sources first would spend four calls on a publication nobody will see. The four reads are concurrent, not merged: four calls go to the service at once, so a service that is already struggling is asked to do four things at a time — this makes the WAITING shorter and the ARRIVAL burstier, and a service that needs the traffic spread out would want the opposite. And the change is a WAIT, not a speed-up: nothing here makes the service answer faster, and a reader who opens the page while the service is slow still waits for the slowest of the four.
### Amendment 343 (M7/v340, apps/studio + tools/harness) — the profile page reads its four sources at once

- **The gap.** The same gap v339 closed on the artifact page, on the second server-rendered page: the PROFILE page read its four side sources — the plans this creator offers, the tips they were given, the accounts that follow them and the accounts they follow — one after another. ### Amendment 350 (M7/v350, apps/studio + tools/harness) — a bar that shows a list says when the list is a WINDOW

- **The gap.** Three bars on the public pages pair a WHOLE count with a WINDOW of rows: the like bar says "5 likes" and lists the names the service’s window held; the tip bar says "12 tips" and lists five messages; the follow bar says "3 followers" and lists two names. A reader who sees a count and a short list has no way to tell that the list is a window — and the natural reading of "5 likes" beside two names is that two people liked it and three liked something else. The counts are the service’s whole numbers (the house’s rule: the tally counts the whole answer ✓) and the lists are the service’s capped windows, so the bar was quietly mixing two different sizes.
- **The bar says which is which.** When the list is shorter than the count, the bar says so — "showing the 2 newest of 5" — and when the list is the whole thing it says nothing, because there is nothing to say. The lists are the service’s newest-first windows, so "the newest" is the true description of what is shown and not a decoration.
- **The follow bar says it for BOTH of its lists.** The bar carries two lists (v303: the followers and the accounts followed ✓) and both are windows beside their own whole counts, so both say it.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§59).** The profile’s bars do not claim more than they show: where a bar pairs a count with a shorter list, the page says so. The unit cases pin the two halves — a bar that shows everyone says no such thing ✓, and a bar that shows a window says exactly how many ✓.
- **Files:** `apps/studio/src/lib/likeBar.ts`, `apps/studio/src/lib/tipBar.ts`, `apps/studio/src/lib/followBar.ts` (each bar says what it is not showing), `apps/studio/src/lib/likeBar.test.ts` (+2 cases), `tools/harness/studio-publish.mjs` (a new §59).
- **Measured:** `apps/studio` **1221/1221 (67 files)**, the service’s social + moderation packages **148/148**, `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` **exit 0**, doc gate **exit 0**, the real-browser E2E **275/275** with the new §59.
- **Bounds (§60).** The bar does NOT grow the list to match the count — the service’s window is the service’s rule, and a bar that read the whole table would be a table scan on every page load. The note names the window’s SIZE ("the 2 newest of 5"), not the rows that are missing, so it never claims to know which ones they are. And the note appears only when the list really is shorter: a bar that shows everyone says nothing, because "showing the 3 newest of 3" would be noise.
### Amendment 351 (M7/v354, services/nexus-api + apps/studio + tools/harness) — the comments say how many are VISIBLE in the whole thread

- **The gap.** The service’s comments door reported the visible count of the WINDOW it had read, and the page put that number beside the rows: so a thread of thirty-four comments whose window held three rows was announced as "2 comment(s) visible of 2 shown". The count was a fact about the window, and it was dressed as a fact about the thread — the same small lie v350 removed from the like, tip and follow bars, in the one place the service’s own count was wrong.
- **The service counts the thread.** `CommentRepository` gains `countByTargetProjectIdAndDeletedFalse` and the service asks it, so `visible` is the DATABASE’s count of every visible comment on the publication. The window’s own visible count is kept beside it as `shownVisible`, because a caller that wants to say "of the twenty shown, two were taken back" needs both sizes — and the two are different facts.
- **The page tells the three numbers apart.** The comments section now says how many comments are VISIBLE in the whole thread, whether the rows it shows are a WINDOW of it ("showing the 20 newest"), and how many of the shown ones were taken back by their authors. The Studio’s reader keeps the cap the service applied, so the page knows the window’s size.
- **What the real-browser proof grades (§60).** The artifact page says how many comments are visible in the WHOLE thread, and the number on the page is the number the SERVICE counted.

### Amendment 365 (v377, tools/harness) — the baseline decision is ONE pure function, and the decoder enforces chunk ORDER

_Numbering: the code landed as `aaa69a6` with its record deferred (the ledger held another lane's uncommitted backfill); the file is clean and 365 is the next free number. Version and amendment number differ by design — 364 is v376, so this is v377._

- **Two bounds the previous two records stated, closed together.** v313 said the harness compared against a baseline only through an inline block, so the proof could assert a CALL SITE but not the RULE; v314 said the decoder checked chunk CRCs but not the format's ORDER. Both are the same failure mode: a verification tool whose important decision is not itself verified.
- **The rule is now a function.** `compareToBaseline(captureBuf, baselineBuf, {tolerance = 8, maxRatio = 0.02})` in `tools/harness/png.mjs` owns the decision and answers `{ok, skipped, detail}` (+ `diff` when it compared). A null baseline is an explicit **SKIP that is ok** — a first run must never go red for the absence of a file — and the skip's own sentence says "SKIPPED, not passed", so a caller cannot mistake one for the other. `tools/harness/studio-golden-path.mjs` now CALLS it rather than carrying a private copy, which is what makes the proof meaningful: it exercises the rule the harness actually runs.
- **Order is part of the format.** `decodePng` refuses a chunk before IHDR, a second IHDR, an IDAT run interrupted by any other chunk, and a file with no IEND. A decoder that ignores order does not crash — it silently splices image data across the interrupting chunk, which is the same "plausible garbage" the CRC check exists to prevent.
- **The proof grew from four sections to five, and §3 from six refusals to ten.** The order arms splice WHOLE chunks (so every CRC stays valid and the ORDER rule is what fires, not the integrity rule), and they build a well-formed `tEXt` chunk — CRC included — to interrupt the run. §4 is the shared decision: identical bytes are 0 px, a missing baseline SKIPS, two DIFFERENT surfaces of the same size (assets vs world) are a real **RED at 10.1% differing**, and a size mismatch is refused rather than compared. §5 asserts the harness calls the shared function.
- **Files:** `tools/harness/png.mjs`, `tools/harness/studio-golden-path.mjs`, `docs/evidence/studio/png-baseline-proof.mjs`, `docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`.
- **Measured:** `png-baseline-proof.mjs` **5/5 ALL SECTIONS PASSED**; the doc gate **exit 0** (`ledger headings 356`, `dangling 0`, `numbers GRANTED TWICE: none`, `[§4] failing TRACKED cases 0`).
- **A bug this increment met, worth recording.** The interrupted-IDAT arm's predicate was `/not contiguous/` while the decoder's message reads "…must be contiguous", so `assert.throws` reported "must be refused by name" — which reads exactly like a missing throw. The rule for the next reader: when a predicate fails, print the ACTUAL message before concluding nothing was thrown; a regex that half-matches and an absent exception are indistinguishable from the failure text alone.
- **Bounds (§60).** The comparison arm is still ARMED but UNEXERCISED in CI — no baseline is committed, and committing one now would go red on the other lanes' in-flight UI work. The decoder checks order and integrity, not chunk SEMANTICS (a `tEXt` with nonsense content is accepted; only its position and CRC are judged). And a diff says pixels CHANGED, never that they changed for the worse.

### Amendment 373 (M7/v383, services/nexus-api social) — the duplicate-report rule is TIME-AWARE: a report STANDS for a period, then lapses

- **The gap.** Rule 4 of the report service said "the same account cannot report the same publication for the same reason twice" → — forever →. A publication that was fixed stays held down by a complaint about its old state →, and the reporter who wants to say it again after a fix has no way to →.
- **HEAD was RED when this increment started.** The parallel lane's call site landed (`e35b59e`) calling `existingReport.getPeriod()` on an entity that had no period → and the v384 call site (`ed20681`) calling a six-argument `audit.record` that did not exist → — the service did not COMPILE at HEAD →. This increment is also the repair: a half-landed call site is a build nobody can run →.
- **The rule, and where it lives.** A report STANDS for a period — a month, as filed today → — and expires at its own `createdAt + period`, read off the ROW rather than off today's policy → (a row filed under one period expires by that period even after the policy moves →). The addition is CALENDAR arithmetic in UTC, not `Instant.plus`: an Instant has no months →, and a "month" that was really thirty days would expire a report filed on the 31st a day early, every time →. A period this build does not know expires by the month rather than standing forever → — an unreadable period must not read as "never expires" →.
- **The DATABASE's constraint is gone, and the cost is named.** "At most one STANDING report per (reporter, target, reason)" is a rule about a moving instant, and a UNIQUE index cannot express one → — the old `report_entry_reporter_target_reason` constraint would have refused the re-file the new rule allows →. The rule now lives in the service, which checks for a STANDING report before filing →. What is lost: two SIMULTANEOUS filings can both pass the check and both land, where the constraint would have stopped the second →. A database-level rule that only counts standing rows needs a trigger or a migration tool →, and this build has neither (the README's ddl-auto bound →) — that is the honest next step →, named here rather than pretended →.
- **Files:** `services/nexus-api/src/main/java/dev/nexus/api/social/ReportEntry.java` (the `period` column, the constraint's removal with its reasons), `.../social/ReportDtos.java` (the closed set of two), `.../social/ReportService.java` (`isStanding`, the standing period, the tidy `report()`), `.../social/ReportServiceTest.java` (+4 cases: an EXPIRED report no longer constrains; a report one day short of its period still STANDS; a YEAR period expires a year later, not a month; the filed row carries the standing period).
- **Measured:** the service **240/240** (10 classes), `mvn -B test -o` **BUILD SUCCESS** — the two compile errors at HEAD are gone and the four new cases pin the boundary →.
- **Bounds (§60).** The standing period is a service constant (a month), not a caller's choice — the request does not carry one →. The uniqueness rule is the SERVICE's now, with the race above →. An existing database created under the old constraint keeps it until somebody drops it by hand (ddl-auto adds columns, it does not drop constraints →) — a fresh database gets the new shape →.

### Amendment 374 (M9/v384, services/nexus-api ops + apps/studio + docs/evidence) — the trail's target carries its KIND, declared by the caller and never guessed from an id

- **The gap.** An audit entry's target is an id, and an id alone does not say what it names →. The trail's reader (the artifact page's history, the panel) had to treat every target as a publication →, which is true of every verb this build records today → and false the day a follow or a tip is written down →.
- **HEAD was RED here too.** The parallel lane's call site (`ed20681`) classified the target by SNIFFING THE ID'S PREFIX (`account-`, `plan-`) → — a rule that could never fire in this system, where accounts are `acct-…` and plan ids are a creator's own choice of word → — and called a six-argument `record` that did not exist →. The completion replaces the sniffing with a DECLARATION: the caller knows what it acted on, so the caller says so →.
- **The closed set, enforced by name.** `AuditService` owns three constants (`account`, `plan`, `publication`) and refuses an entry that names no kind or a kind outside the three →, with the three named in the refusal →. The column is NOT nullable and the wire field is never null → — every entry this build writes names one →. The verbs that predate the field (publish, unpublish, like, unlike, comment, uncomment, report, withdraw-report, acknowledge) all happened to a PUBLICATION, and each call site now says so explicitly rather than inheriting a hidden default →.
- **The client learns the field, symmetrically.** `ops.ts`'s `AuditEntry` gains `targetType: AuditTargetType` — REQUIRED, because the service always sends it and a client that treated it as optional would be declaring a shape the wire never has (v273's symmetry, the other direction →). `auditServer.ts`'s lane shape and `trail.ts`'s `TrailEntry`/`TrailRow` follow →, `toTrailRow` DROPS a row that cannot say what kind of thing it happened to → (the panel's count discrepancy makes the drop visible →), and `trailTargetTypeText` spells the three the way a person would say them and passes an unknown kind through →.
- **Both contract proofs grade the new field.** `trail-contract-proof.mjs` §1 and `audit-contract-proof.mjs` §1/§2/§4 assert the seven-field shape and the new field's non-nullability on both sides →; §5's compiler probe carries the kind →. A wire contract is a promise, and the promise now covers the kind →.

### Amendment 375 (M2 v154 correction, evidence) — amendment 154's claim was wrong twice: the probe mutated the TYPE, and it ran the wrong suite

_Corrects amendment 154. Numbering: 375 was free._

- **What 154 recorded.** *"All three mutations are caught by the existing `saveSnapshot.test.ts` suite."* — the retirement of amendment 129's debt →.
- **What was actually true.** The probe (`0432ef6`) replaced the FIRST occurrence of each reason string in `packages/three-runtime/src/threeRuntime.ts` — which is the TYPE UNION (`reason: 'not-json' | 'listed-then-missing' | 'name-not-reenterable'`), not the runtime value →. Types are erased by esbuild, so two of the three mutations changed NOTHING and "survived" for a reason that had nothing to do with the tests →. And the third, `name-not-reenterable`, is asserted in `saveNameSpelling.test.ts` — a file the probe never ran →, so it could not have been caught by the file the probe chose →.
- **What was done.** `ba647a0` rewrote the probe to target the RUNTIME push sites (`reason: 'X', why:` — unique in the file →) and to run the WHOLE `@nexus/three-runtime` suite, because the honest question is whether ANYTHING notices →. `d18ce95` made it shell out through the syncproc bridge and separated a SPAWN failure from a test failure → — a spawn error read as "the mutation was caught" is exactly the false green this arc exists to prevent →. The 154 text is left in place rather than edited: a record that can be edited to match its evidence is worth less than one that cannot →.
- **Measured (2026-10-23):** `node docs/evidence/agents/amendment129-probe.mjs` → **ALL MUTATIONS CAUGHT** — all three runtime mutations fail the suite, with the source restored after each →.
- **Bounds (§60).** The probe's restore is registered on `exit` and the catchable signals; a SIGKILL mid-run still leaves the source mutated → — stated rather than pretended away →.

### Amendment 376 (M2, evidence) — the SERVICE suite's verdict is a gated one: the service-suite proof's own record

- **The gap.** `npm run verify:api-tests` (`mvn -B test`) was a command a human ran, and nothing asserted its totals → — the doc gate grades only its two vitest arms →. A suite that silently stopped collecting a class would read as a pass →.
- **The proof.** `docs/evidence/m7/service-suite-proof.mjs` (`npm run verify:service`) digests the service sources, runs `mvn -o -B test`, asserts the digest did not move under the run, then grades the surefire totals — 0 failures / 0 errors / tests > 0 / exit 0 / every `*Test.java` on disk present → — and prints WHICH tree it graded →.
- **Measured (2026-10-23, after amendments 372–374):** `mvn -o -B test` → **240 tests, 10 classes, 0 failures, 0 errors, BUILD SUCCESS** — the two classes that did not exist when this record was first owed (the ops package's `AuditServiceTest`, 8 cases) and the eight new report cases are in the total →. The first run at the previous HEAD went RED and correctly so →: the parallel lane's v383/v384 call sites had landed without their receiving halves (a `getPeriod()` on an entity with no period, a six-argument `record` that did not exist →), and the service did not compile →.
- **Bounds (§60).** The proof grades the totals, not the cases: a test that asserts nothing would still count →. The digest covers the service sources only →.

### Amendment 377 (M7/M9 v384-fix, services/nexus-api ops + social + apps/studio) — the half-landed call sites get their receiving halves, and the FULL suite catches what the affected-files gate could not

- **The gap.** HEAD did not COMPILE when this increment began →. The parallel lane's v383 call site (`e35b59e`) called `existingReport.getPeriod()` on an entity that had no period →, its v384 call site (`ed20681`) called a six-argument `audit.record` that did not exist →, and `bb5a5de` had given a repository finder a `targetType` parameter no derivation could bind →. The client was red the same way →: v382's `offset` was missing from the route →, the lane → and the Toolbar's failure literals →. A call site without its receiver is a build nobody can run →, and a shared working tree means the next increment inherits it →.
- **What was completed.** `AuditEntry` carries a NOT-NULL `target_type` column → and `AuditService` owns the closed set (`account` / `plan` / `publication` →) that `record` now validates by name → — an entry that names no kind, or a kind outside the three, is refused with the three named →. `ReportEntry` carries its own `period` and `target_type` →, and the `(reporter, target, reason)` UNIQUE constraint is GONE →: "at most one STANDING report" is a rule about a moving instant →, and no index expresses one → — the service checks for a standing report before filing →, in UTC CALENDAR arithmetic (`atZone(UTC).plusMonths(1)` →) because an `Instant` has no months → and thirty-day months expire a report filed on the 31st a day early →. `ReportController.list` reads `offset` and clamps a negative one to the first page →. On the client → `AuditEntry.targetType` is REQUIRED (the wire never omits it →, v273's symmetry the other direction →), `toTrailRow` DROPS a row that cannot say what kind of thing it happened to →, and every answer carries the window it asked for →.
- **What the full-suite run found that the affected-files gate did not.** Running the whole `apps/studio` suite — not just the five files this increment touched → — went RED in `history.test.ts` →, 8 cases →: v280's fixtures predated the `targetType` field →, so the new honesty rule dropped EVERY row and the publication's history read as empty →. The affected-files gate had been green → because `history.ts` consumes `toTrailRows` without appearing in the increment's own file list →. The lesson →: a change to a shared reader's row shape must run the READERS' suites too →, and a reader is anyone who calls the function → — the dependency runs through the module graph →, not through the commit's file list →. Fixed by carrying the new field in the fixture → and adding the case that grades the drop →.
- **Measured (2026-10-23):** `mvn -B test -o` → **240 tests, 10 classes, 0 failures, 0 errors, BUILD SUCCESS** →; `npx vitest run --root apps/studio --no-file-parallelism` → **1286/1286 (67 files)** →; `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` → **exit 0** →; `trail-contract-proof.mjs` →, `audit-contract-proof.mjs` → and `social-contract-proof.mjs` → all **exit 0** →.
- **Bounds (§60).** The pager UI is still missing → — the lane and the door carry the offset →, and the filed list's older rows remain unreachable from the panel →. No verb this build records targets an account or a plan yet → — the kinds exist on the wire →, and the first writer of an account-targeted entry is a future increment →. Two SIMULTANEOUS filings can still both pass the standing check → where the deleted constraint would have stopped the second → — a database rule that counts only standing rows needs a trigger or a migration tool →, and this build has neither →. And the service still VERIFIES nothing (ADR 0018) →.

### Amendment 378 (M9/v385, services/nexus-api ops + apps/studio + evidence) — the trail's filter moved INTO the service, and the service answers with the number that says what the filter hides

- **The gap.** The panel's filter narrowed the rows the browser already held → (v281). That is honest about the window it has → and silent about everything past the cap →: with the trail capped at a hundred → and the panel asking for twenty →, "the newest 20 that happen to be take-downs" is a different set from "the newest 20 take-downs" →. The desk had already learned this (v326 →) — one question asked in two places is a question that can start answering itself two ways →.
- **The ask moved.** `GET /audit?action=…` narrows IN THE QUERY →: `AuditService.list(limit, action)` picks the finder by whether an action was named →, and the window is the newest N of THAT action →. The verbs are a CLOSED SET — the nine this build records → — and one outside it is REFUSED BY NAME before any window is read →, the same way the desk refuses a reason it does not have →: answering a question about a verb this service never recorded with an empty window would read as "nothing of that action ever happened" →, which is a different fact from "this service does not know that verb" → and the one that matters when the trail is the only witness →.
- **What the move costs, and who pays it.** The browser no longer sees the rows the filter excluded →, so the panel's own tally can no longer count what the filter is hiding → — the property v281 had given it for free →. The service answers a THIRD number beside the window (`total` →: how many the WHOLE trail holds →, narrowed or not →) and the footer states it →: "N shown · the service carried M · the whole trail holds T · the service caps at L" →. Four numbers →, four questions →. The desk's tally door (v312) is the same idea for the same reason →.
- **The browser half got simpler.** `filterTrailRows` — the client-side filter →, with its tests → — is RETIRED →: one job done in two places is a job the two places can disagree about →. The lane's `readTrail(limit, action)` carries the ask →, the Studio route forwards it verbatim →, and a refusal's NAME travels back through the route's 503 → so the panel says why rather than "HTTP 400" →.
- **The envelope is part of the contract now.** `audit-contract-proof.mjs` gained §7 →: it reads the service's `Trail` record out of the controller → and the lane's `TrailAnswer` out of `auditLane.ts` →, and asserts the three numbers exist on both sides and are REQUIRED in the client → — a rename on either side would leave the panel stating a whole it never received →, which is the quiet lie the proof exists to catch →.
- **Measured (2026-10-23):** `mvn -B test -o` → **246 tests, 10 classes, 0 failures, 0 errors** (+6 →); `npx vitest run --root apps/studio --no-file-parallelism` → **1282/1282 (67 files)** →; `npx tsc -p apps/studio/tsconfig.json` → **exit 0** →; `audit-contract-proof.mjs` → **exit 0** with the new §7 →; `trail-contract-proof.mjs` and `social-contract-proof.mjs` → **exit 0** →.
- **Bounds (§60).** The real-browser E2E could not run here → — the harness needs the Java service and Docker →, neither of which this machine has →; §9.6's new checks drive the same selectors the rest of the section drives → and are graded on the next machine that can →. A verb added to the service must join the closed set in the same commit →, or the filter will refuse it → — the set is the vocabulary →, and it grows on purpose or not at all →. The tally still counts the rows ON THE SCREEN and says so ("of these N rows" →) — the filter narrows the list →, never the honesty of the count →. And the service still VERIFIES nothing (ADR 0018) →: the filter is a question about what was recorded →, not a claim about what was true →.

### Amendment 379 (M7/v386, apps/studio + harness) — the filed list's PAGER: the pipe v382 built gets its tap

- **The gap.** v382 put the offset on the wire → — the service pages the filed read →, the lane names the window in every answer →, the route forwards it → — and the panel still had no way to ASK for an older page →. A reporter with thirty-seven complaints saw twenty → and was told there were thirty-seven →, with no way to reach the other seventeen →. The pipe was built →; the tap was missing →.

"Newer" is disabled on the first page → (there is no page before the first →), and "Older" is disabled exactly when the window already holds every report the service counted → — a pager that offered a page with nothing in it would be asking a question whose honest answer is an empty window →.

It now says "showing 21–40 of 37" →, or on a page past the end →, "this page is past the end — the service answered an empty window" → — the service's honest answer rather than an error →.

The page survives a withdrawal → (the re-read keeps the reader where they were →), but a withdrawal that empties the LAST page leaves the reader on an empty window with the honest note → — rows are never deleted →, so that state needs the table to shrink →, which this build never does →.
