### Amendment 425 (v432, three-runtime) — the STORAGE SEAM’s own rules, graded directly

- **The gap.** `saveStore.ts` is the only module in this package that talks to somewhere outside the process, and the only place every save name passes through (`resolveSavePath` exactly once) — and it shipped with no test file of its own. Measured on HEAD, that left the three stores’ honesty rules ungraded: what a `null` from `read` means, which names may be CREATED versus merely read, what a host that cannot rename, flush or browse is told, and why a listing is refused rather than answered with an empty array.
- **The repair.** One vitest file asks the seam directly, with injected hosts — the way the module was built to be asked →. The naming rule is graded clause by clause: a plain relative name passes, the absolute spellings (`/`, `\`, drive letters) are refused, `..` walks out, empty and `.` segments are refused, and a backslash name is refused by the RE-JOIN rule rather than by scanning segments that the split has already emptied →. `savePathRefusal` hands out the door’s OWN sentence — asserted identical to what `resolveSavePath` throws — so the two can never drift apart →. Creation goes one rule further than reading: the temp suffix is refused naming the shorter save it would collide with, while the READ side keeps accepting a `.tmp` the host already holds, because a leftover is a fact about the host and a browser that browses its own store must not die on one →. The memory store round-trips, answers `null` for “not there” (never “empty file”), answers `false` for a delete that removed nothing, refuses durable writes by name, and replaces atomically in one map mutation →. The fs store refuses a root that itself walks out at construction, confines every path under the root, writes temp-then-rename leaving no debris, refuses an atomic write the host cannot perform BEFORE any byte moves (no `renameSync`; `durable` with no `flushSync`), and on a failed rename leaves the old file untouched and removes the temp — or, when the cleanup also fails, NAMES the leftover instead of hiding it →. Delete throws when the host cannot delete, because `false` would be a lie the store must not tell →. `list` refuses rather than answering `[]` when the host cannot browse, walks nested names with their prefixes, and answers `[]` only where the root is knowably absent →. The localStorage store — the one store that was unconstructible outside a browser until the storage became a seam — is driven headlessly through an injected `StorageLike`: namespaced keys, an index that gives `list` its names without reading bytes, the temp key used and removed, durable refused by name, a quota refusal re-thrown naming the quota AND that nothing was written, and a non-quota error re-thrown untouched →.
- **Files:** packages/three-runtime/test/saveStore.test.ts (new, 28 cases).
- **Measured (2026-10-24):** `npx vitest run --root packages/three-runtime --no-file-parallelism test/saveStore.test.ts` → **28/28**; `npx tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` → exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** The seam is graded with INJECTED hosts: what a real fs does with a cross-device rename, or a real browser with a full quota, is the host’s subject, and the store’s job is only to name what happened →. The fs fake is flat — its directory answers are derived from the keys it holds — so the walk is graded for shape, not for symlink or permission behaviour a real host would add →. And `writeAtomic`’s durability claim stops at the FILE: flushing the directory (the rename itself) is deliberately not attempted, and these cases grade exactly that much and no more →.

### Amendment 426 (v433, world-engine) — the retrieval core’s query contract, graded directly

- **The gap.** `worldRag.test.ts` (7 cases) pinned that a query returns hits, respects scope/filter/limit and can carry a context. What it did not pin is the contract those answers are made of: what ORDER equal scores come back in, what a limit does to the count the answer reports, what the threshold admits when a document shares nothing with the question, what a rebuilt index does to the documents the last world state left behind, and what a document actually SAYS. Measured on HEAD, each of these was reachable only by reading the code — the query answered correctly while its own rules went unasked.
- **The repair.** Nine new cases in the same file ask them directly →. A score tie is broken by ID, so the order is a rule and not a map-iteration accident — and a document that shares nothing sorts LAST at score 0 rather than being dropped, because the default threshold admits it →. A limit truncates the results while `totalHits` keeps counting the whole answer — the window is not the answer’s idea of how many matched →. The default threshold admits a zero-score document and SAYS it is worth 0; a named threshold above the score excludes it and `totalHits` follows →. A filter is exact equality on every key it names, including a null one →. The context is the RANKED hits, each as `[TYPE] title: content`, blank-line separated, and the answer says how long it took →. A second world state REPLACES the index: no document from the last world lingers →. And the documents themselves are graded: a character reads as labelled lines with only ACTIVE goals listed, an absent faction as “none”, a relationship as `id: type (strength)`, and its own `updatedAt`; an event titles itself type + the first 50 characters of its description and keeps its own timestamp; a location — the one builder whose type carries no clock — stamps itself with NOW, and an unconnected place says so with an empty list →.
- **Files:** packages/world-engine/test/worldRag.test.ts (extended, 7 → 16 cases).
- **Measured (2026-10-24):** `npx vitest run --root packages/world-engine --no-file-parallelism test/worldRag.test.ts` → **16/16**; `npx tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` → exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** The scoring itself (`hybridScore`, the hash embeddings) is `@nexus/agent-runtime`’s subject, pinned there; this file grades what the retrieval core DOES with a score — order, threshold, window, count →. The fixtures are minimal worlds built by hand, so what a full WorldEngine timeline looks like is the engine suite’s subject →. And the location builder’s `Date.now()` is pinned as a window (before ≤ stamp ≤ after), because a clock read is the one thing a test cannot make exact →.

### Amendment 427 (v434, ai-providers) — the demo BATCH PRODUCER’s own rules, graded directly

- **The gap.** `compose.test.ts` pins `compose`: the template detection, the tree wiring, the determinism. The function the DemoDesignProvider actually drives is `composeDesignBatch`, which wraps `compose` and turns the tree into the OpBatch the editor applies — and its own decisions had no direct case: where the section enters the page, in what order the nodes travel, what the provenance and the summary say, what clock the batch is stamped with, and what the seed defaults to. Measured on HEAD, every one of those was reachable only by reading the code.
- **The repair.** Seven new cases in the same file (8 → 15) ask them directly →. The section is inserted as ONE `addSubtree` at index 0 of the ACTIVE page — on top, not appended under whatever is already there →. The nodes travel ROOT-FIRST, every non-root naming a parent that appears earlier in the list, so `applyOp` can wire the whole subtree in one pass; the count matches what `compose` produced, no node lost or duplicated →. The provenance names the demo mode and the template that was chosen (`demo:auth`, `demo:dashboard`), so a reader can tell which generator spoke →. The summary quotes the prompt — with the typographic quotes the composer actually writes, pinned as measured — and only its first 60 characters →. The batch is stamped at 0 (the demo authors at clock-zero; the runtime stamps when it applies) and its id derives from the seed →. With no seed named, the prompt IS the seed: two calls with one prompt and one document produce byte-identical batches, and the id is the documented `demoId('batch', hashString(prompt))` →. And the batch applies cleanly to a real document: the section lands on the active page as its first child, the threaded parent survives the apply, and every node the batch carried exists afterwards →.
- **Files:** packages/ai-providers/test/compose.test.ts (extended, 8 → 15 cases).
- **Measured (2026-10-24):** `npx vitest run --root packages/ai-providers --no-file-parallelism test/compose.test.ts` → **15/15**; `npx tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` → exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** The templates themselves — what each builder puts in a section — are `compose`’s subject and stay pinned by the cases above; this file grades the batch the tree becomes →. The document the batch lands on is a fresh `createEmptyDocument`, so what the section does beside EXISTING page content is the editor suite’s subject →. And the summary’s curly quotes are pinned as MEASURED: whether a summary should carry typographic quotes is a decision about the composer’s voice, not a fact this file settles →.

### Amendment 428 (v435, ai-providers) — the EMBEDDING SEAM’s own rules, graded directly

- **The gap.** `hashEmbed` and `cosine` are pure, and both are load-bearing: the router embed/rank surface, the agents-runtime token-bag seam and the vector stores all lean on them, and the runtime hybrid score literally reads `0.6 * cosine(qv, e.vector) + 0.4 * coverage` — a formula that stays bounded only because `hashEmbed` hands back unit vectors while `cosine` stays a raw dot product. Neither half of that contract had a case: the only existing checks ask “same text, same vector” through the router and read one self-similarity at 5 digits. Measured on HEAD, the normalization, the dim parameter, the value range and the behaviour on mismatched lengths were reachable only by reading the code.
- **The repair.** A new `test/embedding.test.ts` asks them directly, 22 cases →. Shape: `EMBED_DIM` is 64 and is the default length, custom dims are honoured (1, 8, 257), dim 0 yields an empty vector rather than a crash or NaN, the empty string is a legal input seeded by the FNV offset basis, and long and unicode text stays finite →. Determinism: byte-identical per text, at every dim, and distinct texts diverge →. Normalization: unit length for every probe (empty, one char, long, unicode), every component inside [-1, 1], and never the all-zero vector that would rank nothing →. `cosine` is pinned as the raw dot product it is: 2,0 × 3,0 = 6 and not 1, orthogonal 0, antipodal -1, signs multiply, symmetric, and two empty vectors score 0 rather than NaN →. Mismatched lengths are zero-padded rather than rejected, so the same text at two dims scores below identity (measured 0.778 — each dim count is its own normalization space) →. And the pair is graded the way the retrieval stack actually uses it: every pair of probe embeddings scores inside [-1, 1], the bound the runtime weighting leans on, while distinct texts sit at effectively independent directions (measured 0.0008), because `hashEmbed` is a per-string projection and NOT token-aware — the token-bag averaging that makes a shared word matter lives in the runtime seam, not here →.
- **Files:** packages/ai-providers/test/embedding.test.ts (new, 22 cases).
- **Measured (2026-10-24):** `npx vitest run --root packages/ai-providers --no-file-parallelism` → **9 files, 95/95** (was 73 across 8 files); `npx tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` → exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** The token-bag composition (`embedTokens`) and the hybrid score that mixes cosine with token coverage are the agents-runtime seam’s subject; here they appear only as the reason the [-1, 1] bound matters →. Whether a hash embedding is the right retrieval primitive at all is ADR 0010’s decision — this file grades the seam that decision installed →. And the two numbers quoted above (0.778, 0.0008) are pinned as MEASURED snapshots of a deterministic generator, not as claims about its distribution →.

### Amendment 429 (v436, studio) — the LIKES DOOR’s write half, graded directly

- **The gap.** `readLikes` had six direct cases (v400). The two writes and the viewer read — `likeOnService`, `unlikeOnService`, `readLikesOnService` — were reached only through the lanes that call them, so nothing ever asked what a write carries or what a refusal answers: whether an unfilled claim field is dropped or named empty, whether a 200 saying `ok:false` counts as a like, whether a refused like comes back with a count, which verb goes where, and whether every ask is bounded. Measured on HEAD, all of it was reachable only by reading the code.
- **The repair.** Fourteen new cases in the same file (6 → 20) ask them directly →. A like is POSTed to the likes door with the claim exactly as the browser built it — the publication in the body, the account, handle, assurance and instant beside it — and an absent handle, assurance or claimedAt is written as `null` rather than dropped, so the service can tell “empty” from “never asked” →. A refusal carries a reason and NO count: a 200 saying `ok:false` is still a refusal, and a count of zero there would show a reader a like the service never took →. The service error body carries no `ok` field (v313), so the reason is read from `message`, and with neither a reason nor a message the HTTP status is named →. A body that is not JSON is a refusal, not a crash →. Unreachable and merely-late are different sentences: a `TimeoutError` names the 15-second budget rather than calling a busy service gone →. Taking a like back is a DELETE naming the claimer and only the claimer — no handle, no assurance, no instant, and no body at all →. The POST names the publication in its body while the DELETE names it in its path, encoded →. The viewer read asks with the viewer when there is one and omits the parameter entirely when there is not, and it answers with no window, because it is the who-am-I read and not a page →. And every ask carries the service-call budget signal, so a silent service cannot hang a server-rendered page →.
- **Files:** apps/studio/src/lib/likeServer.test.ts (extended, 6 → 20 cases).
- **Measured (2026-10-24):** `npx vitest run --root apps/studio --no-file-parallelism src/lib/likeServer.test.ts` → **20/20**; `npx tsc --noEmit` (apps/studio) → exit 0.
- **Bounds (§60).** What the SERVICE does with the claim — recording it, verifying nothing (ADR 0018), what it answers — is the nexus-api suite’s subject; this file grades what the Studio sends and what it makes of the answer →. The lanes that call these functions keep their own cases; here the door is asked with an injected fetch and no lane in the way →. And the 15-second budget is `serviceCall.ts`’s constant, asserted here only as PRESENT, not as the right number →.

### Amendment 430 (v437, studio) — the COMMENTS DOOR’s write half, graded directly

- **The gap.** `readComments` had six direct cases (v399). The two writes and the other-side read — `writeComment`, `removeCommentOnService`, `readCommentsWritten` — were reached only through the lanes that call them, so what a comment carries on its way out and what an answer means on its way back were never asked. Two rules here have no counterpart in the likes door and are the reason this is its own increment: a take-back that found nothing is still a SUCCESS (the service answers 200 either way and says which), and the comment a write answers with is the first entry of the answer’s list rather than a field of its own. Measured on HEAD, both were reachable only by reading the code.
- **The repair.** Nineteen new cases in the same file (6 → 25) ask them directly →. The comment a write answers with is the FIRST entry of the answer’s list, and an ok answer carrying none leaves the field absent rather than inventing one →. A refusal carries a reason and no comment; the error body has no `ok` field, so the reason is read from `message` and then from the HTTP status →. A take-back is a DELETE naming the comment and the claimer and only those, with no body →. And the marquee rule: a take-back that found NOTHING is still a success — `removed: false` means “already gone”, not “your take-back failed”, the same rule the un-like keeps (v320) — while `removed` is read as the boolean the service said and not as truthiness →. The author’s own read asks by author and limit with NO window — the other side of the relation, not a page — and answers `visible: 0` when the service does not say, a divergence from `readComments` that leaves the field absent, pinned as measured →. Every refusal and every unreachable call names itself →.

### Amendment 436 (v443, studio) — the SUBSCRIPTION STANDING derivation, graded directly

- **The gap.** `subscriptionStandingOf` has been exercised since v274 only through `toSubscriptionRow`, which asks it once and shows the answer. Asked directly it states a rule no row can show: **the SERVICE’s word wins, and the client’s own computation is the fallback.** A wire that says `cancelled` while carrying `active: true` and a future `expiresAt` is a subscription the service has ended, and a client that recomputed the standing from the flags would show it as standing — answering a question about time with a clock that is not the service’s. Measured on HEAD, the precedence itself was reachable only by reading the code.
- **The repair.** Seven new cases in the same file (69 → 76) ask it directly →. The service’s word wins in both directions: a wire saying `cancelled` beside `active: true` and a future expiry reads `cancelled`, and a wire saying `active` beside `active: false` and a past expiry reads `active` →. A status this runtime does not know — including a wrong-case one — falls through to the client’s own computation →. That computation is pinned rule by rule: not active is cancelled whatever the expiry says; an expiry at or before now is expired, with the boundary INCLUSIVE, so the instant of expiry is already expired; and an expiry that is not a number means no expiry rather than an expired subscription →. Anything that is not a subscription object is cancelled, never active →. And the same wire read at two different nows answers about time and not about the wire →. `subscriptionStandingText` is pinned beside it: the three standings in the words the economy surface already uses, a cancelled one reading `Never` →.

- **Bounds (§60).** What the SERVICE decides a standing is — and whether it may say one thing while its flags say another — is the nexus-api suite’s subject; this file grades what the client makes of the wire it is handed →. Whether the client’s fallback computation should exist at all, or a wire with no status should be refused rather than computed, is a decision about the door’s contract →. And the inclusive expiry boundary is pinned as MEASURED: “expired at the instant of expiry” is the reading this code gives, and a reader who wants the last second covered is asking for a different rule →.

### Amendment 444 (v451, studio) — the ORBIT’s INPUT SCALES, graded directly

- **The gap.** The component (`Scene3D.tsx`) is the only consumer of `ORBIT_RADIANS_PER_PIXEL`, `ORBIT_ZOOM_PER_NOTCH`, `ORBIT_PAN_PER_PIXEL`, `ORBIT_PAN_PER_KEY` and `SCENE_DOCUMENT_DEFAULT_AT`, and it is not a file this suite can run — the suite runs in Node with no DOM and no pointer events. What CAN be asked directly is the scale each constant declares and the arithmetic the component performs with it, fed through the pure orbit functions the suite already believes in. Measured on HEAD, a control whose scale nobody had stated was a control that lied by omission: the five numbers were reachable only by reading the component.
- **The repair.** Five new cases in the same file (142 → 147) state the scales as countable facts →. A hundred dragged pixels is ONE radian, both axes sharing the one scale, so a diagonal drag turns the camera diagonally instead of skewing it →. A wheel notch is a TENTH of the distance the camera stands at — the zoom is multiplicative, so a notch near and a notch far move by different amounts and the same proportion, and the range still binds at the nearest wall →. One key press is worth TWENTY-FIVE dragged pixels — a tap and a drag that agree are one control, not two that happen to move the same target →. The pan box is FORTY-EIGHT key presses wide: the scale is stated against its own limit, and the number a person can count is the number the constants agree on →. And a scene frame lands at `SCENE_DOCUMENT_DEFAULT_AT` when the caller names no place, with a named place winning over the default — the default is a fallback, not a floor →.

- **Bounds (§60).** What the component does with a pointer event — the handlers, the listeners, the canvas the pixels arrive on — is the component’s subject, and this suite cannot run it; what is graded here is the SCALE the handlers apply, expressed as the pure arithmetic they hand to `applyOrbit` and `applyPan` →. Whether the scales are the RIGHT ones — whether a notch should be a tenth and a press twenty-five pixels — is a decision about feel, and this file records what they are now rather than arguing what they should be →. ### Amendment 446 (v453, studio) — the DOM DRIVER SEAM, graded directly

- **The gap.** `createDomDriver` was the one export of `uiRun.ts` no case named: the suite drives the runtime through a hand-written `FakeDriver`, so what the REAL driver does with a page was reachable only by reading it. A tree walker honours tag-QUALIFIED compound selectors, elements know their own tag and classes, and an input’s value accessor lives on the prototype the way a browser’s does — a canned answer per selector string would pass even if the driver asked for the wrong one, so the matcher is real →. `elements()` lists the `.btn` buttons and `.field` inputs and NOTHING else: a div wearing the class is not a button, and nesting and document order hold →. And `type()` writes through the NATIVE setter and fires a bubbling input event — an own-property shadow on the instance, the situation a framework leaves behind, does not block the write, which is the whole reason the trick exists →. The driver reads the document at CALL time, not at creation →.
